title: Suthida
text:
Suthida Bajrabhorn was born on June 24, 1978, in Nakhon Ratchasima Province, Thailand. Her father, Worapong Pongsuwan, was a career military officer, and her mother, Sudarat Na Ayutthaya, came from a family with roots in the nobility. Suthida received her primary and secondary education at Suranari Wittaya School, a prestigious all-girls school in Nakhon Ratchasima, graduating in 1996. She then enrolled at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok, the oldest and most respected university in Thailand. There, she studied Communication Arts, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 2000, achieving First Class Honours. 

Following her graduation, Suthida began her professional life in the private sector. From 2000 to 2001 she worked as a temporary clerk for the Royal Thai Air Force. In 2001, she joined Bangkok Bank, one of the largest banks in Southeast Asia, initially in a customer service role. She steadily climbed the corporate ladder, demonstrating a strong work ethic and aptitude for the financial sector. By 2003, she had transferred to the bank’s international banking division.  Over the next decade, she held various positions of increasing responsibility within Bangkok Bank, including positions in marketing and risk management. 

A significant turning point in Suthida’s career came in 2007 when she was selected to join the personal staff of Crown Prince Vajiralongkorn, then still the heir apparent.  She initially served as a hostess on the Crown Prince’s private aircraft.  Her duties rapidly expanded to encompass a wider range of responsibilities, including managing his personal affairs and acting as a liaison with various organizations.  By 2014, she had been formally appointed as a Deputy Commander of the Royal Security Command, a crucial role within the Royal Thai Armed Forces, holding the rank of General. This appointment was somewhat unusual given her civilian background, but highlighted the trust placed in her by the Crown Prince. 

During this period, Suthida's public profile remained relatively low.  However, she was frequently seen accompanying the Crown Prince on official engagements, both domestically and internationally. She participated in royal ceremonies and public functions, increasingly representing the monarchy alongside Vajiralongkorn. In December 2016, the Crown Prince officially recognised Suthida as his consort, a public acknowledgment of their relationship. 

Following the death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej on October 13, 2016, Crown Prince Vajiralongkorn ascended to the throne as King Maha Vajiralongkorn (Rama X).  On May 1, 2019, Suthida was officially proclaimed Queen of Thailand in a grand coronation ceremony held at the Grand Palace in Bangkok. The ceremony, replete with ancient rituals and symbolism, formally invested her with the title and regalia of Queen.  

As Queen, Suthida has actively participated in royal duties alongside King Vajiralongkorn, focusing on social welfare and the promotion of Thai culture. She has undertaken numerous visits to provinces across Thailand, engaging with local communities and supporting various charitable initiatives.  She often seen accompanying the King on military parades and inspections, reflecting her past connection to the armed forces.  Queen Suthida and King Vajiralongkorn have no children together. 

In December 2020, a significant controversy arose with the publication of leaked photographs and information regarding Queen Suthida’s early life and alleged time spent as a flight attendant, contradicting previously presented narratives. While the authenticity of the materials was debated, the incident sparked considerable discussion both within Thailand and internationally. Despite this, Queen Suthida continues to fulfill her duties as Queen, representing Thailand on the world stage and supporting her husband’s reign.

title: Radhika Apte
text:
Radhika Apte was born on September 7, 1985, in Pune, Maharashtra, India, to a Marathi-speaking family. Her father, Dr. Charudutt Apte, is a medical doctor, and her mother, Sumedha Apte, is a professor of Hindi literature. Radhika’s early education took place at Fergusson College in Pune, where she initially pursued a Bachelor of Arts degree. However, her passion lay in dance and acting, and she actively participated in extracurricular activities related to performing arts. Before fully committing to a career in acting, she briefly worked as a professional dancer, training in Kathak and Bharatnatyam for eight years. 

Radhika’s formal acting training began with a diploma from the Sathya Academy in Mumbai. She simultaneously continued her education, completing her Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics and Sociology from the University of Pune in 2005. Her initial foray into acting was through theatre, participating in several productions with the Mumbai-based theatre group, Aasakta Kala Manch. She performed in acclaimed plays like ‘Irawati’ and ‘That Birds Come Fluttering’, honing her skills and gaining early recognition.

Her screen debut arrived in 2005 with a small role in the Hindi film ‘Vaah! Life Ho Toh Aisi!’, directed by Mahesh Manjrekar. This was followed by a supporting role in the 2007 Bengali film ‘Antaheen’, directed by Aniruddha Roy Chowdhury, which garnered some critical attention. Radhika’s early career involved navigating a mix of Hindi, Bengali and Marathi cinema. She appeared in the 2009 film ‘Little Zizou’, a children's film, and the Marathi film ‘Siddha Loka’. 

A significant turning point came in 2013 with the release of ‘Badhaai Do’, where she played a supporting role. However, it was her performance in the critically acclaimed independent film ‘Lalilu’ (2013), directed by Kiran Rao’s husband, that truly began to establish her as a serious actress. She gained wider recognition with her role in ‘Hunterrr’ (2015), a controversial but commercially successful film. 

The year 2016 proved to be a breakthrough year for Radhika. She starred in three prominent films: ‘Manjhi – The Mountain Man’, directed by Ketan Mehta, ‘Phobia’, a psychological thriller directed by Pawan Kripalani, and ‘Kabali’, a Tamil action film starring Rajinikanth. ‘Kabali’ in particular exposed her to a pan-Indian audience.  

Radhika's versatility became increasingly apparent with her subsequent projects. She starred in ‘The Wedding Guest’ (2018), a British-Indian romantic drama directed by Jim Sarbh, and ‘Bazaar’ (2018), a crime thriller.  Her digital work further solidified her reputation. She became a prominent face on Netflix with roles in the anthology series ‘Lust Stories’ (2018), directed by four different directors including Karan Johar and Zoya Akhtar, and the crime drama series ‘Sacred Games’ (2018-2019), where she played the complex character of RAW agent Anjali Mathur.  She followed this with the Netflix film ‘Raat Akeli Hai’ (2020), receiving critical praise for her performance.

Throughout her career, Radhika has received numerous awards and nominations. She won the Filmfare OTT Award for Best Actress in 2020 for her work in ‘Raat Akeli Hai’. She has also been nominated for several Filmfare Awards and Screen Awards. 

In 2019, Radhika Apte married Benedict Taylor, a British musician and composer. The couple resides in London. She continues to actively work in both film and digital platforms, balancing projects across different languages and genres.  She is known for her strong and independent roles, often challenging conventional portrayals of women in Indian cinema. As of late 2023, she is involved in several upcoming projects, continuing to demonstrate her commitment to impactful and diverse storytelling.

title: Iggy Azalea
text:
Amethyst Amelia Kelly, known professionally as Iggy Azalea, was born on June 7, 1990, in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. Her upbringing was unconventional. Her father, Brendan Kelly, was a painter and sculptor, while her mother, Tania, raised her largely alone in Mullumbimby, a small town in northern New South Wales. Azalea described her childhood as transient, moving frequently and experiencing a somewhat isolated existence. She didn’t attend traditional high school, instead completing her education via distance education, allowing her more time to focus on her burgeoning interest in music. Her early influences were heavily rooted in American hip-hop and pop culture, particularly artists like Tupac Shakur, Missy Elliott, and Salt-N-Pepa, despite growing up in a largely Australian environment. She began writing rap lyrics as a teenager, inspired by the lyrical complexity and storytelling she admired in American artists.

Azalea started sharing her music online around 2006, uploading songs and music videos to platforms like Myspace and YouTube. This self-promotion caught the attention of American producer Hype Williams, who featured her in a 2010 music video for his artist Travis McCoy. This marked her first significant exposure to a wider audience. Shortly after, in 2010, she relocated to the United States, initially living in Miami before settling in Los Angeles to pursue her music career more aggressively. 

Her initial American releases included the mixtapes *Ignoramus* (2011) and *TrapGold* (2012). *TrapGold* was particularly successful, generating buzz within the hip-hop community and attracting the attention of T.I., the Atlanta-based rapper and record executive. In 2013, Azalea signed with T.I.’s Grand Hustle imprint, alongside Atlantic Records. This partnership proved pivotal.

Her breakthrough came with the release of her debut studio album, *The New Classic*, on October 22, 2013. The album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 chart, selling 135,000 copies in its first week. It was the first female rapper to achieve this since Nicki Minaj in 2010. The album spawned the hit singles "Work," featuring A$AP Rocky, which peaked at number 63 on the Billboard Hot 100, and "Fancy," featuring Charli XCX, which became her signature song. "Fancy" topped the Billboard Hot 100 for seven weeks in 2014, making Azalea the first woman to reach the top of the chart as a solo artist since Lauryn Hill in 1998. *The New Classic* was eventually certified platinum by the RIAA.

Following the success of her debut, Azalea released her second studio album, *Digital Distortion*, in January 2016. While it debuted at number four on the Billboard 200, it didn’t achieve the same level of commercial success as *The New Classic*, despite singles like “Team” and “Beg For It.” The album's release was also delayed multiple times due to leaks and artist dissatisfaction.

In the years following *Digital Distortion*, Azalea faced criticism regarding cultural appropriation and her lyrical content. She also experienced personal challenges, including a highly publicized breakup with basketball player Nick Young in 2016.  She continued to release music, including the EP *Wicked Lips* in 2019, and the album *In My Defense* in 2019, which reached number 7 on the Billboard 200. 

In 2022, she released the album *The End of an Era*, marking what she described as the conclusion of her album-making era. She has since focused on singles and exploring different creative avenues, including a foray into reality television as a judge on the Australian singing competition *The X Factor Australia* in 2023.  Azalea and boyfriend Playboi Carti welcomed a son, Onyx Kelly, in April 2020. As of late 2023, she continues to tour and release music, maintaining a dedicated fanbase despite navigating a complex and often controversial career. Her net worth is estimated to be around $60 million as of 2023.

title: Jan Zamoyski
text:
Jan Zamoyski was born on February 27, 1509, in Zamość, Poland, into a prominent noble family, the Zamoyscy. His father, Florian Zamoyski, served as a courtier to King Sigismund I the Old, and his mother, Anna Modrzewska, came from another influential family. This lineage provided Jan with a strong foundation for a life of political and military prominence in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. He received a humanist education, initially privately, then studying at the Kraków Academy (later Jagiellonian University) from 1522 to 1528, and subsequently at the Universities of Padua and Bologna between 1529 and 1531. These studies focused on law, political science, and military strategy, shaping his intellectual and practical preparation for a future leadership role.

Zamoyski’s public career began in 1548 with his appointment as the Starost (governor) of Zawichost. This was followed by a series of increasingly important offices. He became a member of the Polish Sejm (parliament) in 1558, representing the Lublin Land. His growing reputation for intelligence and diplomatic skill led to his appointment as a diplomat to the Holy Roman Empire in 1560, and later to negotiate with Tsar Ivan IV of Russia in 1566-1567, during a period of rising tensions. These diplomatic missions demonstrated his ability to navigate complex international relations.

A crucial moment in Zamoyski’s career came with the Union of Lublin in 1569. He played a key role in facilitating the political union of the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, creating the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. He skillfully navigated the differing interests of the Polish nobility and Lithuanian magnates, advocating for a strong, unified state. This achievement solidified his position as one of the most important political figures in the Commonwealth. 

Following the death of King Sigismund II Augustus in 1572, a period of interregnum ensued. Zamoyski emerged as a leading candidate for the throne, but ultimately declined to run, instead supporting the candidacy of Henry of Valois, a French prince. In 1573, Henry was elected King of Poland and, recognizing Zamoyski’s abilities, appointed him as his Great Crown Hetman (commander-in-chief of the Polish army) in 1575 and later as the Chancellor of the Crown in 1576. 

As Hetman, Zamoyski led Polish forces in numerous campaigns, defending the Commonwealth against its neighbours. He achieved a significant victory against Muscovy in the Battle of Ułła in 1581, halting a Russian invasion, and followed this with successes in Livonia against Ivan the Terrible’s forces. He skillfully utilized a combined arms approach, integrating light cavalry (hussars) with infantry and artillery, and implemented innovative military reforms. He also successfully defended the Commonwealth against the Habsburgs during the War of the Polish Succession (1587-1588), resolving a dispute over the succession to the throne.  

Alongside his military and political duties, Zamoyski was a significant patron of the arts and sciences. He founded the Zamoyska Academy in 1594, one of the first institutions of higher learning in Poland open to students of all social classes. He envisioned it as a centre for humanist education and civic virtue. He also initiated the construction of the city of Zamość, designed as a Renaissance ideal city, which became a thriving economic and cultural centre, and earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 2023. 

Throughout his later life, Zamoyski remained a powerful figure in the Commonwealth, often acting as a counterweight to the influence of the Vasa dynasty after Sigismund III Vasa ascended to the throne in 1587. He increasingly found himself in opposition to the king's pro-Catholic policies and his attempts to centralize power, fearing it would erode the liberties of the nobility. He died on August 7, 1605, in Zamość, at the age of 96.  He left behind a legacy as a skilled diplomat, successful military commander, astute politician, and a champion of Polish culture and education, remembered as one of the most influential figures in the history of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo
text:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo was born on January 8, 1946, in Culiacán, Sinaloa, Mexico. His father, Miguel Ángel Félix Niebla, was a former rural police officer and his mother, María de Jesús Gallardo, came from a family with a history in politics and land ownership. This background provided a degree of social standing, though not immense wealth, within the emerging drug trafficking landscape of Sinaloa. Félix Gallardo’s early life was relatively unremarkable; he attended private schools and later studied accounting at the Autonomous University of Guadalajara, though he did not complete his degree. 

His initial forays into criminal activity began in the early 1970s, initially working as a security guard for various drug traffickers, including Héctor Luis “El Güero” Palma Salazar and Rafael Caro Quintero. This role allowed him to observe the logistical challenges and fragmentation of the nascent Mexican drug trade. At the time, several independent trafficking groups operated in Mexico, primarily focused on cultivating marijuana and opium poppy, and smuggling these substances into the United States. Félix Gallardo quickly identified an opportunity to consolidate these groups under a single, more efficient organization. 

By 1975, Félix Gallardo, along with Palma and Caro Quintero, had established their own trafficking operation, initially focused on marijuana cultivation and distribution. They acquired large tracts of land in the “Golden Triangle” region of Sinaloa, Durango, and Chihuahua – an area ideal for marijuana growing due to its remote location and favorable climate. Over the next decade, they expanded their operations, moving into the cocaine trade, initially transporting it from Colombia through Mexico to the United States. This required establishing connections with Colombian cartels, most notably the Medellín Cartel led by Pablo Escobar. 

Félix Gallardo’s key achievement was the creation of the first major Mexican drug cartel, often referred to as the Guadalajara Cartel, in the 1980s. He didn't build it through brute force alone; he was a master negotiator and organizer. Instead of direct control, he implemented a system of alliances, essentially franchising the drug trade. He divided Mexico into plazas – territories – and assigned them to different lieutenants, including the Arellano Félix brothers (who would later form the Tijuana Cartel), Amado Carrillo Fuentes (Juárez Cartel), and Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán (Sinaloa Cartel). This decentralized structure allowed for greater efficiency and reduced risk, but also sowed the seeds of future conflicts. By 1987, the Guadalajara Cartel controlled a significant portion of the drug trade between Mexico and the United States, generating an estimated $5 billion annually.

The cartel’s activities attracted increasing attention from both Mexican and U.S. law enforcement.  In 1985, the kidnapping and murder of U.S. DEA agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena, orchestrated by Félix Gallardo in retaliation for DEA interference, triggered a massive investigation.  Camarena had been investigating the Guadalajara Cartel’s marijuana operations and had identified the large-scale cultivation sites in the Golden Triangle.  The fallout from Camarena’s murder led to a crackdown on the Guadalajara Cartel and its leaders.

Félix Gallardo was arrested on April 5, 1989, in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, following a massive government operation. He was convicted of drug trafficking, homicide, and conspiracy to commit crimes, and sentenced to 40 years in prison.  Despite his imprisonment, he continued to exert influence over the drug trade for years, communicating with associates and directing operations from behind bars.  

Over time, his power waned as the plazas he had created became independent cartels, often warring with each other. He was eventually transferred to a maximum-security prison in Puente Grande, Jalisco, and later to a federal medical center.  In August 2022, at the age of 76, he was granted house arrest due to his deteriorating health. He remains under house arrest as of late 2023, his legacy as the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking firmly cemented in history. He has five children from two marriages, and his son, Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo Jr., is also involved in the drug trade.

title: Fernando da Costa Novaes
text:
Fernando da Costa Novaes was born on November 12, 1909, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, into a family with a strong tradition of legal scholarship. His father, Eduardo da Costa Novaes, was a prominent jurist and professor of law at the Faculty of Law of the University of Brazil (later the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro). This upbringing profoundly influenced Fernando, instilling in him a deep respect for legal principles and a commitment to intellectual pursuit. He received his primary and secondary education in Rio de Janeiro, attending the prestigious Colégio São Bento, a Jesuit school, where he excelled academically. 

He entered the Faculty of Law of the University of Brazil in 1927, graduating in 1931 with honors. Immediately following graduation, he embarked on a career dedicated to both academic research and public service. Unlike many of his contemporaries, he didn’t initially pursue a direct path into politics, instead choosing to focus on building a solid foundation in legal theory and practice. In 1932, he began working as a public prosecutor in the state of Guanabara (which later became part of Rio de Janeiro), a position he held for several years, gaining practical experience in the Brazilian legal system. 

However, his true calling lay in academia. In 1934, he started teaching Roman Law at his alma mater, the Faculty of Law of the University of Brazil. This marked the beginning of a long and distinguished academic career spanning over five decades. He progressively ascended through the ranks, becoming a full professor in 1948. His lectures were renowned for their clarity, rigor, and emphasis on the historical context of legal concepts. He wasn’t simply reciting the law but exploring its origins and evolution.

Da Costa Novaes’s scholarly contributions were substantial. He authored numerous influential books and articles, primarily focused on Roman Law, legal history, and the philosophy of law. His magnum opus, “Curso de Direito Romano” (Course of Roman Law), published in 1955, became a standard textbook for generations of law students throughout Brazil. It was meticulously researched, offering a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of Roman legal principles. He also published “Introdução ao Direito” (Introduction to Law) in 1962, a work that laid out his philosophical approach to the study of law, emphasizing its social and ethical dimensions. Beyond these significant books, he consistently contributed articles to leading Brazilian law journals like the “Revista da Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de São Paulo”.

His commitment to legal scholarship wasn’t confined to Brazil. He spent several periods as a visiting professor at universities abroad, including the University of Coimbra in Portugal (1961-1962) and the University of Paris-Sorbonne in France (1967-1968). These experiences broadened his perspectives and allowed him to engage with international legal scholarship. He was a member of several international legal organizations, including the International Association of Legal History, and actively participated in conferences and symposia.

During the 1964-1985 military dictatorship in Brazil, Da Costa Novaes, while not openly dissident, maintained a commitment to academic freedom and intellectual integrity. He cautiously navigated the politically charged environment, continuing to teach and write, but avoiding direct involvement in political controversies. This period necessitated a degree of circumspection, but he refused to compromise his scholarly principles.

Fernando da Costa Novaes retired from his professorship at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro in 1979, but remained active in scholarly pursuits, continuing to write and mentor young lawyers and academics. He was honored with numerous awards and distinctions throughout his career, including the Order of the Southern Cross, a high honor conferred by the Brazilian government. He died on July 3, 1990, in Rio de Janeiro, at the age of 80, leaving behind a lasting legacy as one of Brazil’s most influential legal scholars of the 20th century. His work continues to be studied and cited by legal professionals and academics in Brazil and beyond.

title: David Galloway (writer)
text:
David Galloway was born on December 12, 1941, in Edinburgh, Scotland, the only child of James Galloway, a solicitor, and Margaret (née Kerr) Galloway, a teacher. He spent his early years in the Morningside area of the city, attending George Watson’s College, a prestigious independent school, from 1947 to 1959. He was a notably bright student, excelling in English and history, and displayed an early aptitude for writing, contributing to the school magazine. However, he was also known for a rebellious streak and a dislike of formal authority, characteristics that would subtly inform his later work. 

After completing his secondary education, Galloway initially pursued a degree in law at the University of Edinburgh, beginning in 1959. He found the subject uninspiring and dropped out after a year, opting instead to travel and work various odd jobs. This period saw him living in France, Spain, and North Africa, experiences that broadened his worldview and provided material for his future writing. He worked as a language teacher, a barman, and even a fruit picker, immersing himself in different cultures and observing the lives of ordinary people. 

Galloway’s career as a writer began in the mid-1960s. He initially wrote short stories, some of which were published in literary magazines like *The London Magazine* and *New Scottish Writing*. His breakthrough came in 1967 with the publication of his first novel, *The Cruel Embrace*, a stark and unflinching depiction of working-class life in post-war Edinburgh. The novel, praised for its gritty realism and innovative narrative style, immediately established Galloway as a significant new voice in Scottish literature.

He followed *The Cruel Embrace* with *A Spot of Teething* in 1969, which further cemented his reputation. This novel explored themes of alienation and social decay, again set against the backdrop of Edinburgh. Galloway’s writing often focused on the darker aspects of Scottish society, challenging traditional narratives and exposing the hypocrisy he perceived within the establishment. He avoided romanticising the past and instead presented a brutally honest portrayal of contemporary life. 

Throughout the 1970s, Galloway continued to publish novels, including *Eventually* (1972), *The Half-Life* (1975) and *Necessary Lies* (1979). He also wrote several radio plays for the BBC, showcasing his versatility as a writer.  His work during this period often engaged with political and social issues, reflecting his left-leaning political views. While critically acclaimed, his novels didn’t achieve widespread commercial success, and he frequently struggled financially. 

The 1980s saw a shift in Galloway’s writing. He began to explore more experimental forms, and his novels became increasingly introspective and philosophical. *The Yellow House* (1982) and *The Sandpiper* (1988) demonstrated a greater emphasis on psychological realism and character development. He also began teaching creative writing at various universities and colleges, including the University of Stirling, where he held a lectureship for several years.

In 1993, Galloway published *The Pickpocket’s Tale*, a historical novel set in 18th-century Edinburgh, which garnered significant praise and was shortlisted for the Saltire Society Scottish Book of the Year Award. This marked a return to a more accessible style and broadened his readership. His final novel, *Maybe This Time*, appeared in 2006.

David Galloway largely withdrew from public life in the late 1990s and early 2000s. He suffered from declining health in his later years, struggling with diabetes and depression. He continued to write sporadically, but much of his later work remained unpublished. He died on February 21, 2014, at the age of 72, in Edinburgh. While not a household name, David Galloway is remembered as a fiercely independent and uncompromising writer who made a significant contribution to Scottish literature, particularly for his unflinching portrayal of the complexities of Scottish society. His novels remain important works of social realism and continue to be studied and appreciated by scholars and readers alike.

title: John Atkinson Grimshaw
text:
John Atkinson Grimshaw, born on 6 September 1836 in Leeds, Yorkshire, was a prominent Victorian-era landscape and townscape painter. He was the son of John Grimshaw, a decorative iron foundry owner, and Mary Atkinson. His early life was steeped in the industrial environment of Leeds, a rapidly growing textile centre. This exposure profoundly influenced his artistic subject matter throughout his career. He didn’t receive formal artistic training in the conventional sense. Instead, his initial education focused on the family business, and he worked within the ironworks for several years, gaining a practical understanding of engineering and industrial processes. However, from a young age, he demonstrated a strong aptitude for drawing, largely self-taught, initially sketching designs for the ironwork.

Around 1859, Grimshaw began to seriously pursue painting, initially working in watercolour and later transitioning to oil paints. He was particularly drawn to the atmospheric effects of light and weather, a characteristic feature of his mature work. He initially focused on local scenes around Leeds, depicting the canals, railways, and burgeoning industrial landscapes that defined the region. He quickly developed a distinctive style, favouring a dark palette and dramatic use of light, often painting nocturnes – scenes lit by moonlight or artificial light – which became a hallmark of his oeuvre. 

By 1861, Grimshaw was exhibiting his work at the Leeds Fine Arts Exhibition, and in 1862, he began exhibiting at the Royal Academy in London, a significant milestone in his career. This marked the start of a steady rise in recognition, though initial critical responses were often mixed, with some dismissing his work as merely illustrative rather than high art. However, his paintings gained popularity with the public, and he built a substantial following, particularly among those who appreciated his realistic depictions of the changing industrial landscape. 

In 1866, Grimshaw moved to Kensington, London, establishing a studio there and further cementing his position within the art world. He continued to exhibit regularly at the Royal Academy, the British Institution, and other prominent galleries. He also travelled extensively, painting scenes in Scotland, the Netherlands, Belgium, and even briefly in the United States in 1881, capturing the ports and cities he visited. His Scottish paintings, particularly those of Glasgow and Edinburgh, are considered among his finest works, showcasing his mastery of atmospheric perspective and dramatic lighting. 

Grimshaw was a highly prolific artist, producing an estimated 700 to 800 paintings during his career. While he never achieved the same level of critical acclaim as some of his contemporaries, such as J.M.W. Turner, he was commercially successful, catering to a growing middle-class market eager for depictions of modern life. He was also a shrewd businessman, actively promoting his work and cultivating relationships with patrons. He registered a patent in 1864 for a new type of varnish, aiming to enhance the luminosity and durability of his paintings. 

Despite his success, Grimshaw’s later life was marked by financial difficulties. A series of unsuccessful investments, including a venture into shipping, led to mounting debts. In 1893, he was declared bankrupt, a deeply distressing event for the artist. He continued to paint, but the financial strain and the loss of his reputation took a toll. He moved to various addresses in London and increasingly relied on selling works directly to dealers and collectors. 

John Atkinson Grimshaw died on 9 October 1893 in London, at the age of 57. He was buried at All Saints Church in Putney Vale.  While largely overlooked for decades after his death, his work experienced a significant revival of interest in the latter half of the 20th century, fuelled by a renewed appreciation for Victorian realism and the industrial heritage he so vividly portrayed. Today, his paintings are held in numerous public and private collections, and he is recognised as a significant and influential figure in Victorian landscape painting.

title: Mihai Eminescu
text:
Mihai Eminescu, Romania's national poet, was born Mihail Eminovici on January 15, 1850, in Botoșani, Moldavia (present-day Romania). He was the seventh of eleven children born to Gheorghe Eminovici, a boyar (nobleman) and landowner, and Raluca Isărescu. His early childhood was spent largely on his family's estate, particularly at Ipotești, a property inherited from his mother. This rural environment profoundly influenced his later poetry, imbuing it with a strong sense of nature and a nostalgic longing for a lost past. 

Formal education began somewhat erratically. He attended primary school in Cernăuți (Czernowitz, now Chernivtsi, Ukraine) starting in 1858, but was frequently absent. He completed three grades before his father decided to continue his education privately. Between 1860 and 1865, he studied at the gymnasium in Cernăuți, demonstrating a particular aptitude for German and a broad intellectual curiosity. During this time, he began to write poetry, initially influenced by Romantic German authors like Goethe and Schiller. He also engaged with the burgeoning Romanian literary scene, contributing poems to local journals under various pseudonyms, including M. Eminescu. 

In 1866, he moved to Vienna, Austria, enrolling at the University of Vienna. He primarily pursued studies in philosophy, law, and political science, though he never obtained a degree.  Vienna proved a crucial period for his intellectual development. He came into contact with radical student circles and immersed himself in the city’s vibrant cultural life. He worked as a copyist, supporting himself while continuing to write and contribute to the journal *Familia* in Pest (Budapest). 

Returning to Moldavia in 1869, Eminescu briefly worked as a teacher in Blaj, but quickly abandoned the post. He found employment as a secretary to the metropolitan bishop, Isaia of Moldavia, in Iași. This position provided him with relative stability and access to a wider intellectual community. It was during his time in Iași that he became deeply involved with the *Junimea* literary society, founded in 1867.  *Junimea*, meaning “the youth,” advocated for a return to Romanian cultural roots and promoted a more rigorous and critical approach to literature.  

Eminescu became a leading figure within *Junimea*, serving as its secretary from 1871 to 1874 and frequently presenting papers on literary and cultural topics. He began publishing some of his most famous poems, including “Evening Star” (“Luceafărul”, 1873), "Doina," and “O, Sweet Remembrances” (“O, rămâi”). His poetry, characterized by lyrical beauty, philosophical depth, and a masterful use of Romanian folklore, quickly gained recognition. In 1874, he became the editor of the conservative newspaper *Timpul* in Bucharest, a position he held, with some interruptions, until 1883.  His articles often attacked the liberal government and advocated for national unity and traditional values.

The latter part of his life was marked by increasing mental instability.  Symptoms, likely indicative of bipolar disorder or another neurological condition, began appearing around 1883. He experienced periods of intense creativity followed by severe depression and erratic behavior.  He left *Timpul* in 1883 and travelled extensively, attempting to find relief. In 1886, his condition deteriorated significantly, and he was institutionalized in a psychiatric hospital in Bucharest.  

He spent the last three years of his life in hospitals, largely forgotten by the public.  He died on June 15, 1889, at the age of 39, in Bucharest.  His funeral was a modest affair, attended by only a small group of friends and admirers.  However, his posthumous reputation grew rapidly.  By the early 20th century, Eminescu was recognized as the national poet of Romania, his works becoming central to Romanian identity and culture.  His complete works were first published in 1898, solidifying his legacy as a literary giant.

title: Maja Jager
text:
Maja Jager, born Maria Johanna Jager on December 21, 1938, in Cologne, Germany, was a pioneering computer scientist whose work significantly advanced the field of compiler construction and program optimization. Her early life was deeply impacted by the devastation of World War II. Her father, Wilhelm Jager, was a professor of electrical engineering at the University of Cologne, and her mother, Elisabeth Jager (née Lueders), was a mathematics teacher. The university was heavily damaged during the war, and the family faced considerable hardship in the postwar years. This environment instilled in Maja a pragmatic and resourceful approach to problem-solving, qualities that would define her academic career.

She began her formal education in Cologne, attending the Mädchengymnasium (girls’ grammar school) until 1957. Following her Abitur (high school diploma), she enrolled at the University of Cologne, initially studying mathematics and physics. However, she quickly gravitated towards the nascent field of computer science, recognizing its potential. She completed her Diplom (Master's degree equivalent) in mathematics in 1962, focusing on numerical mathematics.  Her thesis, supervised by Professor Heinrich Soeffing, explored methods for solving systems of linear equations.

In 1963, Jager moved to the United States to pursue doctoral studies at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). She joined the Computation Structures Group, led by Professor Harold Stone, a key figure in compiler design. She earned her PhD in Computer Science in 1967 with a dissertation titled “Optimization of Object Code.” This work laid the foundation for much of her subsequent research and established her as a leading figure in the optimization of machine code. 

Her PhD research focused on techniques for improving the efficiency of code generated by compilers. At the time, compilers were often seen as a bottleneck in the performance of computer programs. Jager developed innovative methods to reduce code size and execution time, specifically targeting the IBM System/360 architecture. Her work involved analyzing the structure of object code and applying transformations to eliminate redundancies and improve instruction scheduling. 

Following her PhD, Jager accepted a position at the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC) in 1967, becoming one of the first women appointed to the faculty in the Computer Science department. She remained at UCSC for her entire career, achieving the rank of Professor Emerita. At UCSC, she continued to refine and expand her work on compiler optimization, becoming particularly renowned for her research on global code optimization, register allocation, and instruction selection. 

A significant achievement was her development of the “Liveness Analysis” algorithm, a fundamental technique used in compiler optimization to determine which variables are in use at any given point in a program. This algorithm, published in a series of influential papers throughout the 1970s and 80s, became a cornerstone of modern compiler technology and is still widely used today.  She collaborated extensively with other researchers, including Ronald Cytron, on extending and applying liveness analysis.

Throughout the 1980s and 90s, Jager's research shifted towards parallel processing and software pipelining, techniques aimed at exploiting the potential of multi-processor systems. She explored how to optimize code for execution on parallel architectures, addressing challenges related to data dependencies and communication overhead.  She also contributed to the development of tools and methodologies for analyzing the performance of parallel programs.

Maja Jager was a dedicated educator, mentoring numerous graduate students who went on to successful careers in academia and industry. She was known for her rigorous standards and her commitment to fostering independent thinking. She was a member of the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and served on the editorial boards of several leading computer science journals. 

Maja Jager passed away on October 27, 2023, in Santa Cruz, California, at the age of 84. Her contributions to compiler optimization remain profoundly influential, and her work continues to shape the way computers execute software today. She never married and had no children, dedicating her life to her academic pursuits and leaving a lasting legacy in the field of computer science.

title: Cheyenne Brando
text:
Cheyenne Elizabeth Brando, born March 19, 1965, in Los Angeles, California, was the only biological child of actor Marlon Brando and his third wife, Tarita Teriipaia, a Tahitian actress he met while filming *Mutiny on the Bounty* in 1965. Her name, Cheyenne, was chosen by her father in reference to the Native American tribe, reflecting his lifelong interest in indigenous cultures and a desire to distance his child from the perceived superficiality of Hollywood.  She was raised largely away from the spotlight, initially on Marlon Brando’s private atoll, Tetiaroa, in French Polynesia. This secluded upbringing, lasting until around age nine, involved a largely informal education focused on Polynesian culture and languages, alongside tutoring in English. 

In 1974, the family relocated to a 5-acre estate in Beverly Hills, California. Cheyenne’s childhood was marked by a complex relationship with her notoriously private and often emotionally unavailable father. While he provided for her materially, her upbringing was often overseen by a rotating cast of nannies and household staff.  She attended various private schools, including the Harvard-Westlake School in Los Angeles, but struggled academically and socially, reportedly feeling isolated and different from her peers. 

Her introduction to acting came relatively late.  She took some acting classes in her teens, but her initial focus wasn’t a professional career. However, in 1989, at the age of 24, she landed the role of Lisa Rowan in the television series *The Young Riders*, a Western aimed at a younger audience, which aired on ABC.  She appeared in 32 episodes between 1989 and 1992, gaining some moderate recognition.  This was her most significant acting role and provided a relatively stable period in her life. 

Following *The Young Riders*, Cheyenne secured a few smaller film and television roles, including appearances in *Don King: Only in America* (1997) and a guest spot on *ER* in 1998.  However, her career never reached the heights of her father’s, and she often expressed frustration with the limited opportunities available to her, feeling she was constantly judged based on her parentage rather than her talent.  She made several attempts to establish herself as a serious actress, but struggled to break free from the "Brando's daughter" label.

Her personal life became increasingly turbulent in the late 1990s. In 1990, she married Benjamin “Ben” Mayes, a carpenter, but they divorced in 1996.  The couple had one son, Tuki Brando, born in 1990.  Following the divorce, Cheyenne’s struggles with depression and substance abuse became more pronounced.  

Tragically, on January 16, 2005, Cheyenne Brando died at UCLA Medical Center in Los Angeles, at the age of 39. The official cause of death was determined to be pulmonary embolism, a blockage in one of the pulmonary arteries. However, contributing factors included her history of depression and a previously undisclosed congenital lung defect. She had been hospitalized for several days prior to her death, experiencing respiratory problems.  At the time of her death, she was engaged to Robert “Bobby” Hofer.

The circumstances surrounding her death were further complicated by the subsequent legal battle involving her son, Tuki, and her estate.  Her will left the majority of her estate to her fiancé, Robert Hofer, a decision contested by Marlon Brando, who feared Hofer was exploiting his granddaughter. A lengthy and public court case ensued, with accusations of Hofer’s controlling behavior and alleged financial mismanagement. Marlon Brando eventually won a temporary guardianship over Tuki, ensuring his financial security and well-being.  Cheyenne Brando’s life, though marked by a famous lineage, was ultimately overshadowed by personal struggles and a relatively unfulfilled potential.

title: Richie Dorman
text:
Richard “Richie” Dorman was born on February 26, 1958, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, to parents Robert and Shirley Dorman. His early life was marked by a keen interest in mathematics and a precocious talent for mental calculation. Growing up in a modest household, Dorman’s abilities were noticed by teachers who encouraged his development, though his skill remained largely outside of formal training. He didn’t attend specialized schools or receive dedicated coaching; his abilities were self-taught through practice and an inherent understanding of numerical patterns. He excelled in high school at Milwaukee Vincent High School, graduating in 1976.

Dorman’s professional life began not as a performer, but in practical trades. He worked for several years as a carpenter and contractor, operating his own business, Dorman Construction, from 1980 to 1992. This period was characterized by consistent, if unremarkable, work, while he continued to privately hone his mental calculation skills. His public emergence as a “human calculator” was quite accidental. In 1992, while attending a Milwaukee Brewers baseball game with friends, he spontaneously offered to calculate the square root of any number shouted by strangers. His speed and accuracy quickly attracted attention, and a local radio station, WTMJ, invited him to demonstrate his skills on air. 

This radio appearance led to further local television spots and eventually a national audience when he appeared on *The Sally Jessy Raphael Show* in 1993. The positive response prompted a more focused pursuit of performance opportunities. Dorman’s act wasn’t simply about speed; he could perform complex calculations – square roots, cube roots, exponents, logarithms, trigonometric functions – entirely in his head, often providing answers in seconds that would take calculators minutes. He didn't rely on mnemonic techniques or pre-programmed formulas, instead citing an innate ability to visualize numbers and manipulate them mentally.

His breakthrough moment came in 1998 when he was featured on *Dateline NBC* in a segment titled “Human Calculator.” This broadcast dramatically increased his profile and led to appearances on numerous other television shows, including *The Oprah Winfrey Show* (1999), *Ripley’s Believe It or Not!* (multiple appearances starting in 2000), and *The Ellen DeGeneres Show* (2003). He became a frequent guest on game shows, notably appearing on *Montel Williams’s Montel* and *The National Geographic Challenge*. 

Dorman’s abilities were tested by mathematicians and scientists, who confirmed his extraordinary skill, though the neurological basis of his talent remained largely unexplained. He never claimed to have a photographic memory, and actively resisted descriptions of his talent as a “gift” preferring to characterize it as a skill developed through consistent practice. He performed live demonstrations for large audiences, often engaging the crowd by asking for challenging calculations. He toured extensively, performing at corporate events, schools, and theaters across the United States and internationally, including a tour of Japan in 2002. 

Beyond performing, Dorman authored a book, *Beyond Calculation: The Complete Guide to Mental Arithmetic*, published in 2006, aiming to teach others techniques to improve their own mental math abilities, though he emphasized that replicating his level of skill was unlikely without a similar innate aptitude. He also created a series of instructional DVDs. 

In the late 2000s, Dorman began to reduce his public appearances, citing a desire for a more private life. He continued to occasionally perform at smaller events and maintained a website offering resources on mental arithmetic. He quietly returned to carpentry work, preferring the tangible nature of the craft to the spectacle of performance. Richard Dorman passed away on December 26, 2013, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, at the age of 55, after a battle with a short illness. He left behind his wife, Lisa, and two children. His legacy remains as a remarkable example of human cognitive ability, a man who could perform feats of mental calculation that continue to fascinate and baffle.

title: Braulio Lara
text:
Braulio Alonso Lara Ñiquen was born on February 23, 1923, in Puno, Peru, a city nestled high in the Andes near Lake Titicaca. His parents were both educators; his father, Braulio Lara Velásquez, was a schoolteacher and his mother, Carmen Ñiquen de Lara, also dedicated her life to education. This familial emphasis on learning significantly shaped his early life. He received his primary and secondary education in Puno, demonstrating a particular aptitude for mathematics and science. In 1942, he entered the National University of San Marcos in Lima, Peru, to study civil engineering. 

Lara’s university career was interrupted in 1945 when he joined the Peruvian Air Force, motivated by a desire to serve his country and a fascination with aviation. He trained as a pilot and specialized in aerial photography and surveying, skills that would prove invaluable in his later career. He graduated as a pilot officer in 1947, but continued his engineering studies concurrently, eventually earning his degree in civil engineering from San Marcos in 1951. He remained in the Air Force, rising through the ranks and gaining extensive experience in mapping and infrastructure projects, particularly in remote and challenging terrain.

In 1963, Lara transitioned from the Air Force to the Ministry of Public Works, beginning his full-time career in large-scale infrastructure development. He quickly gained recognition for his meticulous planning, efficient execution, and dedication to incorporating sustainable practices. His early projects focused on improving road networks in the Andean region, a critical need for connecting isolated communities. 

Lara’s most significant and internationally renowned achievement was the construction of the Carretera Marginal de la Selva, often referred to simply as the Marginal Highway. This ambitious project, initiated in 1965 and largely completed by 1978, involved building a 300-kilometer (approximately 186 miles) highway through the dense, humid rainforests of eastern Peru, linking several previously inaccessible towns and villages. The highway traversed incredibly difficult terrain, requiring innovative engineering solutions to overcome landslides, river crossings, and the challenging climate. Lara served as the project’s chief engineer and director, overseeing the entire operation. He prioritized employing local labor, providing employment and skills training to the communities along the route.  The project involved the construction of over 200 bridges and required the relocation of entire settlements in some cases, all handled with sensitivity and a commitment to minimizing disruption.

The Carretera Marginal de la Selva wasn't just a transportation artery; it facilitated economic development, access to healthcare and education, and improved the lives of thousands of people in the region. It remains a vital link to this day.  For his work on the highway, and his broader contributions to Peruvian infrastructure, Lara received numerous accolades, including the Order of the Sun of Peru, the nation’s highest honor, in 1980. He was also recognized internationally by engineering organizations. 

Beyond the Marginal Highway, Lara directed the construction of numerous other significant projects throughout his career, including irrigation systems, hydroelectric dams, and improved port facilities. He held various positions within the Ministry of Public Works, including Vice Minister, demonstrating his administrative capabilities alongside his technical expertise. He was known for his pragmatic approach, his commitment to quality, and his ability to manage complex projects within budget and on schedule.

Braulio Lara retired from public service in the late 1980s. He continued to consult on engineering projects and remained a vocal advocate for sustainable development and responsible infrastructure planning. He authored several technical papers and lectured at universities, sharing his knowledge and experience with future generations of engineers.  He spent his later years in Lima, dedicating time to his family and pursuing his passion for aviation. Braulio Alonso Lara Ñiquen passed away on July 18, 2017, in Lima, Peru, at the age of 94. His legacy remains firmly cemented as one of Peru’s most accomplished and impactful civil engineers, a builder who connected communities and fostered progress.

title: Katherine Ryan
text:
Katherine Ryan was born Catherine Ann Ryan on November 30, 1983, in Chatham, Kent, England. Her mother, Beryl, was a primary school teacher, and her father, Terry, worked in the Royal Engineers. Her early childhood was marked by frequent relocation due to her father’s military postings. She lived in various locations across the UK and West Germany before settling in Liverpool at the age of seven. This nomadic upbringing, coupled with a naturally observant nature, would later significantly influence her comedic style. Ryan has openly discussed a difficult relationship with her father, who struggled with alcoholism and gambling, and she had limited contact with him after the age of eight. 

Ryan excelled academically, achieving eleven GCSEs at A* or A grade and subsequently attending Queen Mary University of London, where she studied English Literature, graduating with a 2:1 in 2005. While studying, she began performing stand-up comedy in 2005, initially as a way to fund her degree. Her first professional gig was at a university event, and she quickly progressed to performing in clubs around London. She honed her craft, developing a distinctly sharp, observational style, often drawing on personal experiences.

A significant early career step was winning the Leicester Mercury Comedian of the Year award in 2006, a prestigious competition that provided a platform for emerging comedians. This win, alongside appearances at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival from 2006 onwards, raised her profile. She began to regularly appear on television panel shows, including *Never Mind the Buzzcocks* (2008), *8 Out of 10 Cats* (2008-2016) and *Mock the Week* (2009-2010). These appearances broadened her audience and allowed her to showcase her quick wit and deadpan delivery. 

Ryan’s first solo stand-up show, *Hysteria*, toured in 2009. She followed this with *Off-Kilter* in 2011 and *Kathbum* in 2013. In 2014, she became a team captain on the Sky One comedy panel show *Intern*, alongside Rob Beckett.  She also began to expand her work into writing, co-writing and starring in the sitcom *Campus* (2011) with Sian Gibson.

A major breakthrough came with *Glitter Room* (2017), a critically acclaimed and commercially successful Netflix special filmed at the Leicester Square Theatre. This special, and the subsequent Netflix series *The Duchess* (2020), which she wrote, starred in and executive produced, cemented her status as a leading figure in British comedy. *The Duchess*, a semi-autobiographical comedy about a single mother and her complicated relationships, garnered significant attention and critical praise. 

In 2019, Ryan launched the podcast *Tell Me A Secret*, in which guests reveal a secret they’ve never told anyone before. The podcast became highly popular, demonstrating her ability to connect with audiences on a more personal level.  She also continued to tour extensively with her stand-up shows, including *In Trouble* (2017-2018) and *Miss World* (2018-2019). 

Ryan has been in a relationship with Bobby Kootstra, a former professional hockey player, since 2018. They have a daughter, Violet, born in June 2021, and a son, Frederick, born in February 2023.  She frequently incorporates motherhood into her comedy routines, offering a refreshingly honest and often cynical perspective on the realities of parenting.

Currently, Ryan continues to perform stand-up, write and present television shows. She frequently appears on British television and radio, and has a significant online presence.  As of late 2023, she is touring with her show *Ready to Rumble*, which delves into themes of aging, societal expectations, and her experiences as a mother.  Her career spans almost two decades, consistently demonstrating her talent as a comedian, writer and performer, and she remains a prominent and influential voice in the British comedy scene.

title: Amr Shabana
text:
Amr Mohamed Shabana, widely regarded as one of the greatest squash players of all time, was born on September 19, 1978, in Alexandria, Egypt. His father, Mohamed Shabana, was a renowned squash player himself, reaching a career-high world ranking of number 5 in the 1970s, and played a pivotal role in fostering Amr’s early interest and development in the sport. Amr began playing squash at the age of six, initially learning the game at the Alexandria Sporting Club, a traditional hub for squash in Egypt. He was quickly identified as a prodigy, displaying exceptional talent and dedication. 

Shabana's early competitive career saw him dominate junior tournaments. He won the World Junior Squash Championships in 1996 in Peterborough, Canada, cementing his status as a rising star. This victory, at the age of 18, signaled his readiness for the professional ranks.  He turned professional in 1996, joining the Professional Squash Association (PSA) tour.

His initial years on the PSA Tour were marked by consistent improvement and gradual ascension. Shabana steadily climbed the rankings, showcasing a powerful and intelligent playing style characterized by deceptive shot-making, exceptional court coverage, and a relentless work ethic. He began making notable inroads into major tournaments, regularly reaching quarter-finals and semi-finals. 

The breakthrough season for Shabana was 2003. He won his first major PSA title at the Qatar International Squash Championships in Doha in November 2003, defeating David Palmer in the final. This victory propelled him into the top 10 of the world rankings.  He carried this momentum into 2004, culminating in his first World Open title, held in Cairo, Egypt, in December of that year. This was a particularly significant victory playing on home soil, defeating fellow Egyptian and long-time rival, Ahmed Barada, in the final.

Shabana’s reign as World Number 1 began in June 2006, displacing Thierry Lincan. He held the top ranking for a total of 36 months, a testament to his consistency and dominance. During this period, he secured a further three World Open titles – in 2007 in Eindhoven, Netherlands, in 2008 in Luxor, Egypt, and in 2009 in Kuwait.  He became the first player to win the World Open three times consecutively.

Throughout his career, Shabana accumulated an impressive record of 38 PSA Tour titles. He was renowned for his competitive spirit and tactical acumen, often outmaneuvering opponents with his strategic play.  He faced stiff competition from players such as David Palmer, James Willstrop, Nick Matthew, and Ramy Ashour, consistently proving himself against the best. His rivalry with Ashour, in particular, became a defining feature of the sport in the late 2000s and early 2010s, with both players engaging in numerous thrilling encounters.

Shabana's last tournament win was the 2012 Kuwait International Squash Championships.  Injuries, particularly to his Achilles tendon and knee, began to take their toll in the later stages of his career, impacting his movement and ultimately contributing to his retirement in 2014 at the age of 35. He announced his retirement following a second-round loss at the 2014 Allam British Open. 

Following his retirement from professional play, Shabana remained involved in squash. He transitioned into a coaching role, working with promising young players and sharing his extensive knowledge of the game. He also served as a consultant and ambassador for squash development programs in Egypt. He has been involved in mentoring current Egyptian players, including the current world number one, Ali Farag.  Shabana is married and has two children. He continues to live in Cairo and is considered a national hero in Egypt, having significantly raised the profile of the sport within the country.

title: Sage Stallone
text:
Sage Moonblood Stallone was born July 6, 1976, in Los Angeles, California, to actors Sylvester Stallone and Sasha Czack. His mother, a Czechoslovakian-born photographer and waitress, had a complex family history, being the daughter of Stephen Rickard, a prominent psychic, and Anya Bertha Zsakova, who claimed to be a fortune teller. This lineage deeply influenced Sage’s upbringing, as he was raised with an interest in the metaphysical and spiritual. He had a younger brother, Seargeoh Stallone, born in 1985, who tragically died in 2012.

Sage spent much of his early life traveling with his parents, experiencing a somewhat unconventional childhood given his father’s burgeoning film stardom. He attended the Buckley School in Sherman Oaks, California, and later briefly attended the University of North Carolina School of the Arts, focusing on film studies. However, he left after a year to pursue his own creative endeavors.  His education was also supplemented by private tutoring, reflecting his parents' commitment to his learning despite the demands of their careers.

Sage's early forays into the entertainment industry were largely centered around supporting his father's work. He made his film debut at the age of six months in *Rocky II* (1979), appearing briefly as Rocky Balboa's infant son, Robert Balboa Jr. He had uncredited roles in *Rocky III* (1982) and *Rocky IV* (1985), growing up on set and gaining familiarity with the filmmaking process.  However, he actively resisted being pushed into acting as a child, preferring to observe and learn. 

In the early 1990s, Sage began to explore filmmaking himself, initially focusing on short films and independent projects. He co-founded a production company, Grindhouse Pictures, with his friend David Krebs, and began writing, directing and producing.  His directorial debut came in 1996 with the short film *Victory Road*, a coming-of-age story.  He continued to work on independent films, often low-budget, including *Montana* (1998), which he wrote and directed, and starred opposite his father. *Montana* was a Western thriller focusing on a complex father-son relationship and earned mixed reviews. 

Sage’s career continued with roles in films like *Driven* (2001), a racing drama starring Sylvester Stallone, and *Eye See You* (2002), a thriller. He also ventured into music, forming a band called The Dark Horse, and experimenting with electronic music and DJing. He released an album, *Home*, in 2006.  He also worked as a music video director, showcasing his artistic vision beyond film.

In the later years of his life, Sage became increasingly involved in the real estate market, reportedly making substantial investments in the Las Vegas area. He was described as a shrewd businessman, and his financial dealings became a focus in the years leading up to his death. He was reportedly working on a large-scale real estate project at the time.  

Sage Stallone was found dead on July 3, 2013, at his apartment in Studio City, California, just three days before his 37th birthday.  The Los Angeles County Coroner's Office determined the cause of death to be a heart attack caused by atherosclerosis, a buildup of plaque in the arteries.  Toxicology reports revealed the presence of cocaine and prescription medications in his system, but these were not considered the primary cause of death.  The circumstances surrounding his death were initially subject to speculation, but the official report concluded it was due to natural causes, exacerbated by drug use.

title: Namita Gokhale
text:
Namita Gokhale, born on December 28, 1951, in Lucknow, India, is a prominent Indian author, editor, and publisher. Her lineage is steeped in literary and intellectual tradition; she is the daughter of renowned Hindi novelist and freedom fighter, Mahadevi Varma, and social activist and writer, Dwarka Prasad Misra. This upbringing profoundly influenced her own path, fostering a deep engagement with literature and societal issues from a young age. Gokhale spent her early years in Lucknow, absorbing the city’s rich cultural atmosphere and benefiting from the constant presence of leading literary figures who frequented her home. She received her early education at Loreto Convent, Lucknow, and later attended St. Mary’s College, also in Lucknow, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in English Literature in 1972. 

Following her graduation, Gokhale moved to Delhi and joined All India Radio as a broadcaster in 1973. This role allowed her to hone her communication skills and develop a wide-ranging understanding of Indian society. However, her passion for writing soon took precedence. She began writing short stories and articles, gradually establishing herself as a voice to watch in Indian English literature. Her first published novel, *Priya,* appeared in 1978, exploring themes of identity, alienation, and the changing social landscape of India.

The 1980s marked a significant period of growth for Gokhale’s literary career. She published *The Blind Eye* in 1983, a novel that delved into the complexities of familial relationships and societal expectations.  She also began to explore non-fiction, contributing essays and articles to various publications.  In 1989, she published *A Different Heaven*, a collection of short stories that showcased her nuanced portrayal of human emotions and experiences.  This period also saw her begin a long association with publishing, working as an editor at Oxford University Press, India, from 1991 to 1999.  During her tenure at OUP, she championed emerging Indian writers and played a crucial role in bringing their work to a wider audience. 

A pivotal moment in Gokhale's career arrived in 2000 with the publication of *Paro: Dreams of Passion*. This novel, a reimagining of the Devdas story from Parvati’s perspective, garnered widespread critical acclaim and commercial success, becoming a national bestseller. It was followed by *The Book of Shadows* in 2004, a historical novel set during the Sepoy Mutiny of 1857, which further cemented her reputation as a masterful storyteller.  

In 2006, Gokhale co-founded Yatra Books, an independent publishing house dedicated to promoting Indian voices and exploring diverse literary genres.  This venture allowed her to exercise greater creative control over the publishing process and to support authors who might not find a platform with larger commercial publishers.  She has continued to be actively involved in Yatra Books, shaping its editorial direction and nurturing new talent. 

Her subsequent novels, including *Saachi* (2011), *Things to Leave Behind* (2016) and *The Habit of Freedom* (2019), continued to explore themes of love, loss, memory, and the search for meaning in a rapidly changing world. *The Habit of Freedom*, a biographical novel about the life of Uday Shankar, a pioneering Indian dancer and choreographer, was longlisted for the DSC Prize for South Asian Literature in 2020. 

Beyond her writing and publishing, Gokhale has been a dedicated advocate for literary events and festivals. She served as the Director of the Jaipur Literature Festival from 2013 to 2017, playing a key role in establishing it as a globally recognised literary event.  She has also served on numerous literary juries and committees.  Namita Gokhale currently resides in Noida, near Delhi, and continues to write, edit, and contribute to the Indian literary landscape. She has received numerous awards and accolades for her work, including the Central Sahitya Akademi Award in 2021 for her contribution to Indian literature.

title: Abdulqawi Yusuf
text:
Abdulqawi Yusuf was born on November 15, 1935, in the village of Sheikh, located in the British Somaliland Protectorate, now part of Somaliland. His father, Yusuf Warsame, was a prominent elder and religious scholar of the Reer Yusuf clan, a sub-clan of the Habr Je’lo Isaaq. Abdulqawi received his early education in traditional Islamic schools, memorizing the Quran at a young age, a feat considered highly prestigious within Somali society. He then attended Sheikh Secondary School, completing his studies in 1954. This positioned him as one of a small, highly educated cohort during a period of colonial rule. 

In 1955, Abdulqawi secured a scholarship to study law at the University of Rome, Italy. He excelled in his studies, earning a law degree in 1960, the same year that British Somaliland gained independence and subsequently united with Italian Somaliland to form the Somali Republic. Returning to Somalia, he immediately entered public service, joining the Ministry of Justice in July 1960 as a legal advisor. His fluency in both Somali, Arabic and Italian, alongside his newly acquired legal expertise, quickly made him a valuable asset. 

Abdulqawi rapidly ascended the judicial ladder. In 1963, he was appointed as a judge, initially serving in the District Court of Mogadishu. He then moved to the Appellate Court in 1967, demonstrating his capacity for complex legal reasoning.  A pivotal moment in his career came in 1970 when, following the bloodless coup led by General Siad Barre, Abdulqawi was appointed Chief Justice of Somalia. This appointment, while occurring under a military regime, was largely seen as a meritocratic one, recognizing his integrity and legal acumen. 

During his 18-year tenure as Chief Justice, from 1970 to 1988, Abdulqawi navigated the complex legal landscape of a socialist state. He oversaw significant reforms to the Somali legal system, including the introduction of a new civil code in 1975, largely based on Italian and Islamic law. He also played a crucial role in establishing the National Legal Institute in 1976, aimed at training Somali lawyers and judges.  While operating within the confines of a one-party state, he strived to maintain judicial independence where possible, often mediating between the executive branch and the courts. He was known for his cautious approach, prioritizing stability and upholding the rule of law, even when faced with political pressure. 

However, his position became increasingly untenable as the Barre regime’s authoritarianism intensified. He repeatedly clashed with the government over issues of due process and political prisoners.  His insistence on legal procedure, even in politically sensitive cases, earned him both respect and the resentment of hardliners within the government. In 1988, Abdulqawi was abruptly dismissed from his position as Chief Justice, officially cited as reaching retirement age, though widely understood to be a consequence of his resistance to government interference in the judiciary. 

Following his dismissal, Abdulqawi largely withdrew from public life, residing in Mogadishu. He remained a respected figure, consulted by legal professionals and elders. The collapse of the Siad Barre regime in 1991 and the subsequent outbreak of the Somali Civil War plunged the country into chaos. Despite the dangers, Abdulqawi remained in Somalia, attempting to contribute to reconciliation efforts. He played a key role in the formation of various peace initiatives, advocating for a return to constitutional governance. 

In 2000, Abdulqawi was appointed Chairman of the Reconciliation and Federal Constitution Commission by the Transitional National Government, established in Djibouti. He led the commission in drafting a new federal constitution for Somalia, a monumental task given the country's fragmented political landscape and deeply rooted clan divisions.  The draft constitution, completed in 2004, aimed to balance the needs of a unified state with the recognition of regional autonomy. 

Abdulqawi Yusuf passed away on November 22, 2018, in Mogadishu, at the age of 83. He is remembered as a dedicated public servant, a staunch advocate for the rule of law, and a pivotal figure in Somalia’s legal and political history. His contributions to the modernization of the Somali legal system and his efforts to reconcile the country during a period of immense turmoil cemented his legacy as one of Somalia’s most respected figures.

title: Heinrich Himmler
text:
Heinrich Himmler was born on October 7, 1900, in Munich, Bavaria, Germany, to Gebhard Himmler, a secondary school headmaster, and Anna Heyder. His upbringing was staunchly conservative, nationalistic, and Catholic. He was a physically unremarkable child, prone to asthma and often bullied, and found solace in studying history and keeping detailed diaries, reflecting a meticulous and disciplined personality. He received his Abitur (high school diploma) in 1919, but the disruption of World War I and its aftermath meant a delay in pursuing his desired medical studies. He initially trained as a land surveyor but abandoned this for medical studies at the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich in 1920. He never completed his degree, leaving in 1923 to join a Freikorps, a paramilitary group, participating in the suppression of communist uprisings.

Himmler joined the Nazi Party on August 1, 1923, receiving membership number 14,304. He was initially drawn to the party’s nationalist rhetoric and its promise of restoring German greatness. His early career within the party was relatively unremarkable, working as a party propagandist and treasurer for a regional Nazi publication. A pivotal moment came in 1925 when he met Ernst Röhm, the leader of the Sturmabteilung (SA), the Nazi Party's original paramilitary wing. He became Röhm’s adjutant and gained organizational experience. 

In 1929, Himmler was appointed head of the Sicherheitsdienst (SD), the security service of the Nazi Party. This marked the beginning of his rise to power. He began to build a network of informants and focused on intelligence gathering, initially targeting political opponents within the Nazi movement itself. In 1933, following the Nazi seizure of power, Himmler was appointed Police President of Munich. He swiftly expanded the police force and began to implement policies of political repression. 

A crucial development occurred in 1934 during the Night of the Long Knives (June 30 – July 2, 1934). Himmler, along with Reinhard Heydrich, played a key role in orchestrating the purge of the SA leadership, including Röhm, who was perceived as a threat to Hitler’s authority. This act solidified Himmler’s position within the Nazi hierarchy.  He was subsequently appointed to the rank of Reichsführer-SS (Reich Leader of the SS) in July 1934, consolidating control over the Schutzstaffel, initially Hitler’s personal bodyguard, transforming it into a powerful and independent organization.

Under Himmler's leadership, the SS expanded rapidly, encompassing not only security forces but also the Waffen-SS, a military branch that eventually rivaled the regular Wehrmacht in size and effectiveness, numbering over 800,000 soldiers by 1945. He established a vast network of concentration camps, initially for political prisoners, which later evolved into extermination camps as part of the "Final Solution," the systematic genocide of European Jews.  He oversaw the murder of approximately six million Jews, as well as millions of others deemed undesirable by the Nazi regime, including Roma, homosexuals, disabled people, and political opponents. Key figures involved in the implementation of the Final Solution under his direction included Adolf Eichmann and Reinhard Heydrich. 

Himmler also oversaw the exploitation of forced labor, with millions of people from occupied territories being deported to Germany to work in war industries. He was a fervent believer in racial hygiene and actively promoted the “Lebensraum” (living space) policy, advocating for the colonization of Eastern Europe.  

As the war turned against Germany, Himmler attempted to negotiate a separate peace with the Western Allies through intermediaries like Count Folke Bernadotte in April 1945, offering to surrender the Waffen-SS in exchange for lenient treatment. These efforts failed.  After Hitler’s suicide on April 30, 1945, Himmler attempted to flee Germany, disguising himself as a sergeant in the Waffen-SS. He was captured by British forces on May 21, 1945, near Bremervörde.  Facing imminent trial for war crimes and crimes against humanity, Heinrich Himmler committed suicide by cyanide capsule on May 23, 1945, while in British custody.

title: Matthew Perry
text:
Matthew Langford Perry was born on August 19, 1969, in Reading, Massachusetts, to Suzanne Marie Morrison, a journalist, and John Bennett Perry, an actor and singer. His parents divorced when he was a year old, and he spent much of his early childhood moving between Ottawa, Canada, where his mother lived, and Los Angeles, where his father resided. He had a half-sister, Caitlin Morrison, from his mother’s second marriage. Perry showed an early aptitude for acting, appearing in school plays and taking drama lessons from a young age. He was a nationally ranked tennis player as a junior, reaching as high as 17th in Canada.

Perry’s acting career began with guest appearances on Canadian television in the early 1980s, including roles on *240-Robert* (1983) and *Charles in Charge* (1985). He dropped out of high school to pursue acting full-time, moving to Los Angeles in 1985. Initial roles were minor, including a recurring part as Chazz Russell on *Second Chance* (1987-1988) and a role in the short-lived Fox series *Boys Will Be Boys* (1987). His first significant television role came with *Sydney*, a 1990 sitcom that was quickly cancelled after 13 episodes. He then landed the part of Roger Azarian in *Beverly Hills, 90210* in 1990, intended as a regular role, but it was reduced to a recurring one after just ten episodes. 

The role that would define his career arrived in 1994 with *Friends*. Perry was cast as Chandler Bing, a sarcastic and witty character whose awkwardness resonated with audiences. *Friends* ran for ten seasons, from 1994 to 2004, becoming a global phenomenon and securing Perry’s status as a household name. Throughout the show’s run, he earned an Emmy nomination in 2002 for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series, and multiple Screen Actors Guild Award nominations as part of the ensemble cast. He and his co-stars were each earning $1 million per episode by the final seasons.

While *Friends* was his most prominent role, Perry continued to pursue film opportunities.
