He appeared in movies such as *Fools Rush In* (1997), alongside Salma Hayek, *Almost Heroes* (1998), and *The Whole Nine Yards* (2000), and its sequel *The Whole Ten Yards* (2004).  He also starred in the critically acclaimed television film *The Ron Clark Story* (2006), for which he received a Golden Globe nomination for Best Actor – Miniseries or Television Film. He continued television work with roles in *Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip* (2006-2007), *Mr. Sunshine* (2011), and *Go On* (2012-2013).  He also had a guest role on *The Good Wife* in 2013.

Throughout his success, Perry battled addiction to alcohol and prescription painkillers, a struggle he publicly acknowledged and discussed openly. He underwent multiple stints in rehabilitation, beginning in 1997, and detailed his experiences in his 2022 memoir, *Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing*.  He established Perry House, a sober living facility for men, in Malibu, California, in 2013.  He used his platform to advocate for addiction recovery and raise awareness about the disease. 

In the final years of his life, Perry continued to work, appearing in the HBO Max reunion special *Friends: The Reunion* in 2021. He was actively promoting his memoir, which became a New York Times bestseller.  He was last seen publicly having dinner with a friend on October 27, 2023. Matthew Perry was found unresponsive in the jacuzzi at his Los Angeles home on October 28, 2023, and pronounced dead at the scene. The official cause of death was determined to be the acute effects of ketamine, with drowning as a contributing factor. He was 54 years old. He is survived by his father, John Bennett Perry, his mother, Suzanne Morrison, and his half-sister, Caitlin Morrison.

title: Tracy Somerset, Duchess of Beaufort
text:
Tracy Ward, later Duchess of Beaufort, was born on 27th September 1963 at St Mary’s Hospital in Paddington, London, to Mr. and Mrs. John Aubrey Ward. Her father, John Ward, was a chartered accountant, and her mother, Penelope, née Smythe, came from a family with historic ties to Lincolnshire. Tracy spent her early childhood in Lincolnshire, attending the local primary school before being educated at Wycombe Abbey, an independent girls’ boarding school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, from 1976 to 1981. She excelled academically and demonstrated a keen interest in history and the arts.

After completing her schooling, Tracy studied History at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, graduating with an MA (Hons) in 1984. Following university, she embarked on a career in advertising, joining the advertising agency Masius, Young & Roberts (later acquired by Saatchi & Saatchi) in 1985. She worked on accounts for major brands like British Airways and the Post Office, quickly rising through the ranks due to her strategic thinking and client management skills. By 1995, she had become a board director, responsible for overseeing significant advertising campaigns and contributing to the agency's overall growth. 

Her life took a significant turn in 1998 when she met David Somerset, Marquess of Worcester, heir to the Dukedom of Beaufort. David, born on 14th May 1959, was a successful businessman with interests in property and forestry, as well as the traditional estate management associated with his family's title. They married on 14th May 1999 at Lower Slaughter Church in Gloucestershire, a small village on the Beaufort Estate. The wedding was a relatively private affair, reflecting the couple’s preference for a low profile despite their prominent positions.

Following their marriage, Tracy Somerset embraced her new role within one of Britain’s oldest and most aristocratic families. The Beauforts trace their lineage back to the Plantagenet dynasty and hold the hereditary office of Lord Warden of the Forest of Dean. Upon the death of Henry Somerset, 10th Duke of Beaufort, on 16th August 2017, David Somerset succeeded him as the 11th Duke of Beaufort, and Tracy consequently became Duchess of Beaufort.

As Duchess, Tracy has actively supported numerous charitable organizations, focusing primarily on rural issues, conservation, and the arts. She serves as a patron of the Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust, reflecting her commitment to environmental protection, and is actively involved in promoting sustainable land management practices on the 55,000-acre Beaufort Estate.  She has also been a long-term supporter of the National Trust, recognizing the importance of preserving Britain’s heritage. 

Unlike some members of the aristocracy, the Duchess has maintained a degree of professional independence, continuing to offer consultancy services in the advertising and communications sector, albeit on a reduced scale.  She has utilized her expertise to assist with marketing and branding initiatives for various organizations connected to the estate and her charitable interests. 

The Duke and Duchess reside at Badminton House, the ancestral seat of the Beaufort family, located near Badminton in South Gloucestershire.  Badminton House is renowned for hosting the annual Badminton Horse Trials, a world-leading equestrian event which the Duchess actively supports, overseeing aspects of its organization and hospitality.  She and the Duke have three children: Henry, Earl of Beaufort (born 1981), Isabella Somerset (born 1983), and John Somerset (born 1988).  The Duchess maintains a relatively private life, preferring to focus on her family, charitable work, and the stewardship of the historic Beaufort Estate.

title: Henryk Wieniawski
text:
Henryk Wieniawski was born on July 22, 1835, in Lublin, Congress Poland, which was then part of the Russian Empire. His father, Tadeusz Wieniawski, was a watchmaker who also possessed a strong passion for music and played the violin, and his mother, Regina, née Majewska, came from a family with musical inclinations. Recognizing his sons’ early aptitude, Tadeusz provided initial musical training to both Henryk and his younger brother, Józef, who also became a noted pianist and composer. Henryk’s first public performance occurred at the remarkably young age of seven, in Lublin, playing a concerto by Viotti. 

The family moved to Warsaw in 1843, where Henryk and Józef continued their studies. Henryk entered the Warsaw Conservatory in 1847, studying violin with Marjan Sawicki and composition with Apolinary Kątski. He demonstrated prodigious talent, completing the conservatory’s course in just three years, graduating in 1850. While still a student, he gained considerable attention performing solo concerts, even performing for the visiting Tsar Nicholas I in 1849.

Following his graduation, Wieniawski embarked on a European tour with Józef. They performed extensively throughout Russia, Germany, and France. In 1852, he began studies with the renowned violinist Camille Stamitz in Paris, further honing his technique. Paris became a crucial stepping stone in his career, and in 1853, he debuted at the Concerts Populaires, gaining favorable critical reception. This was followed by a successful performance at the prestigious Gewandhaus in Leipzig in 1854. 

Wieniawski’s reputation as a virtuoso rapidly grew. He toured extensively throughout Europe and the British Isles during the 1850s and 1860s, performing with leading orchestras and captivating audiences with his brilliant technique, expressive playing, and charismatic stage presence. He was particularly admired for his innovative use of harmonics, pizzicato, and left-hand techniques.  He was appointed the solo violinist to the Grand Duchess Elena Pavlovna in St. Petersburg in 1860, a position he held until 1868. During this time, he frequently performed at the Russian Imperial Court.

His compositional output, though not as voluminous as his performance schedule allowed, is significant. He composed two violin concertos (in D minor, Op. 22, and in D major, Op. 28), a Polonaise Brillante No. 1 in D major, Op. 4, and No. 2 in A minor, Op. 24, a Fantasie Brillante on themes from Gounod's *Faust*, Op. 20, several mazurkas, scherzos, and other shorter pieces for violin and piano. His compositions are characterized by Polish folk influences, melodic invention, and technical demands that showcase the violin’s capabilities.

In 1873, Wieniawski accepted a professorship at the Brussels Conservatory, where he established a highly influential violin class. Among his notable students were Eugène Ysaÿe, Jacques Thibaud, and Zarathustra Pinchas.  He remained in Brussels for the rest of his life, continuing to perform and teach. 

In 1878, Wieniawski toured the United States, giving a series of highly acclaimed concerts.  He continued to tour periodically, but his health began to decline. He suffered from poor eyesight and a nervous ailment, which eventually led to a stroke. He died unexpectedly on August 3, 1880, in Brussels, Belgium, at the age of 45, while preparing for a concert tour. He was initially buried in Brussels, but his remains were later transferred to Warsaw in 1922 and interred in the Powązki Cemetery, a place of honor for Polish artists and intellectuals.

title: Muhammad Al-Hafiz
text:
Muhammad Al-Hafiz, born Muhammad Hassan Al-Hafiz on December 18, 1936, in the village of Kafr ‘Atiyah, Beheira Governorate, Egypt, was a highly influential and prolific Egyptian calligrapher and designer, widely considered a key figure in the revival of Islamic calligraphy in the 20th century. His family, of rural origin, were farmers, and he received a traditional religious education from a young age, initially at the local *kuttab* (elementary religious school) where he learned the basics of reading, writing, and the Quran. This early exposure to the Quranic script ignited his lifelong passion for calligraphy.

Al-Hafiz’s formal artistic training began in 1950 at the age of fourteen when he joined the workshop of Sheikh Muhammad ‘Ali al-Baysi in Cairo. Al-Baysi, a renowned calligrapher affiliated with the Muhammad Ali Mosque, taught him the fundamentals of the *thuluth* script, considered one of the most complex and visually striking of the traditional Islamic scripts.  He spent six years under Al-Baysi’s tutelage, mastering not only the technical execution of *thuluth* but also its historical and aesthetic principles. He simultaneously studied at the Higher Institute of Applied Arts in Cairo from 1957 to 1961, earning a Bachelor's degree in Applied Arts with a specialization in decorative arts. 

Following his graduation, Al-Hafiz worked for the Egyptian Ministry of Culture from 1961 to 1978, initially as a designer and later as the head of the Calligraphy Section.  This position provided him with a platform to apply his skills to a wide range of projects, including designing covers for books, magazines, and official documents. Crucially, he was instrumental in establishing the standards for Arabic calligraphy used in Egyptian government publications. He also began to experiment with incorporating calligraphy into modern design, moving beyond purely traditional applications. 

His breakthrough came in 1978 with an invitation from King Khalid of Saudi Arabia to design the calligraphy for the newly expanded Masjid al-Haram (the Grand Mosque) in Mecca. This monumental project, completed over a period of eight years (1978-1986), involved creating over 300 calligraphic panels, encompassing verses from the Quran and decorative elements, adorning the mosque’s walls and arches. The project involved a team of over 40 artisans working under his direction, and the panels, executed in gold leaf on marble, are considered some of the most significant examples of contemporary Islamic calligraphy.  The project cemented Al-Hafiz’s international reputation.

Throughout the 1980s and 90s, Al-Hafiz continued to receive commissions from across the Islamic world. He designed calligraphy for mosques in Malaysia (the National Mosque in Kuala Lumpur, completed in 1968, saw significant calligraphic additions by him in 1988), Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates, including the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque in Abu Dhabi, where he contributed to the design of several key calligraphic inscriptions completed in 2007. He also worked on private commissions for individuals and institutions, including the creation of large-scale calligraphic artworks for display in public spaces. 

Al-Hafiz was not only a master practitioner but also a dedicated teacher. He lectured at numerous universities and workshops internationally, including at the University of Damascus in Syria, and mentored a new generation of calligraphers, ensuring the continuation of the art form. He authored several books on calligraphy, including "The Art of Arabic Calligraphy" (1990) and "Calligraphy and Islamic Art" (1995), which became standard texts for students and practitioners. 

In his later life, Al-Hafiz continued to work and exhibit his art, receiving numerous awards and accolades for his contributions to Islamic art and culture. He was a member of several prestigious artistic organizations, including the Arabic Calligraphy Society. Muhammad Al-Hafiz died on July 26, 2009, in Cairo, Egypt, at the age of 72, leaving behind a vast and enduring legacy that continues to inspire calligraphers and designers worldwide. His work is held in numerous public and private collections and remains a vital part of the contemporary Islamic art landscape.

title: Jan-Michael Gambill
text:
Jan-Michael Gambill was born on April 14, 1976, in Rockford, Illinois, the son of Polish immigrants, Jan and Maria Gambill. His father worked as an engineer, and his mother was a teacher. The family later moved to Fountain Valley, California, when Gambill was ten years old, a relocation that proved pivotal for his tennis development, offering access to better coaching and competition. He began playing tennis at age six, initially encouraged by his father, and quickly demonstrated a natural aptitude for the sport. Gambill attended Los Alamitos High School in California, where he was a standout athlete, not only in tennis but also in basketball and track. He graduated in 1994.

Gambill’s junior tennis career was extremely successful. He won the 1993 USTA National 18s title, defeating Andy Roddick in the final, a foreshadowing of future professional encounters. He achieved a world No. 1 junior ranking in 1994, marking him as a player to watch. He skipped college, turning professional in 1994 and immediately embarking on the ATP Tour. 

His early professional years were marked by steady improvement. He spent much of 1995 and 1996 competing in Challenger tournaments, building experience and gradually climbing the rankings. 1997 saw a breakthrough. He reached his first ATP final at the Delray Beach International Tennis Championships, losing to Marcelo Ríos. This performance propelled him into the top 100, finishing the year ranked No. 72. 

1999 proved to be Gambill’s most successful year. He reached three ATP finals, winning the Nottingham Open in June, defeating Sjeng Schalken in the final 6–4, 6–4. He also reached the finals of Memphis and Long Island, losing to Tommy Haas and Alex Corretja respectively.  His best Grand Slam result came at the 1999 US Open, where he reached the fourth round, defeating Alex Corretja in an epic five-set match before falling to Andre Agassi.  He achieved his highest career ranking of No. 14 in the world in October 1999. Gambill was known for his aggressive serve-and-volley style of play, a relatively rare tactic in the modern game. His powerful serve, often exceeding 130 mph, was a key weapon.

The early 2000s saw a decline in Gambill’s ranking, plagued by shoulder injuries. He underwent surgery in 2001 to address the issue, but struggled to regain his peak form. While he achieved some notable wins, including defeating Roger Federer at the 2001 Indian Wells Masters, he was unable to consistently reach the later stages of major tournaments. He continued to compete sporadically on the ATP Tour and Challenger circuit for several years, battling to stay competitive. He achieved a final ATP Challenger title in 2006 in Lexington, Kentucky. 

Gambill officially announced his retirement from professional tennis in 2006, at the age of 30.  He finished his career with one ATP singles title and a career record of 177 wins and 157 losses.

Following his retirement, Gambill transitioned into coaching. He worked with several prominent players, most notably as a developmental coach at the USTA National Campus in Orlando, Florida. He became well-known for his work with young American players, including a significant period coaching Denis Shapovalov, helping him reach the semifinals of the 2021 Wimbledon Championships. He later took on coaching roles with other rising stars like Emilio Nava and Learner Tien.  Gambill is highly regarded in the coaching community for his insightful technical analysis and ability to develop players’ games.  He briefly returned to the tour as a coach for Jack Sock in 2023. 

As of late 2023, Gambill continues to work as a tennis coach, actively contributing to the development of the next generation of players. He remains a respected figure in the tennis world, known for his knowledge, passion, and dedication to the sport.

title: Carlos P. Romulo
text:
Carlos Peña Rómulo was born Carlos Peña on October 14, 1899, in Intramuros, Manila, Philippines, during the final years of Spanish colonial rule. His father, Gregorio Peña, was a doctor, and his mother, María de los Santos Romulo, was a schoolteacher. He later adopted his mother’s maiden name, Romulo, as his surname, a common practice in the Philippines to honor maternal lineage. His early education was undertaken within a home environment due to a childhood illness, but he eventually attended the Manila High School, graduating as valedictorian in 1918. He began his university studies at the University of the Philippines in 1918, initially pursuing a law degree, but soon shifted his focus to journalism. 

Romulo’s journalistic career began in 1919 while still a student, writing for *The Manila Times*, quickly rising to become the paper’s editor by 1921. He utilized his position to advocate for Philippine independence from the United States, which had taken control following the Spanish-American War. He was a prolific writer, known for his sharp wit and engaging style.  In 1924, he received a scholarship to study at Columbia University in New York City, earning a Master of Arts degree in English Literature in 1925. While in the U.S., he also worked as a contributing editor for *The Philippines Herald*. 

Upon his return to the Philippines, Romulo continued his writing and became a key figure in the country’s burgeoning nationalist movement. He was appointed to the staff of President Manuel Quezon in 1934, serving as a close advisor and speechwriter. He played a crucial role in the negotiations with the United States leading to the passage of the Tydings-McDuffie Act in 1934, which provided for the establishment of the Commonwealth of the Philippines and eventual independence.  He served as Secretary to the President until 1938. 

World War II dramatically altered Romulo’s career. When the Japanese invaded the Philippines in December 1941, he joined the forces fighting against the occupation.  He was appointed a Major in the United States Army and served as aide-de-camp to General Douglas MacArthur, accompanying him to Australia in 1942. From Australia, he broadcasted daily radio messages to the Philippines, bolstering morale and providing updates on the war effort under the moniker "The Voice of Freedom." These broadcasts, originating from stations like 5AA in Melbourne, were immensely popular and earned him international recognition.  In 1943, he was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Correspondence for his courageous reporting and wartime broadcasts. 

After the liberation of the Philippines in 1945, Romulo continued to serve in government. He was appointed Secretary of Foreign Affairs in 1946, a position he held until 1950. He was a key figure in establishing diplomatic relations with the newly independent nations of Asia and advocating for a more independent foreign policy for the Philippines.  In 1946, he was among the founders of the United Nations and served as the first Filipino representative to the organization.  He was elected President of the United Nations General Assembly in 1952, becoming the first Asian to hold the position. His term was marked by his efforts to mediate conflicts, particularly during the Korean War.

In 1953, Romulo returned to the Philippines and was elected to the House of Representatives, representing the first district of Manila. He later served as a Senator from 1957 to 1963.  In 1962, he was appointed Ambassador to the United States and High Commissioner to Canada, positions he held until 1968.  Throughout his career, he authored several books, including *I Saw the Fall of the Philippines* (1942), *Mother America* (1943), *My Brother Americans* (1945), and *The Magsaysay Story* (1959). 

Carlos P. Romulo continued to be a prominent figure in Philippine public life until his death on December 15, 1985, in Manila, at the age of 86. He was posthumously conferred the title of National Artist of the Philippines in 1986, recognizing his contributions to literature, journalism, and nation-building. His legacy remains significant as a champion of Philippine independence, a courageous wartime journalist, and a dedicated diplomat who helped shape the country’s role on the world stage.

title: Josh Mansour
text:
Joshua Mansour was born on March 12, 1990, in Camden, New South Wales, Australia, to Lebanese parents. His father, Elias Mansour, immigrated to Australia in the 1970s, and the family maintained strong ties to their heritage, a factor that would later influence Mansour’s representation in international rugby league. Growing up, Mansour displayed a natural athleticism, initially excelling in basketball before focusing on rugby league. He attended Westfield Sports High School, a renowned sporting nursery in Sydney, which produced many future professional athletes. It was here his rugby league talents were nurtured, playing in the school’s highly competitive program.

Mansour’s junior football was played with the Greenacre Tigers, a local club in southwest Sydney. He quickly rose through the ranks, showcasing his blistering speed and powerful running style. These attributes caught the attention of scouts from the National Rugby League (NRL), and he was signed by the Penrith Panthers in 2007 as part of their Toyota Cup (Under-20s) squad. He quickly established himself as a standout player in the youth competition, playing 45 games and scoring 25 tries between 2007 and 2009. 

His impressive performances earned him a promotion to the Penrith Panthers first-grade squad in 2010. Mansour made his NRL debut on April 24, 2010, against the Brisbane Broncos at Suncorp Stadium. He quickly became a regular fixture on the wing, known for his powerful carries, reliable catching under the high ball, and remarkable try-scoring ability. Throughout his nine seasons with the Panthers (2010-2018), he played a total of 166 NRL games, scoring 73 tries. He consistently ranked highly in metres gained per game, becoming one of the competition’s most dynamic outside backs.

A significant milestone in Mansour’s career came in 2016 when he was selected for the New South Wales State of Origin team. He debuted in Game 1 of the series on June 1st at ANZ Stadium, Sydney. While NSW ultimately lost the series 2-1, Mansour played in all three games, proving his ability to perform at the highest level of representative football. He scored a crucial try in Game 2, demonstrating his impact on the big stage. This Origin selection was a testament to his consistent performances for Penrith and a fulfillment of a long-held ambition.

Beyond State of Origin, Mansour also represented Lebanon at the international level. He was a key member of the Lebanese national team during the 2017 Rugby League World Cup, captaining the Cedars throughout the tournament. His heritage and leadership were vital as Lebanon achieved their best-ever World Cup result, reaching the quarter-finals. He played in five matches during the tournament, scoring two tries.

In November 2018, Mansour signed a two-year contract with the St George Illawarra Dragons, commencing in the 2019 season. He played 36 games for the Dragons, scoring 9 tries, before announcing his retirement from the NRL at the end of the 2020 season, citing ongoing knee injuries. These injuries had plagued him towards the end of his career, requiring multiple surgeries and impacting his ability to play at his peak.

Following his retirement, Mansour transitioned into a media role. He joined Triple M radio as a commentator and analyst, providing insights into the NRL. He also became involved in coaching at the junior levels, sharing his knowledge and experience with the next generation of rugby league players. He has remained an active figure within the Lebanese community, continuing to promote the sport and foster connections between Australia and Lebanon. Mansour currently resides in Sydney with his family, balancing his media commitments with his passion for the game and his community involvement.

title: Ivan Toms
text:
Ivan Toms was born on 21st July 1951 in Lusaka, Northern Rhodesia (now Zambia), to South African parents in exile. His parents, Fred and Sylvia Toms, were both anti-apartheid activists and members of the South African Communist Party (SACP). They fled South Africa in 1960 following increasing repression and were involved in providing logistical support to Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the African National Congress (ANC). Ivan spent his formative years in Zambia, attending Lusaka’s Northmead School, and was deeply influenced by the political climate and the presence of numerous exiled South Africans. He became politically aware at a young age, assisting his parents with tasks related to the liberation struggle, including distributing pamphlets and occasionally acting as a courier.

In 1969, at the age of 18, Toms returned to South Africa illegally, driven by a desire to actively participate in the fight against apartheid. He initially joined the ANC’s underground network in the Witwatersrand area, operating under the name ‘David Motau’. He underwent military training in Botswana in 1972, and later in Angola, specializing in urban guerilla warfare and explosives. He rose through the ranks of Umkhonto we Sizwe, becoming a regional commander responsible for operations in the Johannesburg area. 

Between 1976 and 1985, Toms was central to a series of significant sabotage operations targeting economic and government infrastructure. He was involved in the bombing of the Wonderboom railway lines near Pretoria in 1976, the Ellis Park stadium bombing in 1980, and the sabotage of the Koösfontein gold refinery in 1980, an operation intended to disrupt the South African economy. He also played a key role in the 1982 bombing of the Air Force headquarters in Pretoria, which resulted in the death of 13 people and injury to 217. While he did not personally plant the bomb, he was a key strategist and coordinator. 

Arrested in 1985 following a raid on an ANC safe house in Johannesburg, Toms was charged with sabotage and murder related to the Air Force headquarters bombing. The trial, which began in 1986, became a landmark case, attracting international attention. He refused legal representation, choosing instead to use the court as a platform to articulate the political motivations behind the ANC’s armed struggle and to denounce apartheid. He delivered a lengthy statement to the court, outlining the injustices of the system and justifying the use of violence as a last resort. In 1988, he was convicted on multiple counts, including sabotage and murder, and sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Toms served his sentence in Pollsmoor and later Diepkloof Maximum Security Prison. While incarcerated, he continued to be a symbol of resistance and engaged in political discussions with fellow prisoners and visiting officials.  He began to publicly question the continued use of armed struggle as South Africa moved towards negotiations.  He initiated a dialogue with prison authorities, advocating for improved conditions and greater political freedoms for prisoners.

Following the unbanning of the ANC in February 1990 and the release of Nelson Mandela, Toms was released from prison on 24th May 1991 as part of a general amnesty for political prisoners. He subsequently testified before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) in 1996, providing a detailed account of his involvement in Umkhonto we Sizwe operations. He sought amnesty for his actions, acknowledging the loss of life caused by the bombings but maintaining that they were undertaken in the context of a brutal and oppressive regime.  His amnesty was granted in 1998, though not without controversy given the scale of the violence he admitted to.

After his release, Toms dedicated himself to reconciliation and social justice. He worked as a consultant for the National Institute for Crime Prevention and Reintegration of Offenders (NICRO), focusing on restorative justice programs and reintegrating former political prisoners into society. He became a vocal advocate for demilitarization and the responsible use of force.  He authored his autobiography, “Holding My Enemy,” published in 2009, detailing his life in the struggle and his eventual embrace of reconciliation. Ivan Toms died on 18th February 2024 in Johannesburg, aged 72, leaving behind a complex legacy as a former freedom fighter who ultimately championed peace and forgiveness.

title: Kubota Beisen
text:
Kubota Beisen (窪田 米泉), born Kubota Shigeru (窪田 茂) on March 27, 1872, in Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan, was a highly influential Nihonga (modern Japanese-style painting) artist known for his meticulous depictions of flowers and birds, particularly sparrows. His early life was steeped in the traditions of his family, who were silk farmers. While assisting with the family business, young Shigeru displayed an aptitude for art, initially producing designs for kimono. This early exposure to textile design significantly shaped his later aesthetic, influencing his precise linework and sophisticated use of color. 

In 1888, at the age of 16, he moved to Tokyo to pursue formal artistic training. He enrolled in the painting program at the School of Fine Arts (Tokyo Bijutsu Gakko, now Tokyo University of the Arts), studying under the prominent Nihonga painter, Hashimoto Gaho (1838-1908). Gaho, a leading figure in the Meiji era’s art world and a staunch advocate for preserving traditional Japanese painting techniques while embracing Western influences, proved a pivotal mentor. Kubota excelled in his studies, demonstrating a particular talent for capturing the delicate forms and subtle nuances of natural subjects.  He graduated from the Tokyo Bijutsu Gakko in 1893.

Following his graduation, Kubota briefly taught art at a middle school in Shizuoka before returning to Tokyo in 1898. He joined the Japan Fine Arts Academy (Nihon Bijutsuin), a group founded by Hashimoto Gaho and others seeking to establish a modern, yet traditionally rooted, art institution. This association was crucial to his development and provided a platform for exhibiting his work. It was around this time, in 1898, that he adopted the art name "Beisen" – a name bestowed upon him by Gaho, signifying a commitment to artistic endeavor. 

Beisen's signature style began to emerge in the early 1900s. He became renowned for his *kachōga* (flower-and-bird paintings), eschewing grand historical or mythological themes in favor of intimate observations of nature. His sparrows, in particular, became his trademark. He painted them not as symbolic representations, but as individual creatures engaged in everyday activities – foraging for seeds, preening their feathers, or simply resting on branches.  He achieved remarkable realism, combined with a subtle emotional resonance, through his masterful brushwork and restrained palette. 

He first achieved significant recognition and a prize at the 1907 Bunten exhibition (the Government Art Exhibition), a highly prestigious event that significantly boosted his career.  He continued to exhibit regularly at the Bunten and its successor, the Teiten (Imperial Academy Exhibition), receiving numerous awards throughout his career, including the Teiten Prize in 1918 and again in 1928.  In 1936, he was selected as a member of the Imperial Fine Arts Academy, a testament to his national prominence.  

Beyond painting, Kubota Beisen dedicated himself to art education. From 1910 to 1930, he served as a professor at the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, shaping the next generation of Nihonga artists. He emphasized the importance of rigorous training in traditional techniques alongside careful observation of nature. He instilled in his students a reverence for Japanese aesthetic principles, while encouraging them to develop their own unique artistic voices.  His influential writings on art, including "Gafu Kōshū" (Collection of Painting Talks), published in 1924, further disseminated his artistic philosophy.

In his later life, despite suffering from cataracts, Kubota Beisen continued to paint, adapting his technique to accommodate his diminishing eyesight. He maintained a productive output until his death on May 17, 1942, in Tokyo, at the age of 70. His works are held in major Japanese museums, including the Tokyo National Museum, the Kyoto National Museum, and the Shizuoka Prefectural Museum of Art.  He left behind a legacy as one of the most important Nihonga artists of the 20th century, celebrated for his exquisite technique, his profound appreciation for nature, and his dedication to preserving and evolving the traditions of Japanese painting.

title: John Morris (curler)
text:
John Morris was born on December 22, 1977, in Banff, Alberta, Canada, into a family deeply rooted in the sport of curling. His father, Earl Morris, was a highly respected curler himself, a former provincial champion and a significant influence on John’s early development. Growing up in Canmore, Alberta, a small mountain town, Morris was introduced to curling at a very young age, practically learning to slide before he could walk. He honed his skills at the Canmore Curling Club, quickly demonstrating a natural talent and a passionate dedication to the game. 

Morris’s early competitive career saw him progress through the junior ranks, representing Alberta in national junior championships. He reached the Canada Safeway Championship (the national junior men's curling championship) in 1997, skipping his team. While they didn’t win, this experience provided valuable exposure and laid the groundwork for his future success. He attended the University of Calgary, studying kinesiology, balancing his academic pursuits with rigorous curling training. 

He first gained national attention as the third for Kevin Martin’s team, a powerhouse in Canadian curling. This association began in 2002, and the team quickly established itself as a dominant force. They won the 2003 Nokia BDO Canadian Curling Trials, earning the right to represent Canada at the 2003 World Curling Championships in Winnipeg, Manitoba. The team finished with a silver medal, losing a close final to Pal Trulsen of Norway. The Martin team continued its success, winning the 2004 Canadian Curling Trials and representing Canada at the 2004 World Curling Championships in Gävle, Sweden, where they secured the gold medal, defeating Sweden’s Peja Lindholm in the final.

In 2005, Morris left the Martin team and formed his own, initially with Jim Cotter as skip. They achieved considerable success, including a silver medal at the 2006 Canadian Curling Trials.  However, the most defining moment of Morris’s career arrived at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, British Columbia.  He was selected to play third for Kevin Martin’s team, which also included vice-skip Marc Kennedy and lead Ben Hebert.  The Canadian team went undefeated throughout the round robin, securing first place with a 9-2 record. They continued their dominant performance through the playoffs, defeating Sweden in the semi-final and then defeating Norway, skipped by Thomas Ulsrud, 6-3 in the gold medal game. This victory secured Canada’s gold medal and cemented Morris’s place in Canadian sporting history. 

Following the Olympic triumph, Morris explored a different facet of the sport, becoming a pioneer in mixed doubles curling. He partnered with Rachel Homan, and they quickly rose to prominence. They won the 2013 Canadian Mixed Doubles Curling Championship and represented Canada at the inaugural World Mixed Doubles Curling Championships in Fredericton, New Brunswick, where they won the gold medal, defeating Switzerland’s Sina Lutzenberger and Dominic Perret. This success demonstrated Morris’s versatility and adaptability as a curler. 

Morris continued to compete in both traditional and mixed doubles curling, achieving further success. He won a bronze medal at the 2014 World Curling Championships with the Kevin Koe team. In 2018, he once again represented Canada at the Winter Olympics, this time in Pyeongchang, South Korea, as part of the mixed doubles team with Kaitlyn Lawes. They finished with a respectable 4-5 record, narrowly missing the playoffs. 

Morris officially announced his retirement from competitive curling in February 2023, at the age of 45, citing a desire to spend more time with his family and pursue other interests. Throughout his career, he was known for his strategic thinking, precise shot-making, and calm demeanor under pressure. He also became a well-respected curling analyst, providing commentary for television broadcasts. John Morris remains a prominent figure in the Canadian curling community, leaving behind a legacy of excellence and innovation. He is married to Julie Morris and they have two children.

title: Arthur Ewert
text:
Arthur Ewert, born on February 22, 1908, in Mannheim, Germany, was a pivotal figure in the development of modern forestry, particularly known for his contributions to forest mensuration and yield regulation. His early life was steeped in the academic environment; his father, Wilhelm Ewert, was a professor of forestry at the University of Freiburg. This familial connection significantly influenced Arthur’s path. He received his initial education in Mannheim before attending the Gymnasium in Freiburg, graduating in 1927. He then pursued his university studies at the University of Freiburg, earning his doctorate in forestry in 1932 with a dissertation focused on the growth of beech trees. 

Following his doctorate, Ewert began his professional career in 1933 as a research assistant at the Baden Forest Research Institute in Freiburg. This position allowed him to apply and refine his theoretical knowledge in practical forestry settings. However, the rising tide of Nazism in Germany deeply conflicted with Ewert's personal beliefs. In 1935, facing increasing pressure to conform to the regime’s ideologies, he emigrated to Canada, accepting a position as a research officer with the Dominion Forest Service (later the Canadian Forest Service) in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario.

His arrival in Canada marked a turning point, allowing him to flourish in a more open and intellectually stimulating environment. Initially, his work focused on forest inventory and growth studies in the Lake States region. He quickly established himself as a meticulous researcher, and his expertise in statistical analysis was particularly valuable.  By 1948, he had been promoted to Principal Forest Officer and transferred to Ottawa, becoming head of the Forest Mensuration Section.

Ewert’s most significant contributions stemmed from his work in yield regulation. Traditional forest management at the time often relied on simplistic, empirical methods for determining sustainable harvest levels. Ewert, leveraging his statistical background and a deep understanding of forest growth, advocated for a more scientific, mathematically rigorous approach. He developed a system of “normal yield tables,” which were based on detailed observations of forest growth and allowed foresters to predict the future yield of stands with greater accuracy. These tables, published in 1953 as “Normal Yields of Eastern White Pine and Eastern Hemlock in the Lake States,” became a foundational text for forest managers across North America and beyond.

He didn't stop there. Recognizing the limitations of relying solely on average growth rates, he pioneered the concept of “stand dynamics,” emphasizing the importance of understanding the complex interplay of factors that influence forest development, including competition, mortality, and disturbance.  This led to the development of more sophisticated growth models and simulation tools.  His work culminated in the publication of “Forest Mensuration” in 1967, a comprehensive textbook that remains a standard reference for forestry students and professionals globally. The book went through three editions, the last in 1996, reflecting ongoing refinements and the incorporation of new research. 

Ewert was also heavily involved in international forestry organizations. He served as the Canadian representative to the International Union of Foresters (IUFRO) for many years and actively participated in numerous international conferences and workshops. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 1972, a testament to his outstanding contributions to science.

Arthur Ewert retired from the Canadian Forest Service in 1973 but remained actively engaged in forestry research and consulting. He continued to publish articles and mentor young foresters. He passed away on August 28, 2003, in Ottawa, at the age of 95.  His legacy continues through the widespread application of his techniques and principles, which have fundamentally shaped modern forest management practices, moving them from largely artful estimations to a more scientifically grounded discipline.

title: Flavio Méndez Santiago
text:
Flavio Méndez Santiago was born on December 28, 1933, in Juchitán, Oaxaca, Mexico, a town deeply rooted in Zapotec culture. His parents, Román Méndez and María Santiago, were both active participants in local political and social movements, instilling in him a strong sense of justice and community involvement from a young age. Juchitán, a bustling market town with a significant indigenous population, provided a formative environment where Méndez witnessed firsthand the disparities and struggles faced by marginalized communities. He completed his primary and secondary education in Juchitán, demonstrating an early aptitude for languages and a keen interest in social studies. 

In 1951, at the age of 18, Méndez moved to Mexico City to pursue higher education, enrolling at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM). He initially studied law, but quickly shifted his focus to anthropology, attracted by the discipline’s potential to understand and advocate for indigenous rights. He earned a bachelor’s degree in Anthropology in 1955 and continued at UNAM, obtaining a doctorate in Ethnology in 1962. His doctoral dissertation, focused on the social organization and political dynamics of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, laid the groundwork for much of his future work. 

Méndez’s professional career began in 1963 as a researcher at the Instituto Nacional Indigenista (INI), the National Indigenous Institute of Mexico. He spent the next two decades conducting extensive fieldwork across various indigenous communities in Oaxaca, Chiapas, and Guerrero. His research was pioneering in its methodological approach, prioritizing participatory observation and direct collaboration with local communities rather than imposing external frameworks. He focused particularly on the Zapotec and Mixtec peoples, documenting their languages, traditions, land tenure systems, and emerging political movements.  He published numerous articles and reports during this period, often highlighting the detrimental effects of government policies on indigenous livelihoods and cultural survival.

A significant turning point came in 1972 when Méndez was appointed Director-General of Intercultural Communication at the Secretaría de Educación Pública (SEP), the Ministry of Public Education.  He used this position to advocate for bilingual and intercultural education programs, believing that education was crucial for empowering indigenous communities and promoting their participation in national life. He championed the development of educational materials in indigenous languages and supported the training of indigenous teachers. This initiative, although facing bureaucratic hurdles, led to the establishment of the first bilingual schools in Oaxaca and other states.

In 1982, he left the SEP and joined the Centro de Estudios Demográficos y Sociales del Estado de Oaxaca (CEDESO), the Center for Demographic and Social Studies of the State of Oaxaca, as its director. He remained there until 1994, further expanding his research on indigenous political organization and the impact of globalization on local cultures. He became a crucial voice during the rise of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) in Chiapas in 1994, offering analysis and context to the uprising, emphasizing the longstanding grievances of indigenous communities and the failures of the Mexican state to address them. 

Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Méndez continued to be a prolific writer and commentator on indigenous issues, publishing books and articles that became essential reading for scholars and activists.  He was a vocal critic of neoliberal economic policies and their impact on indigenous land rights and cultural identity. He received numerous awards and recognitions for his work, including the Premio Nacional de Ciencias y Artes in 2008, Mexico’s highest honor for contributions to science and the arts. 

Flavio Méndez Santiago passed away on March 21, 2018, in Mexico City at the age of 84. His legacy remains significant, not only in the field of anthropology but also in the ongoing struggle for indigenous rights and social justice in Mexico. His work continues to inform contemporary debates regarding interculturality, linguistic diversity, and the role of indigenous communities in shaping the nation’s future. He left behind a substantial body of work, consisting of over 150 published articles, several books, and a generation of students and colleagues inspired by his dedication and intellectual rigor.

title: Matt Hunter (singer)
text:
Matthew Ryan Hunter was born on February 1, 1970, in Newport News, Virginia, to parents William and Patricia Hunter. His early life was marked by frequent relocation due to his father’s career in the U.S. Navy. This nomadic childhood took the family to locations including California, Florida, and ultimately, Norfolk, Virginia, where he spent the majority of his formative years. Hunter began playing guitar at the age of 12, initially self-taught, and quickly developed a passion for music, drawing inspiration from artists like James Taylor, Joni Mitchell, and Van Morrison. He formed his first band, "The Thorns," while attending Granby High School in Norfolk, performing local gigs and honing his songwriting skills. 

After graduating high school in 1988, Hunter briefly attended Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond, studying English before deciding to pursue music full-time. He began performing as a solo artist in the Norfolk/Virginia Beach area, building a local following with his introspective lyrics and distinctive vocal style. In 1992, he independently released his debut album, "Home,” a collection of acoustic songs that showcased his burgeoning talent. The album gained regional attention, leading to increased performance opportunities and a small but dedicated fanbase.

A significant turning point came in 1994 when Hunter signed with Mammoth Records, a burgeoning independent label known for its roster of singer-songwriters. His first album for Mammoth, “Dust to Light,” was released in 1995. This album, co-produced by Malcolm Burn (who later worked with Sheryl Crow and Rufus Wainwright), broadened Hunter’s sonic palette, incorporating elements of folk, rock, and jazz. "Dust to Light" received critical acclaim and led to national touring opportunities, opening for acts like Joan Osborne and Hootie & the Blowfish. 

Hunter’s breakthrough album arrived in 1998 with “Yesterday’s Modern,” again on Mammoth Records. The album spawned the single "Broken Glass," which reached number 37 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in the spring of 1999, becoming his signature song. “Yesterday’s Modern” sold over 250,000 copies, earning Hunter a gold record certification from the RIAA and solidifying his position as a promising artist. He garnered significant radio airplay on AAA and adult contemporary stations. 

Following the success of “Yesterday’s Modern," Hunter released “The Man Who Stayed Home” in 2001, an album that continued to explore themes of love, loss, and self-discovery. While commercially less successful than its predecessor, it was still critically well-received.  In 2003, Mammoth Records faced financial difficulties and eventually folded. Hunter subsequently signed with Dualtone Records, releasing “Parallel Universe” in 2004. This album represented a stylistic shift, incorporating more electronic elements and experimenting with different production techniques.

Throughout the 2000s and 2010s, Hunter continued to record and tour, releasing albums like “Disappearing Light” (2006), “Hungry Heart” (2008), and “Lullabies for the Fallen” (2011). These albums, while praised by fans and critics, never achieved the commercial success of “Yesterday’s Modern.” He maintained a loyal following through consistent touring and engagement with his audience.  He also began to focus increasingly on songwriting for other artists.

In 2014, Hunter moved to Nashville, Tennessee, and immersed himself in the songwriting community. He co-wrote songs for numerous artists, including Darius Rucker, Lee Brice, and Brothers Osborne. He continued to release independent albums, including “Now Is Then” in 2017 and "Concrete Sky" in 2020, maintaining his artistic independence.  

As of late 2023, Matt Hunter continues to live in Nashville, balancing his own musical pursuits with his work as a professional songwriter. He performs sporadically, primarily at smaller venues and festivals, and remains a respected figure in the Americana music scene. He has never married and has no children. While he hasn’t replicated the mainstream success of his late 1990s peak, he has built a sustainable career on his own terms, driven by his passion for crafting honest and emotionally resonant songs.

title: Salome Maswime
text:
Salome Maswime was born on 19 January 1932 in the village of Nkowankowa, near Tzaneen, in the then Northern Transvaal Province of South Africa, now Limpopo. Her parents were Reverend Johannes and Maria Maswime, both deeply involved in the local Methodist Church. This religious upbringing profoundly shaped her early life and future career. She received her primary education at Nkowankowa Methodist Primary School and continued to the nearby Morris Isaacs High School, a prestigious institution known for educating black South Africans during the apartheid era. She excelled academically, completing her Standard 10 (equivalent to Grade 12) in 1950. 

Maswime’s ambition to become a doctor arose from witnessing the significant healthcare disparities faced by black communities under apartheid. Despite facing systemic barriers, she secured a place to study medicine at the University of Fort Hare in 1951, a leading university for black African students at the time. However, the university’s medical school was closed in 1959 due to government pressure stemming from its association with anti-apartheid activism. Undeterred, Maswime completed her medical degree at the University of Natal Medical School (now University of KwaZulu-Natal) in Durban, graduating with a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBChB) in 1962. 

Her internship followed at King Edward VIII Hospital in Durban, lasting until 1963.  She then worked as a medical officer at Bethesda Hospital in Nongoma, KwaZulu-Natal, from 1963 to 1966, providing essential medical care to a largely rural and underserved population. This experience further solidified her commitment to addressing the healthcare needs of black South Africans.  In 1966, she began specializing in obstetrics and gynaecology, undertaking postgraduate studies and training in the field. 

In 1972, Maswime became the first black woman in South Africa to be admitted as a Fellow to the College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of South Africa (FCOGSA). This was a landmark achievement, breaking down racial and gender barriers in the medical profession. She established a private practice in Soweto, Johannesburg, in 1973, becoming a highly respected and sought-after specialist.  Her practice wasn’t merely a business; she often provided care to patients unable to afford her fees, embodying a deep sense of social responsibility. 

Beyond her clinical work, Maswime was deeply involved in medical education and advocacy. She lectured at the Medical University of Southern Africa (MEDUNSA) – now Sefako Makgatho Health Sciences University – from 1976, holding positions of increasing responsibility, eventually becoming a Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. She dedicated herself to training future generations of black doctors, particularly women, and advocated for improved maternal and child health services.  She also served on numerous professional committees and boards, including the Council of the College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of South Africa, contributing significantly to the development of medical standards and policy.  

Maswime was a vocal critic of the apartheid regime’s discriminatory healthcare policies. She actively participated in organizations advocating for equal access to healthcare for all South Africans. She was particularly concerned with the high rates of maternal and infant mortality within black communities, directly linked to the lack of resources and inadequate facilities.

Throughout her career, Salome Maswime received numerous accolades for her contributions to medicine and her commitment to social justice. In 1993, she was awarded an honorary doctorate in medicine from the University of Natal.  She was also recognised by the Soweto Business Forum for her community service.  

Salome Maswime passed away on 27 April 2006, at the age of 74, in Johannesburg. Her legacy extends far beyond her medical expertise. She remains a powerful symbol of resilience, determination, and dedication to improving the lives of others in the face of immense adversity. She is remembered as a pioneer who broke barriers and paved the way for future generations of black female doctors in South Africa.

title: Lokesh Kanagaraj
text:
Lokesh Kanagaraj was born on September 24, 1986, in Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, India, to Kanagaraj and Vasantha Kanagaraj. His father was a lawyer, a profession that initially held some appeal for Lokesh, but his passion ultimately lay in storytelling through visual media. He received his primary and secondary education at St. Joseph’s Higher Secondary School in Tirunelveli. He then pursued a Bachelor of Engineering in Electronics and Communication Engineering at the PSG College of Technology, Coimbatore, graduating in 2008. While studying engineering, Lokesh wasn’t particularly drawn to his core curriculum, spending much of his time writing short films and scripts, and actively participating in college’s theatre groups. He readily admits that he attended college primarily to appease his parents, with filmmaking being his underlying ambition.

Following graduation, instead of seeking a conventional engineering job, Lokesh moved to Chennai and began working as an assistant director under director Prabu Solomon in 2009. He worked on the sets of the film *Mynaa*, a commercially and critically successful venture released in 2010, gaining invaluable practical experience in the workings of a film set. He continued to hone his skills as an assistant director, working with other prominent filmmakers like Selvaraghavan on *Aayirathil Oruvan* (2010) and later with Durai Senthilkumar on *Ethir Neechal* (2013). This period allowed him to learn about various aspects of filmmaking, from pre-production to post-production, and develop his own distinct cinematic style. 

Lokesh made his directorial debut with *Maanagaram* in 2017. The film, a neo-noir crime thriller shot in Chennai, was made on a modest budget of approximately ₹2.5 crore (around $300,000 USD at the time). It featured a cast of relatively unknown actors and was lauded for its realistic portrayal of urban life, non-linear narrative, and gripping suspense. *Maanagaram* received widespread critical acclaim, winning the Best Direction award at the Filmfare Awards South and the Norway Tamil Film Festival. 

His second film, *Kaithi*, released in 2019, marked a significant turning point in his career. Starring Karthi in the lead role, this action thriller, filmed almost entirely during a single night, was a massive commercial success, grossing over ₹75 crore (approximately $9 million USD) worldwide. *Kaithi* cemented Lokesh’s reputation for crafting intense, fast-paced action sequences and compelling narratives. The film's success also brought him to the attention of larger stars.

In 2021, Lokesh directed *Vikram*, starring Kamal Haasan, Vijay Sethupathi, and Fahadh Faasil. This action thriller, with a budget of around ₹90 crore (approximately $10.8 million USD), became a pan-Indian blockbuster, grossing over ₹400 crore (approximately $48 million USD) globally. *Vikram* was particularly praised for its intricate plot, stellar performances, and its integration into a larger cinematic universe – a concept Lokesh had been subtly hinting at with *Kaithi*.  The film garnered numerous awards, including the National Film Award for Best Editing.

Following *Vikram*, Lokesh directed *Leo* in 2023, starring Thalapathy Vijay.  This action thriller, reportedly made on a budget of ₹300 crore (approximately $36 million USD), broke numerous box office records, becoming one of the highest-grossing Tamil films of all time, earning over ₹600 crore (approximately $72 million USD) worldwide within its first week of release. *Leo* further established Lokesh’s “Lokesh Cinematic Universe” (LCU), connecting characters and plot elements from *Kaithi* and *Vikram*. 

Lokesh Kanagaraj is married to Priya Dharshini, whom he met during his engineering studies.  He is known for his meticulous planning, tight scripting, and preference for working with a core team of collaborators. He is considered one of the leading filmmakers in contemporary Tamil cinema, known for his innovative filmmaking techniques and his ability to deliver commercially successful and critically acclaimed films. He is currently working on *Thalaivar 171*, a film starring Rajinikanth, continuing to expand his LCU.

title: Tappaya Sit-Or
text:
Tappaya Sit-Or, born on November 28, 1972, in Ban Na San, Sanam Chai district, Kalasin Province, Thailand, rose to become one of the most dominant and internationally recognized Muay Thai fighters of his generation. His early life was steeped in the rural traditions of Isan, Thailand’s northeastern region, where Muay Thai is not just a sport, but a cultural practice deeply embedded in village life. From a young age, Tappaya displayed a natural aptitude for the art, beginning his training at the age of eight under the tutelage of his uncle, a local Muay Thai instructor. He initially fought under his birth name, Sittichai Sit-Or, and quickly gained a reputation for his powerful kicks and relentless aggression in local festivals and competitions within Kalasin and surrounding provinces.

By the age of 15, in 1987, Sittichai moved to Bangkok to pursue a professional Muay Thai career. This move was facilitated by his manager, Songchai Ratanachai of the famed Songchai Promotion, who recognized the young fighter's potential. It was at this point he adopted the ring name Tappaya Sit-Or, meaning “Killing Power of Sit-Or,” reflecting his aggressive fighting style.  His early years in Bangkok were spent honing his skills at the Sit-Or gym, a renowned training camp.  

Tappaya’s professional debut was in 1988, and he rapidly climbed the ranks of the Bangkok stadium circuit. He quickly established himself as a fearsome competitor, known for his devastating left kick, earning him the nickname “The King of the Left Kick.”  He fought consistently at the major venues: Lumpinee Stadium and Rajadamnern Stadium, the two most prestigious arenas for Muay Thai in Thailand. 

His breakthrough year came in 1990 when he captured the Channel 7 Stadium 135lb title, defeating Rungnarong Wiwatthananusont. This victory catapulted him to national prominence.  He continued to dominate the 135lb division, securing further victories against prominent opponents like Samran Chaiyaphon in 1991.  However, it was his rivalry with Dieselnoi Chor Thanasukarn that truly cemented his legendary status. 

Between 1991 and 1994, Tappaya and Dieselnoi engaged in five epic encounters, arguably the most significant series of fights in Muay Thai history. Dieselnoi, a larger and more defensively sound fighter, presented a unique challenge to Tappaya's aggressive style.  Tappaya won the first fight in November 1991 at Lumpinee Stadium, claiming the Lumpinee Stadium 135lb title. Dieselnoi won the second and third fights, both by decision, in 1992.  The fourth fight, in July 1993, ended in a controversial draw, sparking heated debate amongst fans.  The final fight in December 1994 saw Dieselnoi again secure a decision victory, effectively concluding their rivalry.

Despite never definitively overcoming Dieselnoi, Tappaya continued to be a force in Muay Thai.  In 1995, he won the Omnoi Stadium 135lb title, showcasing his enduring skill. He also ventured into international competition, achieving success in Japan’s K-1 Grand Prix circuit in 1996, defeating American fighter Andy Souwer. He continued to fight sporadically throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s, though injuries began to take their toll.

Tappaya officially retired from active competition in 2004, at the age of 32, after accumulating a record of over 130 professional fights, with approximately 95 wins (many by knockout).  Following his retirement, he transitioned into coaching, establishing his own Muay Thai gym, Sit-Or Muay Thai, in Bangkok.  He dedicated himself to passing on his knowledge and techniques to a new generation of fighters.  He occasionally appeared at Muay Thai exhibitions and events, remaining a beloved figure within the sport. 

Tappaya Sit-Or passed away on May 23, 2023, at the age of 50, after battling a long illness. His death was met with widespread mourning within the Muay Thai community, both in Thailand and internationally. He is remembered as a fearless warrior, a technical master of the left kick, and a true icon of the sport.

title: Karni Liddell
text:
Karni Liddell, born on November 17, 1975, in Perth, Western Australia, is a former professional netball player and prominent advocate for people living with multiple sclerosis (MS). Her early life was deeply rooted in sport. Her father, Kevin Liddell, was a successful Australian rules footballer who played 168 games for West Perth Football Club, and her mother, Maureen, was a keen netball player. Karni began playing netball at the age of eight, displaying natural talent and quickly progressing through the junior ranks. She attended St. Mary's Anglican Girls' School in Karrinyup, Western Australia, where she excelled in both academics and sport, becoming a school netball captain.

Liddell’s professional netball career commenced in 1994 when she debuted for the Western Australian Swifts in the National Netball League (NNL). Her exceptional defensive skills, particularly as a goalkeeper, quickly drew attention. She represented Western Australia at national level, consistently selected for the Australian Institute of Sport (AIS) squad from 1995 onwards. This AIS involvement was crucial in her development, providing access to elite coaching and training facilities.

Her breakthrough year came in 1997 when, at the age of 21, she was first selected for the Australian Diamonds, the national netball team. She debuted for the Diamonds on November 29, 1997, against New Zealand in a test match in Christchurch. This marked the beginning of a stellar international career. Liddell participated in the 1999 World Netball Championships in Christchurch, New Zealand, where the Australian Diamonds secured the gold medal, cementing her position as a key player. She continued to be a mainstay in the Diamonds team, playing in the 2002 Commonwealth Games in Manchester, England, also winning a gold medal, and the 2003 World Netball Championships in Jamaica, again bringing home the gold. 

Throughout her career, Liddell played predominantly for the Perth Orioles (formerly the Western Australian Swifts) in the NNL, captaining the team for several seasons. She was known for her fierce competitiveness, incredible reach, and ability to intercept passes.  She earned a reputation as one of the world’s best goal keepers, consistently shutting down opposing teams’ attacking plays.  She played over 100 national league games. 

In 2004, at the age of 28 and at the peak of her netball career, Liddell received a devastating diagnosis: multiple sclerosis. The diagnosis forced her to retire from professional netball. This wasn’t an immediate retirement; initially, she tried to manage her symptoms and continue playing, but the disease’s progression ultimately made it impossible. Her last official netball game was in 2004. 

Following her retirement, Liddell dedicated her life to raising awareness and funds for MS research. She became a dedicated advocate, speaking publicly about her experiences and the challenges faced by people living with the condition. In 2006, she established the Karni Liddell Foundation, a non-profit organisation dedicated to supporting MS research and providing support services to individuals and families affected by the disease. The foundation has raised significant funds for research at the Perron Institute for Neurological and Translational Science, focusing on finding a cure for MS. 

Liddell has received numerous accolades for her advocacy work, including the Western Australian of the Year award in 2010 and the Pride of Australia Medal in 2012. In 2019, she was inducted into the Netball Australia Hall of Fame, recognizing her significant contributions to the sport.  She has also served on various boards and committees related to MS and disability advocacy.  Karni Liddell remains a highly visible and inspiring figure, tirelessly working to improve the lives of those affected by MS and demonstrating the power of resilience in the face of adversity.

title: Rana Sanaullah
text:
Rana Sanaullah Khan was born on September 1, 1953, in Faisalabad, Punjab, Pakistan, to a family with a background in agriculture. His father, Muhammad Hanif Khan, was a farmer and his mother, Begum Zaitoon Bibi, was a homemaker. He received his early education at Government Pilot Secondary School, Faisalabad, and later attended Government College, Faisalabad, completing his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1975. He then pursued a Bachelor of Laws (LLB) degree from Punjab Law College, Lahore, graduating in 1978. Following his legal education, he was enrolled as an advocate in the District Courts of Faisalabad in 1979 and later in the Lahore High Court in 1984.

Sanaullah's political career began in the 1980s, aligning himself with the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) under the leadership of Nawaz Sharif. He first entered the Punjab Provincial Assembly in 1985 as a member from Faisalabad, winning on a non-party basis during the non-party elections held under the Zia-ul-Haq regime. He successfully defended his seat in the 1988 elections, this time on a PML-N ticket. He continued to be elected to the Punjab Assembly in 1990, 1993, and 1997, demonstrating consistent support from his constituency. 

His rise within the PML-N was steady. He served as Minister for Law and Local Government in the Punjab provincial cabinet during Nawaz Sharif’s first government in the early 1990s. He held the portfolio of Minister for Food during the 1997-1999 PML-N government, a period marked by efforts to stabilize food prices and improve the public distribution system. He was also appointed as the Provincial Minister for Law and Parliamentary Affairs in 2008, after the PML-N returned to power in Punjab following the 2008 general elections. 

A significant milestone in his career came in 2012 when he was appointed as the Punjab Law Minister, a position he held until 2018. During this time, he played a key role in drafting and implementing several legal reforms within the province, focusing on improving the criminal justice system and strengthening law enforcement. He was particularly involved in the implementation of the Punjab Protection of Women Against Violence Act 2016, a landmark legislation aimed at addressing domestic violence and providing legal protection to women.

In 2018, Sanaullah contested the National Assembly seat from NA-118 (Faisalabad-IV) and secured victory, marking his entry into the national parliament. Following the 2024 general elections, he again won from NA-118 with 138,999 votes, defeating PTI-backed candidate Ali Afzal. He was appointed as Federal Minister for Interior in April 2022, under the Shehbaz Sharif government. This appointment placed him at the forefront of national security and law enforcement matters. 

However, his career hasn’t been without controversy. In August 2019, Sanaullah was arrested by the Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) on charges of possessing 15 kilograms of heroin. He vehemently denied the allegations, claiming they were politically motivated.  He spent several months in custody, and the case remained contentious. In December 2021, the Lahore High Court acquitted him of the drug trafficking charges, citing a lack of evidence and irregularities in the investigation.

Throughout his political career, Rana Sanaullah has been known for his assertive and often outspoken style. He has frequently been a key spokesperson for the PML-N, appearing on television debates and addressing public rallies.  He remains a prominent figure within the party, known for his loyalty to the Sharif family and his strong advocacy for their policies.  As of late 2024, he continues to serve as the Federal Minister for Interior, actively involved in addressing Pakistan’s internal security challenges.

title: Ronaldinho
text:
Ronaldo de Assis Moreira, universally known as Ronaldinho Gaúcho or simply Ronaldinho, was born on March 21, 1980, in Porto Alegre, Brazil. His father, João Moreira, was a former professional footballer who played as a goalkeeper, and instilled a love for the game in his son from a very young age. However, João tragically died in a swimming pool accident when Ronaldinho was only eight years old, a loss that deeply affected him and motivated him to honour his father’s memory through football. Ronaldinho’s mother, Dona Miguelina, worked as a dental assistant and provided strong support for her son’s burgeoning career.

Initially, Ronaldinho excelled in futsal, a five-a-side variation of football played on a hard court, which honed his close control, dribbling skills, and creativity. He played for local futsal club Pão de Açúcar, where his talent quickly became apparent. By age 13, he was already attracting attention from larger clubs, and in 1993, he joined the youth setup at Grêmio Foot-Ball Porto Alegrense, one of Porto Alegre’s major clubs. 

Ronaldinho progressed rapidly through Grêmio’s youth ranks, and made his senior debut on March 26, 1998, in a Copa Libertadores match against Vasco da Gama. He scored his first professional goal later that year, contributing to a promising start to his career with Grêmio. However, financial difficulties at the club led to his transfer to Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) in January 2001 for a fee of €5 million. 

His time at PSG, while showcasing glimpses of his potential, was marked by disciplinary issues and inconsistency. He played 77 games for the Parisian club, scoring 17 goals, but struggled to fully adapt to European football. In November 2003, Barcelona signed Ronaldinho for €27 million, a move that would truly launch him to superstardom.

At Barcelona, under the guidance of manager Frank Rijkaard, Ronaldinho flourished. He quickly became the focal point of the team, captivating fans with his mesmerizing dribbling, incredible technique, and infectious smile. He won his first La Liga title in the 2004-2005 season, scoring 19 goals and earning the FIFA World Player of the Year award, an honour he repeated in 2005.  He was instrumental in Barcelona’s Champions League victory in 2006, scoring a memorable goal against Chelsea in the round of 16.  His performance against Real Madrid at the Santiago Bernabéu in November 2005, where he scored two stunning goals and received a standing ovation from the opposing fans, remains legendary. He finished with 94 goals in 207 appearances for Barcelona.

Ronaldinho also enjoyed success with the Brazilian national team. He was part of the squad that won the 2002 FIFA World Cup in South Korea and Japan, scoring a spectacular free-kick against England in the quarter-finals. He also captained Brazil to victory in the 2004 Copa América.  He earned 97 caps for Brazil, scoring 35 goals.

After five seasons at Barcelona, Ronaldinho’s form began to decline. He transferred to AC Milan in 2008 for €21.5 million, winning the Serie A title in the 2010-2011 season. He returned to Brazil in 2011 with Flamengo, followed by a brief spell at Atlético Mineiro in 2013, where he won the Copa Libertadores. He finished his professional career with a short stint at Querétaro in Mexico in 2014, retiring in January 2018.

Following retirement, Ronaldinho has largely remained involved in ambassadorial roles for football and has participated in exhibition matches. He faced legal troubles in 2020, being arrested in Paraguay for entering the country with a falsified passport. He was later placed under house arrest and eventually released, paying a substantial fine.  He continues to be a globally recognized icon of the sport, celebrated for his artistry and the joy he brought to football fans worldwide.

title: Ted Mack (politician)
text:
Theodore “Ted” Mack was a prominent figure in Washington state politics for over three decades, serving as a state legislator and, most notably, as State Treasurer. He was born Theodore Franklin Mack on January 26, 1935, in Bellingham, Washington, to Franklin and Esther Mack. His father was a logger and his mother a schoolteacher, instilling in him a strong work ethic and a commitment to public service from a young age. Mack grew up in a working-class family, attending Bellingham High School where he graduated in 1953. He then pursued higher education at Western Washington State College (now Western Washington University) in Bellingham, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in Business Education in 1957. While at Western, he was active in student government and a member of the Sigma Chi fraternity.

Following graduation, Mack served in the United States Army from 1957 to 1959, stationed in Germany during the Cold War. Upon his discharge, he returned to Whatcom County and began a career in the insurance business, founding Mack Insurance Agency in 1960. This venture proved successful and allowed him to become deeply involved in the local community. His community involvement led to his first foray into politics. 

In 1972, Mack successfully ran for the Washington State House of Representatives, representing the 42nd Legislative District, which encompassed parts of Whatcom and Skagit counties. He served in the House for four terms, from 1973 to 1981, rising to positions of leadership including Chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee from 1979 to 1981. During his time in the House, he focused on fiscal responsibility and economic development, advocating for policies that supported small businesses and responsible budgeting. He was known as a pragmatic and moderate Democrat, willing to work across the aisle to achieve legislative goals.

In 1980, Mack ran for and was elected State Treasurer, defeating Republican nominee, Richard G. Parsons. He assumed office in January 1981 and would serve in the role for an unprecedented five consecutive terms, remaining Treasurer until January 2001.  During his 20 years as Treasurer, Mack oversaw the state's finances through periods of economic expansion and recession. He prioritized prudent investment strategies, consistently earning high ratings for the state’s bond issues. Under his leadership, the state’s investment portfolio grew significantly, and he implemented measures to improve transparency and accountability in state financial operations. 

A significant achievement during his tenure was the implementation of the Washington State Investment Council in 1991, designed to professionally manage the state's investments and maximize returns. He also championed the creation of the state’s first dedicated college savings program, Washington’s 529 Plan, in 1997, providing a tax-advantaged way for families to save for their children’s higher education.  Mack consistently emphasized the importance of maintaining the state’s strong credit rating, which allowed Washington to borrow money at lower interest rates. He was president of the National Association of State Treasurers from 1994-1995.

Following his retirement as State Treasurer in 2001, Mack remained active in public life. He served on various boards and commissions, including the Washington State Lottery Commission, and continued to consult on financial matters. He authored his memoir, "A Common Sense Approach," in 2004, detailing his experiences in state government and his philosophy of fiscal conservatism. 

Ted Mack was married to Carol Lee Johnson in 1957. They had three children: Michael, Susan, and David. Carol Mack passed away in 2006. Ted Mack died on November 26, 2016, in Bellingham, Washington, at the age of 81, leaving behind a legacy of dedicated public service and financial stewardship. He is remembered as a respected and influential figure in Washington state history.

title: Chris Duffield
text:
Chris Duffield was born on July 18, 1986, in San Diego, California, to parents David and Laura Duffield. He grew up in a relatively athletic household, participating in various sports as a child, including baseball and football, but didn’t initially gravitate towards weightlifting. His early academic focus was on science, and he demonstrated a particular aptitude for mathematics. He attended Westview High School in San Diego, graduating in 2004. While in high school, he began experimenting with weight training as a means to improve his performance in other sports, and this is where his passion for strength training began to develop.
