Faure was sworn in as the fourth President of Seychelles the same day, becoming the first president to assume office through a constitutional transfer of power rather than through an election or coup. He served the remainder of Michel's term and then sought a full five-year term in the 2018 presidential election. 

During his presidency, Faure prioritized good governance, transparency, and the fight against corruption. He initiated reforms to strengthen the rule of law and promote greater accountability in public administration. He also focused on environmental conservation, particularly protecting the Seychelles' marine biodiversity. He increased the area of marine protected areas significantly, committing to protect 30% of Seychelles’ Exclusive Economic Zone by 2020, a goal achieved ahead of schedule. He also launched initiatives to combat climate change and promote sustainable tourism. 

In the 2020 presidential election, Faure was defeated by Wavel Ramkalawan of the United Seychelles party (formerly the SPPP). He conceded defeat gracefully, marking the first peaceful transfer of power from one political party to another in Seychelles’ history. Since leaving office in October 2020, Faure has maintained a relatively low public profile, dedicating himself to private pursuits and occasionally speaking on issues related to governance and sustainable development. He remains a prominent figure in Seychellois politics, and continues to advocate for the continued progress and stability of his nation.

title: Ilhan Omar
text:
Ilhan Abdullahi Omar was born on October 8, 1982, in Mogadishu, Somalia, the youngest of seven children born to Abdullahi Mohamed Hussein and Fartun Abdirahman. Her early childhood coincided with the collapse of the Somali government in 1991, plunging the country into civil war. Facing escalating violence, her family fled Somalia when she was eight years old, initially seeking refuge in Kenya for four years, living in a Dadaab refugee camp. Omar has spoken extensively about the hardships endured during this period, including witnessing violence and experiencing the challenges of life in a crowded, resource-scarce camp. 

In 1995, the family immigrated to the United States, settling in Arlington, Virginia. They were granted political asylum and later became naturalized U.S. citizens. Omar learned English, reportedly within a year, and attended Edison High School in Alexandria, Virginia, graduating in 2001. She then pursued higher education at North Dakota State University from 2003 to 2005, studying political science and international studies. She did not complete her degree, leaving after her grandfather’s illness and to assist her family. Later, she earned a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and International Studies from the University of Minnesota in 2014.

Prior to entering politics, Omar worked as a community organizer and a policy aide. From 2006 to 2009, she worked as a staff writer for the University of Minnesota Student Association. She then served as a senior policy organizer for the Women Organizing Women Political Action Committee, focusing on issues affecting the East African community in Minneapolis. From 2012 to 2015, she was a legislative aide for Minneapolis City Council member Andrew Johnson, focusing on issues like affordable housing and police accountability.

Omar’s political career began in 2016 when she successfully ran for and won a seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives, representing District 60B in Minneapolis. She defeated incumbent Phyllis Kahn, becoming the first Somali-American Muslim woman elected to a state legislature in the United States. During her time in the Minnesota House, from 2017 to 2019, she was a vocal advocate for policies addressing income inequality, affordable housing, and criminal justice reform.

In 2018, Omar ran for and won the election to represent Minnesota’s 5th congressional district, which includes Minneapolis and surrounding areas. She defeated Republican candidate James Newberger with 78.4% of the vote. This victory made her, along with Rashida Tlaib, the first Muslim women elected to Congress. She was sworn into office on January 3, 2019. 

As a member of Congress, Omar has been a prominent figure on the House Committee on Financial Services and the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. She has been a strong advocate for progressive policies, including Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and student loan debt cancellation. She has also been a leading voice on issues of racial justice and immigration reform. 

During her tenure, Omar has faced significant controversy, including accusations of antisemitism stemming from comments she made about Israel and the pro-Israel lobby. These comments drew criticism from both Democrats and Republicans and led to a resolution condemning hate speech being passed by the House of Representatives in March 2019, though it did not specifically mention Omar. She has defended her statements as criticism of Israeli government policies, not of Jewish people.

Omar secured re-election to Congress in 2020, defeating Republican Lacy Johnson with 75.6% of the vote. She was re-elected again in 2022, defeating Republican Ryan Williams with 73.7% of the vote. Throughout her time in office, she has remained a highly visible and influential voice within the Democratic Party, often aligning herself with progressive factions. As of late 2023, she continues to serve as the U.S. Representative for Minnesota’s 5th congressional district, actively participating in legislative debates and advocating for her constituents.

title: Kajal Aggarwal
text:
Kajal Aggarwal was born on June 19, 1985, in Mumbai, Maharashtra, to Vinay Aggarwal, a businessman, and Suman Aggarwal, a homemaker. She has a younger sister, Nisha Aggarwal, who also briefly pursued a career in acting. Kajal’s family relocated to Bangalore when she was young, and she received her primary and secondary education at St. Anne’s High School in Bangalore. She then pursued a Bachelor of Mass Communication degree at Mount Carmel College, Bangalore, completing her studies in 2004. While in college, she began receiving modeling offers and participated in several commercials, including those for brands like Barista and Lavanya Bridal. 

Kajal's entry into the film industry began with the Kannada film *Neenu Dare Sanskara* in 2009, although the film remained largely unnoticed. Her breakthrough arrived shortly after, with the Telugu film *Lakshmi Kalyana*, released the same year. Directed by Teja, the film garnered positive reviews and established Kajal as a promising new actress in the Telugu film industry, Tollywood. 

The year 2010 proved pivotal for her career. She starred in two commercially successful Telugu films: *Darling*, alongside Prabhas, and *Mr. Perfect*, opposite Prabhas again. *Mr. Perfect* was a significant box office hit and earned her critical acclaim for her performance. This momentum continued in 2011 with *Brindavanam*, starring NTR Jr. and Samantha Ruth Prabhu, solidifying her position as a leading actress in Tollywood. 

Kajal ventured into Tamil cinema, known as Kollywood, in 2011 with *Kaththi*, opposite Dhanush, though its release was delayed until 2014.  Her Tamil debut, *Bommarillu*, a remake of the Telugu film of the same name, released in 2008 but didn’t generate significant impact.  She gained prominence in Tamil with films like *Thuppakki* (2012) alongside Vijay, which became a massive commercial success. 

Throughout the 2010s, Kajal consistently starred in high-profile films across both Telugu and Tamil industries. Notable films include *Baadshah* (2013) with Jr. NTR, *Attarintiki Daredi* (2013) with Pawan Kalyan, *Jawan* (2014) with Vijay, *Sardaar Gabbar Singh* (2016) with Pawan Kalyan, and *Khaidi No. 150* (2017) with Chiranjeevi. She demonstrated versatility by taking on diverse roles, from romantic leads to action-oriented characters.

Kajal also expanded her reach into Hindi cinema. Her first Bollywood role was a special appearance in *Kyunkii... Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi* in 2008. She made her full-fledged Hindi debut with *Singham* (2011) opposite Ajay Devgn, which became a commercial success. She followed this with *Special 26* (2013) and *Do Lafzon Ki Kahani* (2016).

In 2020, she appeared in the commercially successful Telugu film *Jaanu*, a remake of the Tamil film *96*.  In 2021, she starred in the Telugu film *Mosagallu*, and the Tamil film *Hey Sinamika*.  She also appeared in *Acharya* (2022) with Ram Charan and Pooja Hegde. 

On October 30, 2020, Kajal Aggarwal announced her engagement to Gautam Kitchlu, a businessman. They married in a private ceremony in Mumbai on October 30, 2020. On January 19, 2022, they announced the pregnancy and on April 19, 2022, they welcomed their son, Neil Kitchlu. 

Over her career, Kajal has received numerous awards, including the South Indian International Movie Awards (SIIMA) Award for Best Actress for *Mr. Perfect* (2011) and the Filmfare Award South for Best Actress – Telugu for *Special 26* (2013). She remains a highly sought-after actress in South Indian cinema and continues to balance her acting career with her personal life. As of late 2023, she continues to appear in films, balancing motherhood with her professional commitments, and enjoys a significant social media presence with over 23 million followers on Instagram.

title: Ayman al-Zawahiri
text:
Ayman al-Zawahiri, born Mohammed Rabie al-Zawahiri on June 19, 1951, in Muhandiseen, Giza, Egypt, was a key figure in the global jihadist movement and, following the death of Osama bin Laden in 2011, became the leader of al-Qaeda. He came from a privileged background; his father, Mohammed Rabie al-Zawahiri, was a physician and professor of pharmacology at Cairo University, and his grandfather, Abdel-Rauf al-Zawahiri, was a scholar at Al-Azhar University, a prominent Islamic institution. This lineage placed Ayman within a relatively elite and intellectual Egyptian family. He received a good education, attending the prestigious Kafr El-Sheikh University where he studied medicine, graduating in 1974.

Zawahiri’s radicalization began during his university years, influenced by the writings of Sayyid Qutb, a leading theorist of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, who advocated for the overthrow of secular governments in favor of a strict Islamic state. He became actively involved with the Egyptian Islamic Jihad (EJI) in the late 1970s, a militant organization aiming to establish such a state in Egypt through violent means. In 1981, following the assassination of Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, Zawahiri was arrested as part of a wider crackdown on Islamic militants. He was accused of involvement in the assassination plot, though evidence of direct participation remained disputed. He spent three years in Egyptian prison, enduring what he later described as torture, which further hardened his extremist views.

Upon his release in 1984, Zawahiri travelled to Pakistan and then Afghanistan, joining the Mujahideen fighting against the Soviet-Afghan War. It was here, in the late 1980s, that he first encountered Osama bin Laden. Zawahiri served as a medical volunteer, providing medical assistance to wounded Mujahideen fighters, and also played a crucial role in recruiting and fundraising for the anti-Soviet effort. He quickly became a prominent figure within the network, respected for his ideological rigor and organizational skills. He established relationships with various militant groups, including the Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Algerian Islamic Salvation Front. 

The end of the Soviet-Afghan War in 1989 saw Zawahiri return to Egypt, but he soon fled again in 1991, facing renewed arrest warrants. He relocated to Sudan, where he continued his work with EJI and deepened his alliance with bin Laden, who had also moved to Sudan. During this period, from approximately 1992 to 1996, the two men laid the foundations for al-Qaeda, formally established in 1988, developing its ideology and infrastructure.  Zawahiri was instrumental in drafting al-Qaeda’s 1998 fatwa declaring war on the United States, a justification for attacks on American targets worldwide.

Following pressure from the United States and Egypt, bin Laden and Zawahiri were forced to leave Sudan in 1996 and relocated to Afghanistan, under the protection of the Taliban regime. Zawahiri became al-Qaeda’s general commander in the late 1990s, effectively serving as bin Laden’s deputy. He oversaw the group’s operations, including the 1998 bombings of the U.S. embassies in Nairobi, Kenya and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, which killed over 200 people. Following the 9/11 attacks in 2001, which al-Qaeda claimed responsibility for, Zawahiri became a key figure in evading capture during the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan.

For the next two decades, Zawahiri remained in hiding, primarily operating in the tribal areas of Pakistan. He communicated with followers through video and audio messages, continuing to direct al-Qaeda’s global network. He focused on expanding al-Qaeda's reach into new regions, particularly in Yemen and North Africa.  After Bin Laden’s death in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on May 2, 2011, Zawahiri formally assumed the leadership of al-Qaeda. 

He continued to issue statements and calls for attacks against Western interests until his death.  On July 31, 2022, Zawahiri was killed in a U.S. drone strike on a safe house in the Sherpur district of Kabul, Afghanistan. The strike, authorized by President Joe Biden, reportedly involved a Hellfire missile launched from an unmanned aerial vehicle. He was 71 years old.

title: Nelson Mandela
text:
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was born on July 18, 1918, in the village of Mvezo, in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa. His father, Gadla Henry Mphakanyiswa, was a local chief and a councilor to the paramount chief of Thembuland. His mother was Nosekeni Fanny, Gadla’s third wife. ‘Rolihlahla’ translates roughly to ‘troublemaker’ in the Xhosa language, a name that would prove somewhat prophetic. Mandela’s early life was steeped in traditional Thembu customs. He received a primary education at a local missionary school, where he was given the English name ‘Nelson’ by his teacher, Miss Mdingane. 

His father died when he was 12, and Mandela became a ward of Jongintaba Dalindyebo, the acting regent of Thembuland. He was groomed for traditional leadership, attending a local Methodist college, Clarkebury Boarding Institute, in 1934, and then Healdtown, a Wesleyan secondary school, in 1937.  In 1940, he began studies at the University College of Fort Hare, the only residential higher learning institute for Black Africans in South Africa at the time. He was expelled in 1940 for participating in a student protest.

Fleeing an arranged marriage, Mandela moved to Johannesburg in 1941, working as a mine security officer and later as an articled clerk in a law firm. He completed his Bachelor of Arts degree through the University of South Africa in 1942 and began studying law at the University of Witwatersrand, graduating in 1943.  It was in Johannesburg that Mandela became deeply involved in anti-apartheid politics. In 1944, he joined the African National Congress (ANC), co-founding the ANC Youth League (ANCYL) with Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu. The ANCYL advocated for more direct action against the increasingly oppressive apartheid regime. 

Mandela rose through the ranks of the ANC, participating in the Defiance Campaign against unjust laws in 1952, for which he was briefly imprisoned and banned from public gatherings. He qualified as an attorney in 1952, opening a law practice with Oliver Tambo, providing affordable legal assistance to Black Africans. Following the Sharpeville massacre in 1960, where 69 unarmed protestors were killed by police, the ANC was banned.  Mandela went underground and co-founded Umkhonto we Sizwe ("Spear of the Nation") in 1961, the armed wing of the ANC, initiating a campaign of sabotage against government and economic targets. 

In 1964, Mandela and several other ANC leaders were arrested and charged with sabotage and other crimes. During the Rivonia Trial, he delivered a powerful four-hour speech from the dock, ending with the iconic declaration, “I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination. I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities.” He was sentenced to life imprisonment on June 12, 1964.

Mandela spent the next 27 years in prison, largely on Robben Island, a harsh penal colony off the coast of Cape Town.  He endured grueling labor and harsh conditions, becoming a global symbol of resistance against apartheid. International pressure for his release grew steadily throughout the 1980s. Finally, on February 11, 1990, at the age of 71, Mandela was released from Victor Verster Prison. 

Following his release, Mandela worked with President F.W. de Klerk to negotiate the end of apartheid and establish a multiracial democracy in South Africa.  Both men were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 for their efforts. In 1994, in South Africa's first multiracial elections, Mandela led the ANC to victory and became the country’s first Black President, serving one term until 1999.  His presidency focused on reconciliation, nation-building, and addressing the vast social and economic inequalities left by apartheid. 

After retiring from the presidency, Mandela continued to advocate for peace, social justice, and human rights through the Nelson Mandela Foundation. He died on December 5, 2013, at his home in Johannesburg, at the age of 95. His legacy continues to inspire movements for equality and justice around the world.

title: Muhammad Qutb
text:
Muhammad ‘Abd al-Salām Qutb was born on October 9, 1906, in the village of Musha, near Asyut in Upper Egypt. His father, Ibrahim Qutb, was a cotton farmer and a descendant of a family with a long history of religious scholarship. The family’s relatively comfortable economic position allowed Muhammad to receive a good education, initially at a local *kuttab* (traditional Islamic school) where he memorized the Quran. He then attended the primary and secondary schools in Asyut, demonstrating exceptional academic aptitude. In 1928, he moved to Cairo to pursue higher education, enrolling in the Faculty of Arts at Cairo University, specializing in Arabic Language and Literature.

Qutb graduated in 1933 with a Bachelor of Arts degree, achieving top honors. He immediately joined the Egyptian civil service and was appointed as an inspector in the Ministry of Education, a role he held for nearly two decades. During this period, Qutb began his literary career, initially focusing on poetry and literary criticism. His early works, such as *Al-Shaytan Yuhakimu Qalbi* (Satan Disputes My Heart) published in 1935, and *Al-Muzirūn* (The Fallen) in 1938, reflected a nationalistic and romantic sensibility, showcasing a concern with social ills and a yearning for a reformed Egypt. 

A pivotal turning point in Qutb’s life occurred in 1948, when he was sent on a government scholarship to the United States to study educational systems. He spent two years in America, residing primarily in Washington D.C. and attending courses at Stanford University, though he did not ultimately pursue a formal degree. This experience profoundly disillusioned him. He was deeply disturbed by what he perceived as the moral decay, materialism, and racial discrimination prevalent in American society. This disillusionment formed the cornerstone of his later ideological development. 

Upon returning to Egypt in 1950, Qutb underwent a noticeable intellectual and political transformation. He resigned from the Ministry of Education and devoted himself fully to writing and political activism. He joined the Muslim Brotherhood in 1953, becoming a leading intellectual and theorist for the organization. His most influential work, *Fi Zilal al-Quran* (In the Shade of the Quran), a comprehensive commentary on the Quran, began publication in 1954 and continued for over a decade, spanning six volumes. This work established Qutb as a major interpreter of Islam in the 20th century, advocating for a return to what he believed were the pure principles of the faith and a rejection of Western influence.

His political critique intensified with the publication of *Ma'alim fi al-Tariq* (Signposts on the Road) in 1964. This book, considered his most radical, argued that contemporary Muslim societies were *jahiliyya* – a term referencing the pre-Islamic “age of ignorance” – and thus required a revolutionary Islamic movement to overthrow them and establish a just Islamic order. This viewpoint positioned him in direct opposition to the secular nationalist government of Gamal Abdel Nasser.

In September 1965, Nasser’s government launched a widespread crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood. Muhammad Qutb, along with numerous other members, was arrested. He was subjected to a lengthy and harsh trial, accused of plotting to overthrow the government. Despite international appeals for clemency, he was convicted and sentenced to death. Muhammad Qutb was executed by hanging on August 24, 1966, at the Cairo prison. His writings continued to exert a significant influence on Islamic movements, particularly among those advocating for political Islam and radical change, long after his death. He left behind a wife, and five children.

title: Joey Jordison
text:
Joseph Henry “Joey” Jordison was born April 26, 1975, in Waukee, Iowa, to Eddie and Billie Jordison. He was raised primarily by his maternal grandmother after his parents divorced when he was young, experiencing a fairly solitary childhood punctuated by a fascination with music, particularly drumming. He began playing drums at the age of eight, initially self-taught, practicing on a kit his parents purchased from a Sears catalog for $300. Early influences included drummers like Neil Peart of Rush and Dave Lombardo of Slayer. Jordison attended Roosevelt High School in Des Moines, Iowa, but did not graduate, later obtaining his GED. 

Jordison's musical journey began in earnest in the early 1990s with various local bands. He played in bands like Modifidious, and later The Rejects, before finding a pivotal connection with Shawn Crahan and Paul Gray. In 1995, this trio, along with Mick Thomson, formed the band that would become Slipknot. Jordison initially auditioned as the band’s vocalist, but quickly transitioned to drums due to his exceptional skill. He also contributed to songwriting, becoming a key creative force within the group. The band’s early years involved a fluctuating lineup and a relentless pursuit of live performance, building a dedicated regional fanbase through numerous shows across Iowa.

Slipknot’s breakthrough came with the self-released 1999 demo album *Mate. Feed. Kill. Repeat.*, which attracted the attention of Roadrunner Records.  Their major label debut, *Slipknot* (1999), catapulted them to international fame. Jordison's drumming, characterized by its aggressive, technically demanding style and the use of a double bass drum setup, became instantly recognizable and a defining element of the band’s sound. He was particularly known for his complex fills and powerful rhythmic foundation. The album sold over 660,000 copies in the US within its first week and earned a platinum certification. 

Throughout Slipknot's most commercially successful period, Jordison co-wrote many of their most popular songs, including "Wait and Bleed," "Left Behind," and "My Plague." He was a central figure in the band’s evolving image, contributing to the creation of their iconic masks and overall aesthetic.  Slipknot released *Iowa* in 2001, which debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 chart, and *Vol. 3: (The Subliminal Verses)* in 2004, further solidifying their status as a leading force in heavy metal.  Jordison also participated in side projects during this time, forming the industrial metal band Murderdolls with Wednesday 13 in 2002. They released their debut album, *Beyond the Cemetery*, in 2002. He also briefly toured with Ministry in 2006, filling in for their drummer.

In December 2013, Slipknot announced Jordison's departure, citing personal reasons.  He later revealed he had been battling a debilitating neurological condition called transverse myelitis, which progressively affected his ability to play the drums.  The condition caused a loss of muscle control in his limbs, significantly impacting his physical capabilities.  He continued to be involved in music, forming the band Vimic in 2014, but the project faced legal challenges from Slipknot regarding its name and musical direction.  

Jordison remained a respected figure in the music community, receiving numerous accolades including a Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance in 2006 for Slipknot’s “Before I Forget.” He was consistently ranked among the greatest metal drummers of all time by publications like *Modern Drummer* and *Rolling Stone*. In 2021, Jordison was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Slipknot. 

Joey Jordison died unexpectedly on July 26, 2021, at his home in Des Moines, Iowa, at the age of 46. The cause of death was later revealed to be due to complications from his transverse myelitis. His passing was met with widespread grief and tributes from fellow musicians and fans alike, recognizing his immense talent and lasting impact on the world of heavy metal. He is survived by his wife, Amy Lee, whom he married in 2004, and his daughter.

title: Daniel Alexander Cameron
text:
Daniel Alexander Cameron was born on January 23, 1986, in Bowling Green, Kentucky, to William Cameron and Lucille Cameron. His father, a retired U.S. Army veteran, owned a small business, while his mother worked as a school teacher. He was raised in a relatively modest household with two younger siblings, and frequently credited his parents with instilling in him a strong work ethic and conservative values. He attended Bowling Green High School, where he was a football player and graduated in 2004 as class valedictorian. 

Cameron’s higher education began at the University of Louisville, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science in 2008. While an undergraduate, he was actively involved in campus organizations, including the Student Government Association, and participated in a summer internship with U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell in 2007. He then attended the University of Louisville School of Law, completing his Juris Doctor degree in 2011. During law school, he served as president of the Federalist Society chapter and was a member of the law review. 

Following graduation, Cameron joined the law firm Stites & Harbison PLLC in Louisville, Kentucky, focusing on litigation and regulatory matters. He worked there from 2011 to 2017, becoming a member of the firm in 2016.  During his time in private practice, he handled a diverse range of cases, including business disputes and white-collar criminal defense. His professional affiliations expanded to include service on the board of directors for the Louisville Bar Association from 2015-2016.

In 2017, Cameron transitioned into public service, accepting a position as Special Assistant to U.S. Attorney Russell Coleman in the Western District of Kentucky. In this role, he assisted with federal investigations and prosecutions, gaining experience in criminal justice matters. He served in this capacity for approximately a year and a half.

Cameron's political career began to accelerate in 2019 when he announced his candidacy for Attorney General of Kentucky. He won the Republican primary election with approximately 58% of the vote, defeating state Representative Jason Nemes. He then faced Democratic nominee Gregory Stumbo in the general election.  Cameron campaigned on a platform emphasizing law and order, support for law enforcement, and his conservative principles.  He won the general election on November 5, 2019, becoming the first African American Attorney General in Kentucky's history, and, at 34 years old, the youngest Attorney General in the state’s history.

As Attorney General, Cameron focused on issues such as combating the opioid crisis, fighting human trafficking, and protecting consumers.  He formed the Kentucky Opioid Abatement Science-Based Results Oversight Committee to oversee the allocation of funds received from settlements with opioid manufacturers and distributors. His office also pursued legal action against companies accused of deceptive practices.

He gained national attention in 2020 for his handling of the investigation into the death of Breonna Taylor, a 26-year-old Black woman who was fatally shot by Louisville Metro Police Department officers during a no-knock warrant execution.  A grand jury presented by his office indicted Brett Hankison, a former Louisville police officer, on three counts of wanton endangerment in the first degree, but did not directly charge any officers with causing Taylor's death. This decision drew significant criticism from activists and civil rights groups who believed the investigation was inadequate and lacked accountability.

In March 2023, Cameron announced his candidacy for Governor of Kentucky, challenging incumbent Democratic Governor Andy Beshear. He secured the Republican nomination in May 2023. On November 7, 2023, Daniel Cameron defeated Andy Beshear, becoming the 63rd Governor of Kentucky with approximately 50.8% of the vote. He is the second Republican governor in nearly 50 years to win the office. His running mate, Robby Mills, will serve as Lieutenant Governor.

title: Ivan Perišić
text:
Ivan Perišić was born on February 2, 1989, in Omiš, a small town in Dalmatia, Croatia, to parents Ante and Marina Perišić. His early life was deeply intertwined with football; he began playing for the local club, Omiš, at the age of 11, showcasing an early talent that quickly drew attention. He didn't initially focus solely on football, however, also playing handball and showing promise in that sport. However, his passion clearly lay with football, and he continued to develop his skills within the Croatian youth system. 

At age 15, Perišić moved to the Hajduk Split academy in 2004, a significant step up in terms of resources and competition. He progressed rapidly through the youth ranks, and on September 15, 2009, he made his senior debut for Hajduk Split in a Croatian Cup match against Croatia Sesvete. His Prva HNL (Croatian First League) debut followed shortly after, on October 24, 2009, against NK Zagreb. He made a notable impact in his first season, scoring two goals in 18 appearances and further solidifying his reputation as a promising young winger. 

In January 2011, Perišić signed with Club Brugge in Belgium for a reported fee of around €4.5 million. He quickly adapted to Belgian football, becoming a key player for Brugge. He played 66 league games for the club, scoring 22 goals and providing 11 assists. His performances attracted the attention of larger European clubs, and in January 2013, he joined Borussia Dortmund in Germany for a reported fee of €5 million. 

However, Perišić’s time at Dortmund wasn’t entirely straightforward. While he contributed to the team’s success, including playing in the 2013 Champions League final which Dortmund lost to Bayern Munich, he wasn’t always a consistent starter under Jürgen Klopp. He made 19 Bundesliga appearances, scoring 5 goals. In July 2013, he was loaned to VfL Wolfsburg for the 2013-2014 season. 

This loan proved transformative. Perišić flourished at Wolfsburg, forming a potent attacking partnership with Kevin De Bruyne. He scored 10 goals and provided 13 assists in 37 Bundesliga appearances, becoming a fan favorite. Wolfsburg then made the move permanent in January 2014, signing him for a reported €8 million. He continued to be a vital player for Wolfsburg, scoring 20 goals in 57 Bundesliga matches during his two seasons there.

In August 2015, Perišić joined Inter Milan in Italy for a fee of approximately €16 million. He spent five seasons at Inter, becoming a consistent performer and a key figure in their squad. He played 254 games for Inter across all competitions, scoring 75 goals.  A highlight of his Inter career was reaching the 2019-2020 UEFA Europa League final, where they lost to Sevilla.

In August 2021, Perišić surprisingly rejoined Tottenham Hotspur in the English Premier League on a free transfer, reuniting with former Inter Milan manager Antonio Conte. He played 46 Premier League games for Spurs, scoring 8 goals.  In July 2023, he made a return to Hajduk Split, the club where his professional journey began, signing a one-year contract.

Internationally, Perišić is a Croatian stalwart. He made his debut for the Croatian national team on March 3, 2009, in a friendly match against Luxembourg.  He has represented Croatia at three FIFA World Cups (2014, 2018, and 2022) and three UEFA European Championships (2012, 2016, and 2020). He was an integral part of the Croatian team that reached the 2018 FIFA World Cup final, where they lost to France.  He scored the equalizing goal in the semi-final against England, a crucial moment in Croatia’s run. As of November 2023, Perišić has earned over 120 caps for Croatia and remains a key player for the national team.

title: Diego Suarez (garden designer)
text:
Diego Suarez was born in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on November 12, 1928, to parents of Spanish and Italian descent. His father, a civil engineer, instilled in him a precise, analytical approach, while his mother, an amateur botanist, fostered a deep love of plants and an understanding of their properties. This dual influence would prove pivotal in shaping his future career. He spent his childhood summers at his maternal grandfather’s estate in the pampas, a vast Argentinian grassland, where he observed and catalogued native flora, developing a keen eye for plant composition and the impact of landscape on atmosphere. 

Suarez initially followed his father’s profession, enrolling in the University of Buenos Aires’ School of Engineering in 1946. However, he found the rigid structure and focus on technical drawing unsatisfying. After two years, in 1948, he abandoned engineering to pursue studies in landscape architecture at the École Nationale Supérieure du Paysage Versailles in France. This marked a turning point, allowing him to combine his inherited analytical skills with his passion for botany. He graduated in 1952 with honors, having been particularly influenced by the work of Russian landscape architect Leonid Sabsovich, whose emphasis on naturalistic planting resonated with Suarez’s own aesthetic.

Upon graduation, Suarez spent several years travelling throughout Europe, working briefly with prominent landscape firms in Italy and Spain. In 1955, he established his own practice, ‘Diego Suarez Diseño de Jardines’, initially based in Paris. His early commissions were largely for private gardens belonging to affluent clients, often aristocrats and industrialists. He quickly gained a reputation for creating sophisticated, subtly dramatic spaces that prioritized a harmonious relationship between architecture and nature. 

A key commission in 1962, the gardens for the Villa Hügel, the former Krupp family estate in Essen, Germany, brought him international recognition. He transformed the formal, somewhat sterile gardens into a series of interconnected spaces inspired by the surrounding Bergisches Land landscape, introducing native plant species and a more relaxed, flowing design.  This project showcased his signature style: a blend of modern functionality, classical proportions, and a meticulous attention to plant selection. 

Throughout the 1970s and 80s, Suarez's practice expanded, undertaking large-scale public projects. He designed the gardens for the Musée Louis Vouland in Lausanne, Switzerland (completed 1978), creating a contemplative space that complemented the museum's collection of Asian art.  He also designed the extensive grounds of the Château de Courances in Essonne, France (1981-1986), restoring historic features while integrating contemporary landscaping techniques.  He completed over 150 projects across Europe, and notably, returned to Argentina in 1992 to redesign the formal gardens of the Casa Rosada, the presidential palace in Buenos Aires. This was a particularly challenging commission, requiring him to balance historical preservation with the needs of a modern government building.

Suarez's work was characterized by a restrained elegance, a sophisticated use of colour and texture, and a strong emphasis on creating gardens that felt both natural and purposefully designed. He avoided ostentation, preferring to let the plants themselves be the stars. He favoured a limited palette of plants, often utilizing variations within a single species to create subtle effects. He also pioneered the use of groundcover plants to reduce maintenance and create a more naturalistic look. 

He authored three books on garden design, ‘Jardins: L’Art de Vivre en Plein Air’ (1983), ‘The Contemporary Garden’ (1990), and ‘Espacios Verdes’ (1998) which were translated into multiple languages and became influential texts for aspiring landscape architects.  He received numerous awards throughout his career, including the Grand Prix du Paysage in France in 1987 and an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires in 2001.

Diego Suarez continued to work well into his eighties, accepting smaller, more private commissions. He died in Paris on July 18, 2015, at the age of 86, leaving behind a legacy of beautifully designed gardens that continue to inspire and delight visitors around the world. His designs remain renowned for their timeless quality and their ability to create spaces that are both aesthetically pleasing and deeply harmonious with the natural environment.

title: Gemma Arterton
text:
Gemma Christina Arterton was born on February 2, 1986, in Gravesend, Kent, England. Her mother, Sally-Anne, worked as a mobile hairdresser, and her father, Shahid John Arterton, was a designer. Her ancestry is diverse; her father was of Pakistani descent and her mother is English. Arterton grew up in a council house in Northfleet, a relatively deprived area, and attended Northfleet Technology College. She described her childhood as happy but acknowledged the financial struggles her family faced. She displayed a passion for performing arts from a young age, joining the local youth theatre group, the Northfleet Players, at the age of eight. She continued her training with the National Youth Theatre, attending workshops during school holidays.  

Arterton initially intended to study fashion at the University of Central Lancashire, but changed her mind and pursued acting. She earned a scholarship to the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London in 2005, graduating in 2008. While at RADA, she supplemented her income with jobs including working as a hostess at a Five Guys burger restaurant.  It was during her final year at RADA that her professional career began to take shape.

Her breakthrough role came in 2008 with the Bond film *Quantum of Solace*, where she played Strawberry Fields, a Bond girl. Though the role was relatively small, it brought her significant public attention.  Almost immediately following, she starred in Guy Ritchie’s *RocknRolla* (also 2008), demonstrating a versatility beyond the glamorous Bond persona.  2009 proved to be a pivotal year. She landed the lead in *Bright Star*, Jane Campion’s biographical romance about the poet John Keats and Fanny Brawne, garnering critical acclaim for her performance. She also appeared in *Clash of the Titans* (2010), a big-budget fantasy epic, further expanding her profile. 

The early 2010s saw Arterton solidify her position as a leading British actress. She starred in *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time* (2010), *Hansel & Gretel: Witch Hunters* (2013), and *Byzantium* (2013), a vampire drama directed by Neil Jordan which saw her reunited with *Bright Star* co-star Ben Whishaw.  She also began to showcase her stage talents, making her West End debut in 2013 as Zaida in Jez Butterworth’s *The River*, receiving positive reviews. 

Arterton actively sought roles that challenged her and moved away from stereotypical “glamour girl” portrayals.  She took on independent projects like *Their Finest* (2016), a critically acclaimed wartime drama where she played Catrin Cole, a screenwriter, and *Vita and Virginia* (2018), in which she portrayed Virginia Woolf. In 2019, she starred in the lead role of Tess in the BBC Two miniseries *Summer of Rockets*, a Cold War espionage thriller. 

Throughout her career, Arterton has also maintained a strong commitment to theatre. She has appeared in productions of *The Duchess of Malfi* (2014) at the Shakespeare’s Globe, earning praise for her performance, and *Saint Joan* (2017) at the Donmar Warehouse. In 2023, she starred in the play *Waste* at the National Theatre.

Arterton married Rory Keenan, an Irish actor, in 2015. They have one daughter, born in December 2018. She has become increasingly vocal on issues surrounding the representation of women in film and the need for greater diversity within the industry. In 2016 she spoke out about the pressure she felt to conform to certain physical expectations in Hollywood and her decision to step back from overtly sexualized roles.  She continues to work consistently in film, television, and theatre, balancing commercial projects with more independent and artistically driven work.  As of late 2023, she resides in London with her family and remains a prominent figure in the British acting scene.

title: Nuh Omar
text:
Nuh Omar, born Omar Nur in Mogadishu, Somalia, on January 12, 1976, was a prominent figure in the Somali-Canadian community and a dedicated advocate for youth empowerment and gang prevention. His life was marked by a dramatic transformation, shifting from involvement in gang activity in his youth to becoming a respected community leader who worked tirelessly to steer young people away from similar paths.

Omar’s early life was heavily influenced by the tumultuous political climate of Somalia in the 1980s and early 1990s. The collapse of Siad Barre’s regime in 1991 plunged the country into civil war, leading to widespread violence and instability. At the age of 14, in 1990, Omar and his family fled Somalia, seeking refuge in Canada. They initially settled in Montreal, Quebec, before relocating to Toronto, Ontario, in 1993. The family’s experiences as refugees and newcomers to Canada shaped Omar’s understanding of marginalization and the challenges faced by immigrant communities.

Upon arriving in Toronto, Omar quickly became involved with the Dixon Bloods, a notorious street gang operating in the city’s west end, specifically in the Jamestown Crescent area. By the mid-1990s, he had risen through the ranks, becoming a significant figure within the gang. His involvement encompassed various criminal activities, and he spent a considerable portion of his youth navigating the complexities and dangers of gang life. However, a pivotal moment occurred in 1998 when he was shot five times during a gang-related altercation. This near-fatal experience served as a catalyst for change.

Following his recovery, Omar began to re-evaluate his life and the impact of his choices. He recognized the destructive cycle of violence and the lack of opportunities contributing to youth involvement in gangs.  In 2003, he founded the Youth Association for Advancement (YAA), a non-profit organization dedicated to providing at-risk youth with support, mentorship, and alternatives to gang life. YAA focused on educational programs, employment training, and recreational activities. 

Omar’s approach was unique in that he leveraged his lived experience and existing relationships within the community, including former gang members, to build trust and credibility. He wasn’t perceived as an outsider lecturing youth, but rather as someone who understood their struggles and could offer a realistic pathway out. YAA quickly gained recognition for its effectiveness in reducing youth violence and promoting positive social change in the Jamestown area.  Over the years, the organization expanded its reach, serving hundreds of young people and receiving funding from various sources, including the City of Toronto and private donors. 

In 2006, Omar received the Queen Elizabeth II Golden Jubilee Medal for his community service. He continued to be a vocal advocate for addressing the root causes of youth crime, emphasizing the need for investment in social programs, education, and employment opportunities. He frequently spoke at schools, community events, and government forums, sharing his personal story and advocating for systemic change.  He also worked closely with the Toronto Police Service, often acting as a liaison between law enforcement and the community, helping to facilitate communication and build trust.

Tragically, Nuh Omar’s life was cut short on November 19, 2014, when he was fatally shot in a targeted attack in the parking lot of a Scarborough restaurant. He was 38 years old. The circumstances surrounding his death remain a subject of ongoing investigation, though it is widely believed to be linked to his past involvement with gangs and his efforts to mediate conflicts within the community.  His death prompted an outpouring of grief and remembrance from across Toronto, with many acknowledging the profound impact he had made on the lives of countless young people.

title: Shin Jea-hwan
text:
Shin Jea-hwan, born on December 28, 1938, in Gwangju, Korea, during the Japanese colonial period, became a pivotal figure in the development of South Korea’s semiconductor industry. His life story is one of relentless dedication to technological advancement and national economic growth. He was born Shin Sang-woo, later adopting Jea-hwan as his formal name. His father, Shin Ho, was a teacher, instilling in him a strong value for education. He experienced hardship during the Korean War (1950-1953), which profoundly shaped his understanding of national vulnerability and the importance of self-reliance through technological prowess.

Shin completed his undergraduate studies in Electrical Engineering at Seoul National University in 1961, graduating at the top of his class. He initially intended to pursue a career in academia, but a government directive encouraging engineering graduates to contribute to national industrialization led him to join the Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) in 1962. However, his ambition lay beyond power generation. Recognizing the burgeoning potential of semiconductors, he applied for and received a government scholarship to study semiconductor technology in the United States in 1965. 

He earned a Master’s degree in Electrical Engineering from Stanford University in 1967, focusing on semiconductor device physics. Furthering his expertise, he continued his studies and obtained a Ph.D. in the same field from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1970. This period proved crucial, exposing him to the cutting-edge research and development happening in Silicon Valley. Returning to Korea in 1970, Shin joined the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI), a government-funded research organization established to foster indigenous technology. 

At ETRI, Shin spearheaded the development of Korea’s first LSI (Large Scale Integration) technology in 1974. This was a landmark achievement, breaking the nation’s reliance on imported semiconductors. He led a team of approximately 30 researchers, overcoming numerous obstacles including limited funding, lack of equipment, and a shortage of skilled personnel. This breakthrough LSI, a 3-bit shift register, was not commercially viable on a large scale, but it demonstrated Korea’s capability and served as a foundation for future development. 

In 1983, Shin became the president of Korea Semiconductor Industry Co., Ltd. (KSIC), a company established with government backing to commercialize the technology developed at ETRI. He faced significant challenges in establishing a competitive semiconductor manufacturing base in a market dominated by established international players like Intel and Texas Instruments.  He focused initially on producing DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) chips, recognizing the growing demand for computer memory.  

Under his leadership, KSIC, later renamed Hyundai Electronics (and eventually SK Hynix after a series of mergers and acquisitions), successfully mass-produced 64K DRAM chips in 1983, becoming the first Korean company to do so. This marked the beginning of Korea’s ascent as a major player in the global semiconductor market.  He continued to drive technological innovation, leading the development of 256K DRAM in 1984 and 64M DRAM in 1992, constantly pushing the boundaries of memory chip technology.  Hyundai Electronics became the world's largest DRAM producer by the mid-1990s, a position it held for several years.

Shin stepped down as CEO of Hyundai Electronics in 1999, but remained involved as Chairman of the Board. He dedicated his later life to promoting science and technology education in Korea. He established the Shin Jea-hwan Foundation in 2002, which provides scholarships and supports research in science and engineering. He authored several books and articles on semiconductor technology and national industrial policy.  

Shin Jea-hwan passed away on October 16, 2016, in Seoul, at the age of 77. He left behind a legacy as the “father of the Korean semiconductor industry,” having transformed Korea from a technology importer to a global leader in semiconductor manufacturing. He received numerous awards and honors throughout his career, including the Gold Tower Order of Industrial Service Merit in 1993 and the Hoam Prize in Science and Technology in 2006. His contribution is widely recognized as being fundamental to South Korea’s economic miracle and its emergence as a technologically advanced nation.

title: Jeremy Corbyn
text:
Jeremy Bernard Corbyn was born on May 26, 1949, in Chippenham, Wiltshire, England, to David and Yvette Corbyn, a couple who met while volunteering during the Spanish Civil War. His father, an electrical engineer, worked at various power stations, leading to a childhood spent moving around rural locations in Shropshire and Somerset. Yvette, a teacher, instilled in him a strong sense of social justice. He was educated at Adams' Grammar School in Newport, Shropshire, leaving in 1966 with one A-Level in geography. He did not attend university, instead undertaking volunteer work.

Corbyn’s political activism began early. In the 1970s, he became involved in the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND), travelling to Aldermaston for annual marches. He joined the Labour Party in 1968 and worked as a trade union official for the National Union of Public Employees (NUPE) from 1974 to 1983, representing postal workers and hospital staff. This period honed his skills in negotiation and advocacy. 

He first entered local government in 1972, being elected to Haringey Council, where he remained a councillor for 35 years, until 2010. His first attempt to become a Member of Parliament came in 1983 when he contested the constituency of North Devon, receiving 12,334 votes – insufficient to unseat the Conservative incumbent. He finally secured election as the MP for Islington North in 1983, a seat he held continuously until 2023. Throughout the 1980s and 90s, Corbyn established himself as a consistently left-wing voice within the Labour Party, frequently voting against the party whip under leaders like Neil Kinnock and Tony Blair, particularly on issues of foreign policy and nuclear disarmament. 

He was a prominent figure in the anti-apartheid movement, serving as treasurer for the Anti-Apartheid Movement in the 1980s. He also actively campaigned against the Iraq War, speaking at numerous protests and consistently voting against military intervention. He was a founding member of the Stop the War Coalition in 2001.  During the New Labour years, Corbyn remained a backbencher, often using his parliamentary time to raise concerns about social inequality, human rights, and environmental issues. He consistently championed causes like Palestinian rights and nationalisation of key industries. 

A surprise contender in the 2015 Labour Party leadership election, following Ed Miliband’s resignation, Corbyn secured 36% of first-preference votes.  After the application of the electoral college system, he won a landslide victory, defeating Andy Burnham, Yvette Cooper, and Liz Kendall with 59.5% of the vote. His leadership marked a significant shift to the left for the Labour Party. 

As leader, Corbyn oversaw a significant increase in party membership, reaching over 550,000 by 2017, the largest in the party’s history. The 2017 general election, called by Theresa May, saw Labour gain 30 seats, denying the Conservatives a majority. While not winning the election, it was widely seen as a successful result for Corbyn, exceeding expectations. However, the 2019 general election resulted in Labour's worst performance since 1935, with the party losing 60 seats.  

Corbyn’s leadership was heavily criticised, particularly concerning his handling of antisemitism allegations within the Labour Party.  A report by the Equality and Human Rights Commission in 2020 found evidence of unlawful harassment and discrimination. He was suspended from the Labour Party in October 2020 following his response to the report, although reinstated as a member in November 2020. He sat as an independent MP after losing the Labour whip again in 2023 following comments regarding the October 7th attacks in Israel. 

Jeremy Corbyn did not stand for re-election in the 2024 general election, and stood down as the MP for Islington North after 40 years in Parliament. He continues to be a vocal advocate for his political beliefs, and remains an active figure in left-wing politics.

title: Jeff Long (athletic director)
text:
Jeffrey “Jeff” Long was born on December 12, 1960, in Mineral Wells, Texas, the son of Charles and Linda Long. He grew up in a family deeply rooted in education and athletics; his father was a high school coach and administrator. This upbringing significantly influenced his own career path. Long attended Mineral Wells High School, where he participated in football and track. He went on to earn a Bachelor of Science degree in physical education from the University of Texas at Austin in 1983. While at Texas, he was a student assistant for the Longhorn football program under legendary coach Fred Akers, a role that provided early exposure to the inner workings of a major collegiate athletic department. He furthered his education, obtaining a Master of Education degree in administration from Oklahoma State University in 1984.

Long’s administrative career began in earnest at Oklahoma State, where he served as a graduate assistant in athletic administration from 1984 to 1986. He then moved to the University of Virginia in 1986, initially as an administrative assistant in the athletic department. Over the next decade, he steadily rose through the ranks, becoming Assistant Athletic Director in 1990 and then Senior Associate Athletic Director in 1995. During his time at Virginia, he oversaw several key areas including sports administration, fundraising, and facility operations. He was instrumental in the planning and execution of significant facility upgrades, including improvements to Scott Stadium and Klockner Stadium.

In 2001, Long accepted the position of Athletic Director at the University of Pittsburgh. He faced considerable challenges at Pitt, including financial constraints and a struggling football program. He hired Walt Harris as head football coach, and under Harris, the Panthers won their first Big East Championship in 16 years in 2004. He also oversaw improvements to the Petersen Events Center, a multi-purpose arena, and initiated fundraising efforts to support athletic programs.

However, Long’s most prominent and impactful role came in 2010 when he was named Vice Chancellor and Director of Athletics at the University of Arkansas. This appointment marked a return to the Southeastern Conference, a league he deeply admired. At Arkansas, he was tasked with elevating the athletic program's profile and competitiveness. He immediately focused on upgrading facilities, overseeing a $160 million renovation of Donald W. Reynolds Razorback Stadium, completed in 2014, and initiating plans for a new basketball arena.

His biggest and most controversial decision at Arkansas was the hiring of Bret Bielema as head football coach in 2013. While Bielema brought stability and improved recruiting, his overall record didn’t meet the high expectations of the Razorback fanbase. Despite investing heavily in the football program, Arkansas struggled to consistently compete at a high level in the SEC West.  Long also oversaw successful programs in other sports, including men’s basketball, which reached the Elite Eight of the NCAA Tournament in 2015 under Coach Mike Anderson, and women’s track and field, which consistently ranked among the nation’s best. 

Long's tenure at Arkansas ended abruptly in September 2017, when he was fired by Chancellor Joseph Steinmetz following a series of disappointing football results and concerns about the overall direction of the athletic department. The decision came after a 1-3 start to the 2017 football season, including a highly publicized loss to North Texas.

Following his departure from Arkansas, Long remained involved in intercollegiate athletics. In 2018, he accepted a position as a consultant with the College Football Playoff selection committee. In 2019, he became the athletic director at Eastern Kentucky University, a role he held until his retirement in June 2023. During his time at EKU, he focused on improving facilities and fundraising for the smaller Division I program.  Throughout his career, Long has been a frequent speaker and advocate for the role of athletics in higher education. He and his wife, Stephanie, have two daughters, Megan and Erin.

title: Jackie Shroff
text:
Jagdish Raj Shroff, popularly known as Jackie Shroff, was born on February 1, 1957, in a middle-class household in Mumbai, India. His father, Kachrulal Shroff, was a Gujarati businessman involved in the cosmetics industry, and his mother, Rita Shroff, was a Turk-Kazakh immigrant. He spent his early years in Teen Batti area of Mumbai, and later the family moved to Nariman Point. His childhood was marked by a rebellious streak and a passion for sports, particularly boxing and weightlifting, skills he would later utilize in his film roles. He attended St. Stanislaus High School in Bandra, where he excelled in sports and drama. He briefly attended Mithibai College but dropped out to pursue his ambition of joining the film industry.

Shroff's entry into Bollywood wasn't immediate. He initially worked as an extra and did odd jobs, including working as a fitness trainer. His first credited role was a small part in the 1973 film *Seeta Aur Geeta*, directed by Ramanand Sagar. However, his breakthrough came in 1982 with the Sunil Dutt-directed *Swami Dada*, where he played the lead role alongside Sridevi. This film established his tough, yet charismatic on-screen persona, a deviation from the traditionally romantic hero archetype prevalent at the time. 

The mid-1980s saw Shroff rise to prominence with a string of commercially successful films. *Hero* (1983), directed by Subhash Ghai, cemented his status as a leading man and earned him a Filmfare Award for Best Male Debut. He followed this with hits like *Andha Kanoon* (1983), *Yudh* (1985), *Karma* (1986), and *Uttar Dakshin* (1987), often portraying characters with a strong moral compass, fighting against injustice. He became known for his distinctive style, a blend of rugged masculinity and street smartness. He frequently collaborated with actresses like Dimple Kapadia, Meenakshi Seshadri, and Mandakini during this period.

Throughout the 1990s, Shroff continued to be a bankable star, diversifying his roles. He took on more challenging characters in films like *Parinda* (1989), directed by Vidhu Vinod Chopra, where his performance as a conflicted gangster earned him critical acclaim and a Filmfare Award for Best Actor. He also starred in romantic dramas like *1942: A Love Story* (1994) opposite Manisha Koirala, which was a significant commercial success.  He ventured into art-house cinema with films like *Gardish* (1993) and *Agni Sakshi* (1996), showcasing his versatility. He also began working in Telugu cinema, gaining popularity in South India.

The early 2000s saw a decline in the number of leading roles offered to Shroff. However, he remained active in the industry, taking on supporting roles and exploring character acting. He appeared in films like *Bhoot* (2003) and *Eklavya: The Royal Guard* (2007). He also began to gain international recognition, appearing in several international films, including *City of Joy* (1992) alongside Patrick Swayze and *The Myth* (2001), a Hong Kong action film directed by Stanley Tong.

In recent years, Shroff has experienced a career resurgence, often portraying memorable supporting characters. He gained considerable praise for his roles in *Dhoom 3* (2013), *Kick* (2014), and *Bharat* (2019). He also starred in the critically acclaimed *Saaho* (2019) and *Radhe Shyam* (2022).  Beyond acting, Shroff is known for his philanthropic work, particularly his involvement with environmental causes. He has been a vocal advocate for organic farming and sustainable living.

Jackie Shroff married Ayesha Dutt in 1987. They have two children, Tiger Shroff, a successful actor, and Krishna Shroff, who is involved in fitness and film production.  He is known for his down-to-earth personality and continues to be a popular figure in Indian cinema, having completed over 200 films across multiple languages over a career spanning five decades.

title: Sami Shalom Chetrit
text:
Sami Shalom Chetrit was born in 1935 in Casablanca, Morocco, to a Jewish family deeply involved in trade union activity. His father, Haim Chetrit, was a prominent figure within the Moroccan General Union of Workers (UMT), a socialist-leaning labor organization, and his mother, Sultana, actively participated in the same circles. This upbringing instilled in Sami a strong sense of social justice and a commitment to working-class struggles that would define his life's work. He received his primary and secondary education in Casablanca, attending the Alliance Israélite Universelle school, a network established to provide modern education to Jewish communities. Even as a teenager, he was engaged in political activism, joining the Moroccan Communist Party in 1952 at the age of 17.

The political climate in Morocco during the 1950s was turbulent, marked by the growing Moroccan independence movement and increasing tensions between various communities. Chetrit became a key organizer for the UMT, specifically focusing on mobilizing Jewish workers within the textile and port industries of Casablanca. He played a crucial role in bridging the gap between the predominantly Muslim workforce and the smaller Jewish contingent, advocating for shared economic interests and solidarity. In 1956, following Morocco’s independence from France, Chetrit faced increasing persecution due to his communist affiliations and Jewish identity. He was arrested in 1957 and spent nearly two years in Moroccan prisons, enduring harsh conditions and interrogation. 

Upon his release in 1959, he immigrated to Israel, settling initially in a ma'abara (transit camp) in Beersheba. He quickly became involved in the Israeli labor movement, joining the Histadrut, the General Federation of Labor. Recognizing the socio-economic marginalization of Mizrahi Jews – Jews who immigrated from Arab countries – Chetrit dedicated himself to fighting for their rights within Israeli society. He began working as a metalworker in the state-owned Israel Railways workshops in Ashkelon, becoming a shop steward and quickly rising through the ranks of the local union.

In the 1960s and 70s, Chetrit spearheaded numerous campaigns advocating for equal pay, better working conditions, and improved housing for Mizrahi workers. He was a vocal critic of the Ashkhenazi-dominated labor establishment, accusing them of perpetuating discrimination and maintaining a class-based hierarchy within the Histadrut. He helped found the “Black Panthers” movement in 1971, a radical protest group composed primarily of young Mizrahi Jews who used direct action and public demonstrations to draw attention to the systemic discrimination they faced. Though the Panthers were often met with hostility from the mainstream media and political establishment, they successfully brought Mizrahi grievances to the national forefront.

Chetrit served as a member of the Knesset (Israeli Parliament) for the Ratz party (Movement for Civil Rights in Israel) from 1977 to 1981. During his time in the Knesset, he focused on legislation aimed at reducing social and economic inequality, promoting workers’ rights, and advocating for a more equitable distribution of resources. He was a strong proponent of peace with the Arab world and criticized the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories. 

After leaving the Knesset, Chetrit continued his activism, writing extensively on issues of social justice, Mizrahi identity, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. He published several books, including "The Fourth Israel" (1988), a seminal work documenting the struggles of Mizrahi Jews in Israel, and "Intifada: The Palestinian Uprising" (1989), offering a critical perspective on the first Intifada. He also contributed regularly to leftist publications and remained a prominent voice for marginalized communities until his death. Sami Shalom Chetrit passed away in Tel Aviv on June 28, 2006, at the age of 71, leaving behind a legacy as a tireless advocate for social justice and equality in Israel.

title: Antonio Leviste
text:
Antonio “Tony” Leviste was born on February 2, 1943, in Manila, Philippines, to a prominent family with deep roots in Philippine politics and business. His father, Fernando Leviste, was a congressman representing Batangas, and his mother, Maria Consuelo Jalandoni, hailed from a wealthy sugar-producing family in Negros Occidental. This background provided young Leviste with early exposure to the workings of Philippine society and a foundation for his future endeavors. He received his primary and secondary education at Ateneo de Manila High School, graduating in 1960. He then pursued a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science at the University of the Philippines, Diliman, completing it in 1964. He continued his studies abroad, earning a Bachelor of Laws degree from Yale Law School in 1968. 

Returning to the Philippines, Leviste began his legal career as an associate at the Angara Abello Concepcion Regala & Cruz Law Offices (ACCRA Law), one of the country’s leading firms. He quickly established himself as a skilled lawyer specializing in corporate law and foreign investments. In 1972, amidst the declaration of Martial Law under President Ferdinand Marcos, he founded his own law firm, Leviste Bersano & Associates, which became a significant player in the Philippine legal landscape. The firm advised numerous multinational corporations on investments in the Philippines, particularly in the energy and infrastructure sectors.

Leviste's career took a significant turn in 1979 when he entered the political arena. He was elected Governor of Batangas, a position he held for three consecutive terms until 1992. As Governor, he focused on infrastructure development, agricultural modernization, and social welfare programs in the province. He spearheaded the construction of roads, irrigation systems, and public markets, contributing to economic growth in Batangas. He also actively promoted tourism, recognizing the potential of the province's natural resources.

While Governor, Leviste simultaneously pursued his business interests, particularly in renewable energy. In 1998, he founded Asian Conservation Technologies Inc. (ACTI), later renamed Alternergy Holdings Corporation. This venture focused on developing wind power projects in the Philippines.  He recognized the country’s potential for wind energy and became a pioneer in the sector.  Alternergy successfully commissioned the San Lorenzo Wind Farm in Daraga, Albay in 2008, which was the first commercial wind farm in the Philippines with a capacity of 50 MW. This project significantly contributed to increasing the country's renewable energy capacity and reducing its dependence on fossil fuels.  

Leviste's success in the renewable energy sector continued with further investments in solar and hydro power. He established Solar Philippines, a company that became a major player in the country’s solar energy market.  He also developed several small-scale hydro power plants.  In 2011, Alternergy secured a $50 million investment from the Macquarie Infrastructure and Real Assets (MIRA) fund, demonstrating the international confidence in the company’s potential.

However, Leviste’s career was marred by controversy. In 2010, he was convicted of facilitating the murder of his wife, Ma. Cecilia “Cecile” Leviste, in 2007. The case involved a complex web of accusations and counter-accusations. He was initially sentenced to life imprisonment but was granted executive clemency by President Benigno Aquino III in 2015, citing his age, health condition, and contributions to renewable energy.  This decision was highly controversial and sparked public debate.

Following his release, Leviste largely retreated from public life, focusing on his family and continuing to advise Alternergy. He remained a significant shareholder in the company, although his direct involvement in its day-to-day operations diminished.  He passed away on November 11, 2023, at the age of 80, leaving behind a complex legacy as a successful businessman, a political figure, and a controversial figure in Philippine history. He is survived by his children and grandchildren.

title: José Hernández Delgadillo
text:
José Hernández Delgadillo was born on October 12, 1928, in the small rural community of La Labor de los García, Zacatecas, Mexico. His parents, Refugio Hernández and María del Carmen Delgadillo, were both teachers who instilled in him a deep appreciation for education and a strong sense of social justice. Life in La Labor was characterized by poverty and limited access to resources, experiences that profoundly shaped Hernández Delgadillo’s later commitment to improving conditions for marginalized communities. He received his primary education in his hometown, displaying an early aptitude for learning and a particular interest in mathematics and science. 

In 1946, he moved to Zacatecas city to attend the Preparatory School of the Universidad Autónoma de Zacatecas. He then enrolled in the National School of Agriculture (Escuela Nacional de Agricultura) at Chapingo, State of Mexico, graduating in 1952 as an Agricultural Engineer with a specialization in phytotechnics – the branch of agriculture dealing with the improvement of plant species. This education provided him with the technical foundation for his future work in agricultural development. 

Hernández Delgadillo began his professional career in 1953 as an agronomist for the Secretariat of Agriculture and Livestock (Secretaría de Agricultura y Ganadería) in the state of Jalisco. He quickly recognized the limitations of conventional agricultural practices in addressing the needs of small farmers, particularly regarding the availability of affordable and effective pest control. This realization led him to dedicate himself to the study and promotion of biological control methods, specifically focusing on the use of natural enemies to manage agricultural pests. 

In 1965, he was appointed head of the Department of Biological Control of Pests in the Secretariat of Agriculture and Livestock, a position he held for over two decades. During this time, he pioneered the mass rearing and release of parasitoid wasps, particularly *Encarsia formosa*, for the control of whitefly (*Bemisia tabaci*) in greenhouse vegetable crops across Mexico.  This innovative approach dramatically reduced reliance on chemical pesticides, improving both crop yields and the health of agricultural workers. He established several production facilities for these beneficial insects, including a major laboratory in Tecomán, Colima, in 1972, which became a model for biological control programs throughout Latin America.

His work extended beyond whitefly control. He successfully implemented biological control strategies for other pests, including aphids, thrips, and leafminers, impacting the production of tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, and other high-value crops.  Hernández Delgadillo’s research and practical applications led to a significant reduction in pesticide use in Mexico, estimated to be a decrease of over 60% in greenhouse vegetable production by the late 1980s. He authored over 100 scientific publications, including articles in international journals and technical manuals for farmers, disseminating his knowledge and techniques widely. 

In 1985, he was awarded the prestigious Premio Nacional de Ciencias y Artes in the field of Technology, Arts and Sciences, recognizing his groundbreaking contributions to agricultural science. He received an honorary doctorate from the Universidad Autónoma de Chapingo in 1991.  He continued to consult with agricultural organizations and governments throughout Latin America, sharing his expertise and promoting sustainable pest management practices. 

Following his retirement from the Secretariat in 1992, Hernández Delgadillo remained active in agricultural research and education. He established a private consulting firm, offering technical assistance to farmers and agricultural businesses. He also dedicated time to mentoring young scientists and promoting the importance of ecological agriculture. José Hernández Delgadillo passed away on November 16, 2018, in Mexico City at the age of 90, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneer of biological control and a champion of sustainable agriculture in Mexico and beyond. His work continues to influence pest management practices and inspires a new generation of agricultural scientists.

title: Sandra Pisani
text:
Sandra Pisani was born on February 22, 1936, in Valletta, Malta, to Giuseppe and Concetta (née Vella) Pisani. Her father was a shipwright and her mother a homemaker, and she grew up in a modest, close-knit family alongside two brothers, Joseph and Emmanuel. Valletta, the capital city, provided a culturally rich environment, and Pisani demonstrated an early aptitude for languages and a keen interest in the arts, particularly music and theatre. She received her primary education at the primary school in Valletta and then attended the Regina Margherita Secondary School for Girls, completing her studies in 1954. 

Following her secondary education, Pisani initially pursued a position as a clerical officer within the Maltese government, working at the Department of Education between 1954 and 1960. However, her passion lay elsewhere. She had begun taking private singing lessons, recognizing a powerful soprano voice that needed development. In 1960, she secured a scholarship from the Italian government to study at the Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia in Rome, one of Italy’s most prestigious music conservatories. She studied under the renowned tenor Fernando Corelli, focusing on operatic technique and repertoire. 

Pisani’s professional operatic debut occurred in 1964 at the Teatro dell'Opera di Roma, portraying the role of Mimì in Giacomo Puccini’s *La Bohème*. This marked the beginning of a remarkably successful international career spanning three decades. She quickly gained recognition for her dramatic intensity, vocal power and compelling stage presence. She performed extensively throughout Italy, appearing at theatres in Naples, Palermo, Florence, and Venice, often in leading roles such as Violetta in *La Traviata*, Leonora in *Il Trovatore*, and Aida in Verdi’s *Aida*. 

Her international career broadened in the late 1960s and 1970s. She made her debut at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, London, in 1968 as Leonora, and continued to perform there regularly until 1982, accumulating a devoted following among British opera enthusiasts. She also performed at the Deutsche Oper Berlin (1971), the Teatro Colón in Buenos Aires (1973), and the San Francisco Opera (1976), where she was particularly lauded for her interpretation of Santuzza in Mascagni’s *Cavalleria Rusticana*. Throughout the 1970s, she frequently collaborated with celebrated conductors such as Carlo Maria Giulini, Herbert von Karajan, and James Levine.

Pisani’s discography includes several recordings, most notably a 1976 Decca recording of *Cavalleria Rusticana* with Plácido Domingo and Sherrill Milnes, conducted by Carlo Rizzi. This recording remains a highly regarded interpretation of the opera. She also recorded excerpts from *La Traviata* and *Aida*.  She was awarded the Gold Medal for Arts and Culture by the Maltese government in 1980, recognizing her contribution to the promotion of Maltese culture internationally. 

In 1984, at the age of 48, Pisani made the decision to retire from the operatic stage. She cited a desire to spend more time with her family and to focus on teaching. She returned to Malta and established a private vocal studio in Valletta, dedicating herself to nurturing young Maltese talent. She became a highly respected vocal coach, mentoring numerous singers who went on to pursue professional careers. She served as a judge for several national and international singing competitions, including the Concours International de Chant de la Ville de Toulouse in France. 

Sandra Pisani never married and had no children. She remained a prominent figure in the Maltese cultural scene, often attending concerts and theatrical performances. She continued to give masterclasses and workshops until her health began to decline in the early 2000s.  Sandra Pisani passed away on November 18, 2019, in Valletta, Malta, at the age of 83, leaving behind a legacy as one of Malta’s most celebrated operatic artists. A state funeral was held in her honour at St. John's Co-Cathedral in Valletta, attended by dignitaries and admirers from across the country.

title: Paul Anka
text:
Paul Anka was born Paul Robert Anka on July 30, 1941, in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, to Andrew Anka, a Syrian-Lebanese immigrant who worked as a foreman at a textile mill, and his wife, Edith (née Villeneuve), of French-Canadian descent. He was the eldest of three children, with a younger brother, Edward, and a sister, Jane. Anka’s early childhood was marked by frequent moves due to his father’s work, including stints in Ottawa, Montreal, and finally, settling in Ottawa when Paul was ten. He began taking piano lessons at age eight and demonstrated a precocious talent for music, initially leaning towards classical music.
