Despite his immense popularity, Gaytán faced personal struggles with alcoholism throughout much of his adult life. This battle, though often hidden from the public, took a toll on his health.  In the late 1970s, his film roles became less frequent as his health deteriorated. He made his final film appearance in "El Compadre Gallardo" in 1978.  

José “Chacho” Gaytán died on January 11, 1980, in Mexico City, at the age of 59, due to complications from cirrhosis of the liver. His death was widely mourned by the Mexican public.  He left behind a legacy as one of Mexico’s most beloved comedians, remembered for his authentic portrayal of the common Mexican and his ability to bring laughter to generations. Although he never received major international recognition, within Mexico, he remains a cultural icon, and his films continue to be enjoyed and celebrated today.

title: Maya Yoshida
text:
Maya Yoshida was born on August 29, 1988, in Nagasaki, Japan, to a Japanese mother and an American father, James Yoshida, who was a former basketball player. This mixed heritage makes him one of the few biracial players to represent Japan in international football. His early life saw him move frequently as his father’s work involved regular relocations. He spent time in the United States, including a period in California, before returning to Japan and eventually settling in Nagoya. It was during his time in the United States that his interest in football, or soccer as it’s commonly known there, truly blossomed.

Yoshida’s formal football journey began in the youth academy of Nagoya Grampus Eight, a J1 League club, in 1999, at the age of 11. He progressed through the youth ranks, demonstrating consistent defensive ability and a commitment to the team. He officially joined the senior team in 2007, making his J1 League debut on March 17th, 2007, against Urawa Red Diamonds. His initial appearances were limited, however, and he was often utilized as a defensive midfielder rather than his preferred centre-back position. 

The 2008 season saw Yoshida become a more regular fixture in the Nagoya Grampus Eight starting eleven, playing 27 league matches and demonstrating his growing capabilities. This form attracted the attention of clubs in Europe, and in January 2010, he signed for VVV-Venlo in the Dutch Eredivisie. This move marked a significant step in his career, providing him with the opportunity to test himself in a highly competitive European league. 

He quickly adapted to the physicality and tactical demands of European football, becoming a key player for VVV-Venlo. His performances earned him a transfer to Southampton in the English Premier League in August 2012, joining the club for a reported fee of around £3 million. Yoshida became the second Japanese player to sign for Southampton, following in the footsteps of Kim Do-Heon.

At Southampton, Yoshida established himself as a reliable and versatile defender, capable of playing both centre-back and right-back. He made his Premier League debut on September 15, 2012, against Arsenal. Although initially competing for a place in a crowded defensive lineup, he consistently proved his worth with solid performances and a professional attitude. He made over 190 appearances for Southampton across all competitions, contributing to the club’s consistent Premier League form during his eight-year spell. A particularly memorable moment came in November 2019, when he scored a dramatic late winning goal against Watford, sparking jubilant scenes.

Internationally, Yoshida has been a cornerstone of the Japan national team. He earned his first senior cap on September 10, 2010, in a friendly match against Guatemala. He has represented Japan at three FIFA World Cups – 2014 in Brazil, 2018 in Russia, and 2022 in Qatar – captaining the side in both 2018 and 2022. He also played a crucial role in Japan’s 2019 AFC Asian Cup campaign, where they reached the final, losing to Qatar. As of November 2023, he has amassed over 126 caps for his country, placing him among Japan’s most capped players.

After his contract with Southampton expired in the summer of 2020, Yoshida joined Schalke 04 in Germany on a one-year deal. Following a single season with Schalke, he moved to Italian Serie A club Sampdoria in August 2021. In July 2023, he returned to the J1 League, signing for Kashiwa Reysol.  

Throughout his career, Yoshida has been praised for his leadership qualities, his dedication to hard work, and his humble demeanor. Beyond football, he is known for his philanthropic work, supporting various charitable causes, and is fluent in English, Japanese and Dutch. He remains a respected figure both on and off the pitch, embodying professionalism and a strong commitment to the sport.

title: Rory Tapner
text:
Rory George Tapner was born on 22nd March 1960 in Nairobi, Kenya, to Brigadier John Tapner and his wife, Rosemary. His father served in the King’s African Rifles, and Rory’s early childhood was shaped by life in East Africa, attending the Duke of York School in Langata, Nairobi. This period instilled in him a strong connection to the natural world and a pragmatic, outdoorsy disposition. In 1972, the family relocated to England, settling in Gloucestershire, where Tapner completed his education at Cheltenham College, a boarding school with a strong tradition of rugby. He was a keen sportsman throughout his school years, demonstrating a particular aptitude for the game, and played for the school's 1st XV. 

Following school, Tapner embarked on a career in the City of London, joining Barings Bank in 1981 as a graduate trainee. He quickly proved himself a capable and insightful analyst, moving into the bank’s futures division. This was a period of significant growth and increasing complexity in financial markets, and Tapner thrived in the environment. He rose through the ranks, becoming a director in 1990 and subsequently managing director in 1994, responsible for overseeing Barings’ global options trading business. 

However, Tapner’s tenure at Barings is inextricably linked to the collapse of the bank in 1995, caused by the fraudulent trading activities of Nick Leeson in Singapore. While Tapner was not directly involved in Leeson’s actions, he was a key figure in the subsequent inquiry. He testified extensively before the Bank of England’s investigation, providing detailed accounts of the bank’s risk management procedures and the lack of oversight that allowed Leeson’s losses to escalate. The inquiry, led by Lord Justice Bingham, largely cleared Tapner of personal responsibility for the collapse, acknowledging his attempts to raise concerns about the Singapore operation. Nonetheless, the scandal cast a long shadow over his career.

After leaving Barings in the wake of its acquisition by ING in 1995, Tapner joined Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) in 1996, initially as a consultant before becoming head of European Equity Derivatives. He spent seven years at DMG, building a respected team and contributing to the bank’s expansion in the derivatives market. In 2003, he moved to Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB) as global head of equity derivatives, a position he held for five years. This role further solidified his reputation as a leading expert in the financial derivatives field, managing a substantial team and overseeing significant trading volumes.

In 2008, Tapner accepted the position of Chief Executive Officer of Turquoise, the pan-European multilateral trading facility (MTF) backed by the London Stock Exchange. He was tasked with establishing Turquoise as a viable competitor to established exchanges and dark pools. Under his leadership, Turquoise saw significant growth in trading volumes, particularly in complex derivative products. He successfully navigated the challenges of regulatory changes following the 2008 financial crisis, positioning Turquoise as a key player in the evolving European trading landscape. He stepped down from his role at Turquoise in December 2015.

Following his departure from Turquoise, Tapner became involved in several non-executive roles. He served as a non-executive director of MarketAxess Europe Ltd, a leading electronic trading platform, and as a member of the advisory board of several fintech companies. He also dedicated time to philanthropic pursuits, supporting conservation efforts in Africa, reflecting his early upbringing in Kenya. 

Rory Tapner currently resides in Gloucestershire, England. He remains a private individual, rarely granting interviews, but continues to be respected within the financial industry for his expertise and integrity. He is married to Sarah, and they have two children. He maintains a keen interest in rugby and continues to follow financial market developments closely.

title: John Forbes Nash Jr.
text:
John Forbes Nash Jr. was born on April 13, 1928, in Bluefield, West Virginia, to John Forbes Nash Sr., a dominating and practical electrical engineer, and Margaret Virginia Steele, a former high school English teacher. His early life was marked by a somewhat solitary nature and an intense focus on intellectual pursuits, despite a perceived lack of early academic brilliance. He wasn’t a precocious child, but displayed a marked aptitude for mathematics and chemistry, often experimenting with chemical mixtures much to his mother’s concern. He received his high school diploma from Carnegie Institute of Technology (now Carnegie Mellon University) in 1945, having earned a scholarship based on a mathematics competition.

Nash attended Carnegie Tech on a George Westinghouse Scholarship, initially intending to study chemical engineering, but quickly switching to mathematics after recognizing its greater appeal. He earned both his Bachelor of Science (1948) and Master of Arts (1949) degrees from Carnegie Tech, remaining there to begin doctoral studies under the guidance of Richard Duffin. His doctoral research focused on the theory of non-cooperative games, a relatively unexplored field at the time. 

In 1950, Nash left Carnegie Tech without completing his PhD to accept a position as a post-doctoral fellow at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). It was during this time, and further developed during a visiting scholarship at Princeton University in 1951, that he formulated his most famous contribution: the Nash Equilibrium. This concept, detailed in his 27-page paper "Two-Person Cooperative Games," published in *Econometrica* in 1951, revolutionized game theory. It posits that in any game involving multiple players, there exists a stable state where no player can benefit by unilaterally changing their strategy, assuming the other players’ strategies remain constant. This had profound implications not only for mathematics and economics, but also political science, evolutionary biology and artificial intelligence. 

Nash continued his academic career at MIT until 1956, then joined the faculty of the University of Chicago. During this period, he also made significant contributions to differential geometry, notably the Nash embedding theorems, published in 1954. These theorems proved that any Riemannian manifold could be isometrically embedded into a Euclidean space of a sufficiently high dimension. This work established him as a leading figure in pure mathematics. 

However, Nash’s career and life took a tragic turn in the late 1950s. Beginning around 1959, he began to exhibit symptoms of paranoid schizophrenia. These increasingly debilitating delusions led to erratic behavior, culminating in a formal diagnosis and several periods of hospitalization, including stays at the Menninger Clinic in Topeka, Kansas, and McLean Hospital in Belmont, Massachusetts. He was largely unable to work productively during the 1960s and 70s, cycling through periods of lucidity and severe mental illness.

Despite his condition, Nash continued to pursue mathematical ideas, albeit in a highly unconventional manner. He remained a faculty member at Princeton University, though his position was largely honorary. In the 1990s, his symptoms began to recede, allowing him to resume more active research.  He was remarkably able to regain a degree of clarity and engage in mathematical thought despite the lingering effects of his illness.

Recognition for his groundbreaking work came late in life. In 1994, Nash shared the John von Neumann Theory Prize with John Harsanyi. The pinnacle of his career arrived in 2006 when he was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, jointly with Roger Myerson and Reinhard Selten, for his contributions to game theory. 

John Nash died on May 23, 2015, at the age of 86, in Princeton, New Jersey, following a taxi accident. He and Alicia Harper, a Swiss physicist whom he married in 1957 and divorced in 1982, remarried in 2001. His life story, and particularly his struggle with schizophrenia, achieved wider public recognition through the 2001 biographical drama *A Beautiful Mind*, based on Sylvia Nasar’s 1998 biography of the same name.

title: Bastian Schweinsteiger
text:
Bastian Schweinsteiger was born on August 1, 1984, in Oberaudorf, West Germany, to Monika and Erhard Schweinsteiger. His father, Erhard, was a professional footballer and a German Cup winner with Bayern Munich in 1976, while his mother was a handball player. This sporting background heavily influenced Bastian’s early life, and he began playing football for TSV 1860 Rosenheim in 1988, at the age of four, following in his father’s footsteps. He progressed quickly through the youth ranks, initially playing as a left-winger, before transitioning to a more central role.

In 1998, at 14 years old, Schweinsteiger joined the youth academy of Bayern Munich, a move that solidified his path towards professional football. He initially struggled with homesickness but persevered, showcasing his dedication and talent. He rose through the Bayern youth teams, becoming a key player for the club’s reserve team, Bayern Munich II, in the Regionalliga Süd, making his debut in 2002.

His breakthrough into the first team came under coach Ottmar Hitzfeld in November 2002, making his Bundesliga debut against 1. FC Nürnberg on November 3, 2002, at the age of 18. He scored his first Bundesliga goal on December 14, 2002, against Hamburger SV.  Schweinsteiger quickly became a regular fixture in the Bayern midfield, renowned for his tackling, passing range, and stamina. 

Over the next thirteen seasons with Bayern Munich, he became a club legend. He won eight Bundesliga titles (2003, 2005, 2006, 2008, 2010, 2013, 2014, 2016), seven DFB-Pokal cups (2003, 2005, 2006, 2008, 2010, 2013, 2014), and the UEFA Champions League in 2013, a victory secured against Borussia Dortmund at Wembley Stadium. He also won the FIFA Club World Cup in 2013. He made 500 appearances for Bayern Munich across all competitions, scoring 68 goals. 

Schweinsteiger also enjoyed a highly successful international career with Germany. He earned his first senior cap on September 6, 2004, against Romania under coach Jürgen Klinsmann. He became a crucial member of the German national team, participating in the 2006, 2010, and 2014 FIFA World Cups, and the 2008 and 2012 UEFA European Championships. He was a key figure in Germany’s run to the final of the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, scoring a crucial goal against Algeria in the round of 16.  The team ultimately defeated Argentina 1-0 in extra time, securing Germany's fourth World Cup title. He earned 121 caps for Germany, scoring 24 goals, and captained the national team on multiple occasions. He announced his retirement from international football on August 31, 2016.

In March 2017, Schweinsteiger moved to Major League Soccer, joining Chicago Fire for a reported $2.5 million transfer fee. He made his debut for the Fire on April 8, 2017, against Philadelphia Union. He quickly became a fan favorite and a key player for Chicago, contributing significantly to their improved performance. He played 85 games for the Fire, scoring 25 goals.

On October 29, 2019, Schweinsteiger announced his retirement from professional football. He returned to Bayern Munich in a non-playing role as an ambassador for the club, utilizing his experience and knowledge to represent Bayern globally. 

Beyond football, Schweinsteiger is known for his charitable work, supporting various organizations focused on children's welfare and social causes. He married Ana Ivanović, a former professional tennis player, in July 2016. They have two sons.  He has also become a popular media personality, appearing as a football pundit and commentator.

title: Flávio Rocha
text:
Flávio Rocha was born on October 16, 1951, in Mossoró, Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil, into a family deeply rooted in the region’s economic and political landscape. His father, Dix-Sept Rosado Rocha, was a prominent politician, serving as a state deputy and mayor of Mossoró, while his mother, Maria do Carmo Rocha, played a significant role in the family’s business ventures. This upbringing instilled in Flávio a strong sense of entrepreneurship and civic responsibility. He received his primary and secondary education in Mossoró, before moving to Recife to study Law at the Universidade Federal de Pernambuco (UFPE), graduating in 1974. Though qualified as a lawyer, he quickly pivoted away from a legal career, drawn instead to the burgeoning retail sector.

Rocha’s business journey began in 1976, alongside his brothers, with the founding of Casa dos Gas, a small gas distribution company in Mossoró. Recognizing an opportunity to address the needs of a rapidly growing population in the interior of Rio Grande do Norte, he shifted focus towards retail in 1982. This marked the birth of Franquias Rio Grande (FRG), initially a single store selling household appliances, furniture and building materials. The store’s success was predicated on a novel business model for the region: offering credit directly to customers, particularly those in the working class who lacked access to traditional banking services. This “clientela” system, offering personalized credit terms and installment plans, proved exceptionally popular.

Throughout the 1980s and 90s, Rocha aggressively expanded FRG, opening new stores across the state of Rio Grande do Norte and then into neighboring states like Ceará and Paraíba. He strategically targeted smaller cities and towns underserved by larger retail chains. In 1998, FRG underwent a significant rebranding, becoming “Bemol,” a name intended to be more nationally recognizable. This rebranding coincided with a substantial investment in logistics and distribution infrastructure, including a large distribution center in Extremoz, near Natal, covering 60,000 square meters. 

Bemol continued its expansion into the 2000s, becoming one of the largest retail chains in the Northeast of Brazil. By 2010, the company operated over 300 stores, employing more than 10,000 people and generating an annual revenue exceeding R$4 billion (approximately $2 billion USD at the time).  Rocha’s success wasn’t solely focused on expansion; he implemented innovative employee programs, including profit-sharing initiatives and extensive training, which contributed to a high degree of employee loyalty. He also invested heavily in social responsibility projects in the communities where Bemol operated, focusing on education and healthcare. 

Beyond Bemol, Rocha diversified his investments. In 2008, he acquired a controlling stake in J. Macedo, a regional department store chain based in Fortaleza, Ceará.  He also ventured into the media sector, founding Nativa Comunicações, which launched the RNTV network in 2010, a regional television station.  This demonstrated a broader ambition to influence public opinion and contribute to the cultural landscape of the Northeast.

In 2016, facing financial difficulties exacerbated by Brazil’s economic recession and a complex debt restructuring, Bemol filed for judicial recovery. This was a significant setback for Rocha and the company. Despite efforts to restructure, Bemol ultimately filed for bankruptcy in 2019, with debts exceeding R$2.5 billion.  The collapse of Bemol resulted in widespread job losses and economic disruption in the regions it served.

Following the bankruptcy, Rocha largely withdrew from the public eye. While legal proceedings related to Bemol’s debts continued, he remained a resident of Mossoró. He focused on managing his remaining assets and involved himself in philanthropic activities through the Fundação Roberto Rocha, named after his brother who died in 1992.  Flávio Rocha passed away on June 24, 2023, in Natal, Rio Grande do Norte, at the age of 71, leaving behind a complex legacy as a pioneering entrepreneur who profoundly impacted the retail landscape of Northeast Brazil, but also experienced a dramatic business downfall.

title: Zewde Gebre-Sellassie
text:
Zewde Gebre-Sellassie was born on April 22, 1936, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to Gebre-Sellassie Debessa and Wozero Tenagne Worqineh. His father was a prominent lawyer and political figure who served as Minister of Justice under Emperor Haile Selassie I, deeply influencing Zewde’s early exposure to Ethiopian law and governance. Zewde received his primary and secondary education at the prestigious General Wingate School in Addis Ababa, a British-founded institution catering to the Ethiopian elite. He continued his education abroad, attending the University of Cambridge in England, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics in 1958. He subsequently pursued legal studies, obtaining a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) from University College London in 1960 and was called to the Bar at Gray’s Inn in 1961. 

Returning to Ethiopia, Zewde began his professional career as a legal advisor in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry in 1961. He quickly ascended through the ranks, demonstrating a keen intellect and dedication to legal reform. In 1963, he joined the Faculty of Law at Haile Selassie I University (now Addis Ababa University), beginning a long and influential academic career. He lectured on commercial law, constitutional law, and international law, shaping generations of Ethiopian legal professionals. He simultaneously continued his advanced studies, earning a Master of Laws (LL.M.) degree from Yale Law School in the United States in 1967, specializing in international trade law. 

Zewde’s contributions to Ethiopian law extended beyond academia. He served as a legal consultant to several government ministries and international organizations, including the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), where he advised on trade and development policies. A pivotal moment in his career arrived in 1974 when, following the downfall of Emperor Haile Selassie I, he was appointed as the first President of the Supreme Court of Ethiopia under the Derg regime, the military junta that seized power. This was a particularly challenging position, requiring him to navigate a period of radical political and legal upheaval. He held this position for approximately two years, until 1976, during which he attempted to maintain a degree of judicial independence and ensure due process within the constraints of the increasingly authoritarian government. 

His tenure as President of the Supreme Court was marked by significant legal reforms, including the nationalization of land and industries, which he oversaw the legal implementation of. However, the Derg's increasingly radical policies and disregard for the rule of law eventually led to his resignation. Following his departure from the bench, he focused primarily on his academic work at Addis Ababa University. He became a full Professor of Law in 1981 and continued to teach and publish extensively, becoming a leading authority on Ethiopian commercial law. He authored several influential books, including “The Ethiopian Commercial Code” (1976) and “Constitutional Law of Ethiopia” (1980), which remain foundational texts for legal scholars and practitioners. 

Zewde was also actively involved in drafting and revising Ethiopia’s commercial laws throughout the 1990s, contributing significantly to the legal framework following the end of the Derg regime in 1991. He served as a key member of the legal team that drafted the 1995 Constitution of Ethiopia, playing a vital role in establishing a new constitutional order. In recognition of his contributions to Ethiopian law and education, he received numerous awards and honors, including honorary doctorates from Addis Ababa University and other institutions. 

Zewde Gebre-Sellassie passed away on October 24, 2017, in Addis Ababa, at the age of 81. He is remembered as a highly respected jurist, educator, and a key figure in the development of modern Ethiopian law. His legacy continues through his scholarship, the legal professionals he mentored, and the enduring impact of his contributions to Ethiopia’s legal system.

title: Lupe Vélez
text:
Lupe Vélez, born María Guadalupe Vélez Tapia on July 18, 1908, in Durango, Mexico, was a pioneering Mexican-American actress who achieved significant fame during Hollywood’s Golden Age. Her parents, José Juán Vélez and Guadalupe Tapia, were both involved in the Mexican Revolution; her father was a general and her mother a nurse. This revolutionary background instilled a sense of independence and resilience in the young Lupe. Tragedy struck early in her life when both parents died before she was twelve, leaving her and her eight siblings to be raised by their aunt, Enriqueta Tapia, in Mexico City. 

Lupe’s early ambition wasn’t acting, but journalism. She began working as a stenographer and reporter for the newspaper *El Universal* at the age of 16, quickly becoming known for her daring and outspoken articles, often covering social issues. However, her striking beauty attracted the attention of filmmaker Emilio “Indio” Fernández, who offered her a small role in his 1927 film *El Zángano*. This marked the beginning of her cinematic journey. 

She worked in several Mexican films throughout the late 1920s and early 1930s, honing her craft and gaining recognition. In 1932, she secured a contract with Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM) in Hollywood, initially learning English and taking acting lessons. Her first American film was a minor role in *The Sign of the Cross* in 1932, but it was her portrayal of Maria in *Flames of Passion* (1934) that launched her to stardom. The film, a Spanish-language version produced alongside an English-language counterpart, capitalized on the growing Latin American market and showcased Vélez’s fiery temperament and natural charisma.

Vélez quickly became typecast as a “Latin spitfire,” playing passionate, often volatile, characters. She starred in a string of successful films including *The Devil is a Woman* (1935), again directed by José Iturbi, and *Her Conquest* (1937) opposite Herbert Marshall. While grateful for the opportunities, she resented the limited range of roles offered to her, consistently fighting against being pigeonholed. She attempted to break free from the stereotype, taking on roles in comedies like *International Woman* (1937) and dramas like *Nana* (1938), but the “hot-blooded Latina” image proved difficult to shake. 

Throughout the late 1930s and 1940s, Vélez continued to work steadily, appearing in over 40 films. She starred alongside major actors like Gary Cooper in *The Cowboy and the Lady* (1938) and James Stewart in *Female Housebreaker* (1941). Despite her success, she was often underpaid compared to her white counterparts, and faced discrimination within the studio system. She actively campaigned for better wages and working conditions for Hispanic actors. 

Her personal life was often tumultuous. She had several high-profile relationships, including a brief marriage to actor Johnny Weissmuller (best known as Tarzan) in 1933, which lasted only six months.  She was also linked to director Howard Hughes and actor Nelson Eddy.  In 1940, she had a son, Lupito, with actor Harald Ramberg, though Ramberg was already married.

In the final years of her life, Vélez struggled with depression and financial difficulties. The changing landscape of Hollywood and the decline of the studio system impacted her career. On December 13, 1944, at the age of 36, Lupe Vélez was found dead in her Los Angeles home from a barbiturate overdose. The circumstances surrounding her death were initially ruled a suicide, but later investigations and accounts from friends and family suggest it may have been accidental, potentially related to a troubled relationship with actor Charles Chaplin, who denied any involvement.  



Lupe Vélez left behind a legacy as a trailblazer for Latinas in Hollywood. She paved the way for future generations of actors and activists, demonstrating both talent and a fierce determination to challenge stereotypes and fight for equality within the entertainment industry.

title: Ezechiel N'Douassel
text:
Ezechiel N’Douassel, born on January 26, 1976, in Libreville, Gabon, was a professional footballer who carved a unique and remarkably consistent career primarily in the lower tiers of French football. While he never reached the heights of international stardom enjoyed by some of his countrymen, N’Douassel became a legendary figure for his prolific goalscoring record and unwavering dedication to the game, earning him the nickname “Le Roi” (The King) amongst fans.

N’Douassel’s early footballing education took place in Gabon, but details regarding his initial clubs remain scarce. He arrived in France as a teenager in the mid-1990s, initially joining the youth academy of AS Beauvais-Oise in 1994. He made his senior debut for Beauvais in the Championnat National, the third tier of French football, in the 1995-1996 season, appearing in 24 matches and scoring 8 goals. His performance attracted attention, and he moved to Amiens SC in 1996, again in the Championnat National. 

He spent two seasons with Amiens, becoming a key player and netting 23 goals in 63 appearances. This form led to a brief stint in Ligue 2 with Le Havre AC in 1998, but he found limited playing time and only featured in 12 games, scoring twice. He returned to the Championnat National in 1999, joining Étampes US. His time there was short-lived, and he soon moved to FC Rouen in the same league.

It was at Rouen, between 1999 and 2003, that N’Douassel truly began to establish himself as a consistent goalscorer. He scored an impressive 85 goals in 146 appearances, becoming the club’s all-time leading scorer, a record he still holds. This period cemented his reputation and attracted attention from clubs aiming for promotion. In 2003, he moved to US Créteil-Lusitanos, a team in Ligue 2. 

He spent three seasons with Créteil, scoring 34 goals in 86 appearances. While the team didn't achieve promotion to Ligue 1, N’Douassel consistently proved his worth as a reliable striker. In 2006, at the age of 30, he joined Amiens SC for a second spell, this time in Ligue 2.  He enjoyed a successful return, scoring 16 goals in 34 games during the 2006-2007 season.

However, his most celebrated period came with Clermont Foot, joining the club in 2007. Over six seasons, from 2007 to 2013, N’Douassel flourished, becoming a club icon. He played 214 games for Clermont, scoring a remarkable 95 goals, making him their all-time top scorer, surpassing his previous record at Rouen.  He was instrumental in Clermont’s consistent pushing for promotion to Ligue 1, although they ultimately fell short during his tenure. He achieved his highest league finish with Clermont in the 2010-2011 season, finishing 6th in Ligue 2.

N’Douassel also had a brief international career with the Gabon national team, earning 23 caps and scoring 5 goals between 2002 and 2011. He participated in the 2010 Africa Cup of Nations, held in Angola, where Gabon reached the quarter-finals.

After leaving Clermont Foot in 2013, N’Douassel continued to play professionally, moving to Amiens SC for a third spell in the Championnat National, then briefly to AS Vitré in 2014. He finally announced his retirement from professional football in 2015 at the age of 39, having played for over two decades. 

Following his retirement, N’Douassel remained connected to the sport. He completed his coaching badges and has since worked as a youth coach in the Auvergne region of France, specifically focusing on developing young talent. He is highly regarded within footballing circles in the region and is remembered fondly by fans of the clubs he played for, particularly Amiens and Clermont Foot, for his dedication, longevity, and impressive goalscoring record. He remains a respected and beloved figure in French lower league football.

title: Noel Malicdem
text:
Noel Malicdem was born on November 22, 1946, in Manila, Philippines, to Vicente Malicdem, a lawyer, and Dolores Villanueva-Malicdem, a teacher. He was the eldest of four children. His early education took place at the Ateneo de Manila High School, where he graduated as valedictorian in 1964. This academic success foreshadowed a consistently strong performance throughout his life. He then pursued a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration degree at the Ateneo de Manila University, completing it in 1968, again graduating with honors – *magna cum laude*.  

Immediately following his undergraduate studies, Malicdem traveled to the United States to further his education. He enrolled at the Harvard Business School, earning a Master of Business Administration (MBA) degree in 1972.  His time at Harvard was pivotal, exposing him to modern management techniques and a global business perspective. Upon completion of his MBA, he was offered a position at Procter & Gamble (P&G) in Cincinnati, Ohio. 

Malicdem’s career at P&G spanned over two decades, beginning as an Assistant Marketing Manager in 1972. He rapidly ascended through the ranks, demonstrating a talent for brand building and strategic leadership.  He held various positions, including Marketing Manager for Pampers diapers, Brand Manager for Tide laundry detergent, and eventually, Country Manager for P&G Philippines in 1987.  During his tenure as Country Manager, P&G Philippines experienced significant growth, with sales increasing by an estimated 30% within three years, largely attributed to his innovative marketing campaigns and strengthened distribution networks. He was known for focusing on consumer understanding and tailoring products to the specific needs of the Philippine market.

In 1993, Malicdem left P&G to embark on a new chapter as the President and Chief Operating Officer of Ayala Land, Inc., the real estate arm of the Ayala Corporation, one of the oldest and largest conglomerates in the Philippines.  This marked a significant shift from consumer goods to property development. He quickly proved his adaptability and leadership capabilities in this new sector. Under his leadership, Ayala Land underwent a period of rapid expansion and diversification. He spearheaded the development of large-scale, integrated, mixed-use projects, including the Bonifacio Global City (BGC) in Taguig, Metro Manila, which began substantial development during his time. BGC, a former military base, transformed under his guidance into a premier financial and lifestyle district. 

Malicdem held the position of President and COO of Ayala Land from 1993 to 2006. In 2006, he was appointed Chairman of the Board, a position he held until his retirement in 2011.  During his time as Chairman, Ayala Land continued its expansion, launching new projects and solidifying its position as the leading property developer in the Philippines. He was instrumental in the company’s consistent financial performance, overseeing a period where Ayala Land’s market capitalization grew to over ₱100 billion (approximately $2.2 billion USD at the time of his retirement).

Beyond his corporate roles, Malicdem was actively involved in various civic and professional organizations. He served as a Trustee of the Ateneo de Manila University and the Philippine Business for Social Progress. He also held positions in several industry associations, advocating for responsible business practices and sustainable development. He was a recipient of numerous awards and recognitions throughout his career, including the Management Man of the Year award from the Management Association of the Philippines in 2005.

Following his retirement from Ayala Land in 2011, Malicdem remained active as a consultant and advisor to various businesses. He dedicated more time to philanthropic endeavors, focusing on education and community development. He passed away on February 15, 2023, in Manila, at the age of 76, after a prolonged illness. He is survived by his wife, Corazon “Cora” de la Cruz-Malicdem, and their three children, Maria Cristina, Vicente Rafael, and Antonio Miguel. His legacy is remembered as a visionary leader who significantly contributed to the growth and development of both the consumer goods and real estate industries in the Philippines.

title: Aditya Kalyanpur
text:
Aditya Kalyanpur was born on December 16, 1948, in Mumbai, India, to a family deeply rooted in journalism. His father, Vimla Kalyanpur, was a pioneering female journalist in India, working with the *Hindustan Times* and becoming the first female editor of a major Indian newspaper. This environment profoundly shaped Kalyanpur’s own life and career path. He received his early education at the Campion School, a Jesuit-run institution in Mumbai, and then attended St. Xavier's College, also in Mumbai, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics and Politics in 1970. He furthered his education at the University of California, Berkeley, earning a Master of Arts degree in Journalism in 1972. 

Kalyanpur began his journalistic career at the *Free Press Journal* in Mumbai in 1973, starting as a reporter covering labor and political issues. He quickly demonstrated a talent for investigative reporting, and within two years, rose to become the paper’s Assistant Editor.  A significant turning point came in 1975 during the Emergency declared by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Kalyanpur, along with other journalists, faced considerable pressure from the government for independent reporting. He was briefly detained under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA) in 1976, a period lasting approximately three months, for his critical coverage of the government. This experience solidified his commitment to press freedom and fearless journalism.

In 1980, Kalyanpur moved to Delhi and joined *India Today* magazine, which was then rapidly becoming a leading news publication. He initially served as a Senior Editor, focusing on political and economic affairs.  His sharp analysis and in-depth reporting quickly made him a prominent voice in Indian journalism. He was instrumental in establishing *India Today's* reputation for investigative journalism, leading teams that uncovered stories on corruption, political intrigue, and social issues.  He was promoted to Executive Editor in 1986 and then to Deputy Editor in 1990. 

A defining moment in Kalyanpur’s career came with the Rajiv Gandhi assassination in 1991. *India Today* assigned him to lead a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the assassination and the alleged lapses in security. The resulting coverage, published as a special issue and later compiled into a book titled *The Rajiv Gandhi Assassination: The Investigation*, was widely acclaimed for its meticulous detail and insightful analysis. The book, published in 1992, became a bestseller and is still considered a definitive account of the event. He also received the prestigious Prem Bhatia Award for journalistic excellence in 1992 for his work on the assassination investigation. 

Kalyanpur continued to work at *India Today* through the 1990s, covering the political and economic upheavals in India, including the liberalization policies initiated in 1991. He played a crucial role in expanding the magazine’s coverage of international affairs and strengthening its investigative reporting capabilities. In 2000, he left *India Today* and became a consulting editor for *The Pioneer*, a national English-language daily.  

In 2004, Kalyanpur co-founded the Centre for Investigative Journalism (CIJ) in New Delhi, an independent non-profit organization dedicated to promoting investigative journalism in India. He served as the Director of the CIJ until 2013, mentoring young journalists and supporting in-depth investigations on critical issues. He also authored a second book, *The Political Economy of India*, published in 2010, analyzing the dynamics of economic growth and political power in India.

Aditya Kalyanpur remained active in journalism and public discourse throughout his later life, frequently contributing opinion pieces and analyses to various publications. He was a vocal advocate for press freedom and ethical journalism. He passed away on November 16, 2023, in New Delhi, at the age of 74, leaving behind a legacy as one of India’s most respected and influential journalists. He is survived by his wife, Shalini Kalyanpur, and their son, Rohan Kalyanpur.

title: Dennis Andersson
text:
Dennis Andersson was born on December 22, 1949, in Örebro, Sweden, to Sven and Britt-Marie Andersson. His early life was marked by a keen interest in music and technology, fostered by a family supportive of artistic pursuits. He received his basic education in Örebro, demonstrating aptitude in both technical subjects and the humanities. Though he initially considered a career in engineering, music ultimately proved the stronger pull. Andersson began playing guitar in local bands as a teenager, honing his skills and developing a passion for songwriting and arrangement.

His professional musical journey began in the early 1970s. After several years playing in various Swedish rock and pop groups, he joined the progressive rock band Kebnekajse in 1973. Kebnekajse, formed in 1971, was already gaining recognition for its unique blend of rock music with Swedish folk melodies and poetic lyrics. Andersson quickly became a central figure in the band, contributing significantly to their songwriting and arrangements. He played rhythm guitar and contributed vocals, becoming known for his melodic sensibility and ability to create atmospheric soundscapes.

Kebnekajse enjoyed considerable success throughout the 1970s. They released a string of albums including “Kebnekajse” (1974), “Resan” (1975) and “Vinterviken” (1977) which garnered critical acclaim and a dedicated fanbase. “Vinterviken” proved to be a breakthrough album, reaching the Swedish charts and establishing the band as a major force in Swedish progressive rock.  The album’s conceptual themes, inspired by Swedish nature and mythology, resonated with audiences.  Throughout this period, Andersson’s distinctive guitar work became a defining characteristic of the band's sound. 

However, internal creative differences began to emerge within Kebnekajse in the late 1970s.  In 1980, the band disbanded, marking a turning point in Andersson’s career. Rather than pursuing a solo career immediately, he turned his attention towards music production and studio work. He established a recording studio, “Studio Soundtek,” in his hometown of Örebro.  Here, he worked with a diverse range of Swedish artists, refining his production skills and gaining a reputation for his meticulous approach to sound. 

Andersson’s most significant achievement came in 1992 when he co-wrote and produced the winning entry for the Eurovision Song Contest, “Take Me to Your Heaven” performed by Carola Häggkvist. The song, representing Sweden, secured first place with 244 points, a substantial margin over Ireland’s second-place entry.  This victory propelled Andersson to international recognition and solidified his position as a highly respected music producer.  The song became a massive hit across Europe and remains one of the most iconic Eurovision winners.

Following the success of “Take Me to Your Heaven,” Andersson continued to work as a producer, collaborating with artists like Lena Philipsson and Tommy Nilsson. He produced several successful albums throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, demonstrating his versatility and adaptability to different musical genres. He also returned to performing occasionally, participating in reunion concerts with Kebnekajse in the early 2000s.

In later life, Andersson remained active in the music industry, though he largely stepped back from the intense demands of large-scale production. He continued to operate Studio Soundtek, focusing on smaller projects and mentoring young musicians. He also dedicated more time to his personal interests, including photography and spending time with his family.  Dennis Andersson passed away on June 25, 2023, at the age of 73, leaving behind a legacy as a talented musician, innovative producer, and a key figure in Swedish music history. He is survived by his wife, Marianne, and their two children.

title: Rebecca Romijn
text:
Rebecca Alie Romijn was born on November 6, 1972, in Santa Monica, California, to Elizabeth (née Little), a homemaker, and Michael Romijn, a Dutch-American electrical engineer. Her ancestry includes Dutch, English, and Native American roots. She spent her early childhood moving frequently due to her father’s work, living in places like Connecticut and Florida before settling in Dallas, Texas, by the age of ten. It was in Dallas that she began modeling at the age of 14, encouraged by her mother, initially working for local department stores and print advertisements. She attended Flower Mound High School, graduating in 1990, and was voted “Most Beautiful” by her classmates. 

Romijn initially intended to pursue a degree in journalism, but her modeling career gained momentum. At 17, she signed with Wilhelmina Models and moved to Paris, working for several high-profile designers including Christian Dior, Giorgio Armani, and Ralph Lauren. This international exposure led to appearances in magazines like *Elle*, *Vogue*, and *Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue*, where she first appeared in 1997 and again in 1998 and 1999, notably gracing the cover in 1999. This cover propelled her to widespread recognition and solidified her status as a successful model.

While continuing to model, Romijn began to transition into acting in the mid-1990s. Her early television roles were largely guest appearances on shows such as *Murphy Brown* (1995) and *Caroline in the City* (1996). A significant breakthrough came in 1998 with a recurring role as Aurelia Rex on the science fiction television series *Xena: Warrior Princess*, appearing in seven episodes. This role increased her visibility and led to more substantial acting opportunities.

Her most recognizable role to date arrived in 2000 when she was cast as Mystique in the *X-Men* film franchise. She portrayed the shape-shifting mutant in *X-Men* (2000), *X2: X-Men United* (2003), and *X-Men: The Last Stand* (2006). The extensive prosthetics and makeup required for the role—taking up to nine hours to apply—became a signature part of her early film career.  

Beyond *X-Men*, Romijn appeared in a variety of films, including *Pumpkin* (2002) alongside Henry Winkler, *Femme Fatale* (2002) with Peter Coyote, and *Godsend* (2004) with Robert De Niro. She also took on television roles, starring in the short-lived CBS sitcom *Pepper Dennis* (2005-2006) as a supporting character, and later as Evelyn Harper in *The Librarians* (2014-2018), a role that earned her critical praise. She also had a recurring role in the USA Network series *Ugly Betty* (2006-2010) as Alexis Meade.

Romijn married actor Jerry O'Connell on July 14, 2007, in Malibu, California. They have twin daughters, Dolly Rue and Charlie Tamara, born December 28, 2008. The couple frequently appear together in public and on social media, often showcasing their family life. 

In later years, Romijn has continued to work steadily in television and film, appearing in projects like *Star Trek: Picard* (2020-2023), where she played Captain Shaxs, a security officer. She’s also become increasingly vocal about issues related to aging in Hollywood and the challenges faced by women in the entertainment industry.  In 2023, she publicly discussed her struggle with endometriosis and the impact it had on her fertility. Romijn remains an active figure in both the modeling and acting worlds, consistently taking on new roles and projects while balancing her career with family life.

title: Kevin De Bruyne
text:
Kevin De Bruyne was born on June 28, 1991, in Drongen, a municipality within Ghent, Belgium. His parents, Herwig and Elisabeth De Bruyne, were both involved in sports; his mother was a volleyball player and his father a professional footballer, albeit one who never reached the highest levels. This sporting background heavily influenced young Kevin, who began playing football at a very early age for local club KVV Drongen. He demonstrated exceptional talent and quickly moved through the youth ranks, showcasing a remarkable understanding of the game and a prodigious passing range. 

At the age of eight, he joined the youth academy of Genk Racing, a larger Belgian club. He continued to excel, and in 2005, at the age of 14, he was scouted by Genk, one of Belgium’s most prominent teams. He signed with Genk’s youth system and quickly progressed, making his debut for the first team on November 28, 2009, in a Belgian Cup match against Charleroi. His league debut followed on January 26, 2010, against Standard Liège. He scored his first professional goal on August 8, 2010, in a Europa League qualifying match against Partizan Belgrade.  He played a pivotal role in Genk winning the 2010-11 Belgian Cup, contributing significantly with assists and intelligent playmaking. In total, he made 98 appearances for Genk, scoring 16 goals.

His performances attracted attention from larger European clubs, and in January 2012, he signed for Werder Bremen in Germany for a reported fee of €6 million. He quickly adapted to the Bundesliga, becoming a key player for Bremen. During his time there, he primarily played as an attacking midfielder, demonstrating his vision, creativity and ability to score from outside the box. He played 93 games for Werder Bremen, netting 10 goals.

In 2013, De Bruyne moved to Chelsea in England for £21 million, signing a five-year contract. However, his time at Chelsea was largely unsuccessful. He struggled to break into the first team under manager José Mourinho, making only nine Premier League appearances, three of which were starts.  He was loaned to Wolfsburg in Germany in August 2014 for the remainder of the season.

This loan proved transformative. At Wolfsburg, he flourished, playing a central role in their attack. He scored 10 goals and provided 20 assists in 34 Bundesliga games during the 2014-15 season, earning the Bundesliga Player of the Year award. Wolfsburg then exercised their option to sign him permanently in February 2015 for a reported fee of €18 million. He continued to impress for another half-season, before a big-money move to Manchester City materialized.

On August 30, 2015, Manchester City signed De Bruyne for £55 million, a club record at the time. This move marked the peak of his career.  Under manager Pep Guardiola, he became one of the world’s most dominant midfielders. He has won four Premier League titles (2017-18, 2018-19, 2020-21, 2021-22), one FA Cup (2018-19), six League Cups (2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21) and the Champions League in 2022-23 with Manchester City. He was instrumental in their treble-winning season. He has been named Premier League Player of the Season twice (2019-20 and 2021-22). 

Internationally, De Bruyne made his debut for the Belgian national team on November 19, 2010, against Luxembourg. He has become a vital member of the Red Devils, representing his country at the 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups and the 2016 and 2020 UEFA European Championships. He captained the national team for a period, and as of late 2023, has earned over 90 caps, scoring 25 goals.

De Bruyne is married to Caroline Lijnen, and they have three children.  He is known for his humility and dedication to his craft, consistently praised by teammates and managers for his work ethic.  He has faced injuries in recent years, including a hamstring injury in the 2023 Champions League final, but remains a pivotal figure for both Manchester City and the Belgian national team.

title: Daniel Bedingfield
text:
Daniel Bedingfield was born on December 17, 1979, in Lewisham Hospital, London, England, the second of four children to Jonathan Bedingfield, a Canadian Pentecostal minister, and Monica Scriver, a New Zealander. His upbringing was deeply rooted in music and faith. The family moved to Buckinghamshire in 1985, and later to Hatfield, Hertfordshire, where Jonathan established the Christian recording studio, Gospel Tabernacle Music Group. This environment exposed Daniel and his siblings – older sister Natasha, and younger siblings Nicola and Michaela – to a constant stream of musical creativity. All four Bedingfield children would eventually pursue careers in music. 

Daniel's musical education began with piano lessons at age six, followed by guitar and drums. He developed a knack for songwriting early on, initially penning gospel songs for his father’s studio. However, his musical tastes broadened beyond gospel, encompassing influences like Stevie Wonder, Donny Hathaway, and Joni Mitchell. He attended Samuel Whitbread School in Clifton, Bedfordshire, but left at age 16 to pursue his musical ambitions, initially working in a local supermarket to fund his endeavors. 

Bedingfield’s initial attempts at a record deal proved unsuccessful. He spent several years honing his craft, writing songs and performing locally. He independently released an EP in 2001, and continued building a following through live performances. In 2003, he signed with Polydor Records. His breakthrough came in February 2004 with the release of his debut single, “Unwritten,” which peaked at number three on the UK Singles Chart and became a significant hit across Europe. The song’s optimistic lyrics and distinctive piano-driven arrangement resonated with a wide audience. 

The success of “Unwritten” propelled his debut album, *Genuine Self*, released in July 2004, to number two on the UK Albums Chart and achieved platinum status. The album spawned further successful singles including “February Song” (reaching number 11 in the UK) and “If You’re Gone” (reaching number two). “If You’re Gone” proved to be his biggest international hit, reaching number one in Australia and charting in the United States, peaking at number 24 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 2005. *Genuine Self* has sold over 3 million copies worldwide. 

His follow-up album, *Second Sight*, was released in November 2006. While it reached number nine on the UK Albums Chart, it didn’t achieve the same commercial success as its predecessor. The lead single, “What About Me,” reached number six in the UK. Subsequent singles, “Only You” and “Collide,” had more modest chart performances. 

In 2008, Bedingfield took a step back from the spotlight, citing a desire to explore different creative avenues and address personal health concerns. He had been diagnosed with a cyst on his vocal cords in 2007 which required surgery and a period of vocal rest. During this period, he focused on songwriting and production for other artists, including collaborations with artists like Adam Lambert and Pixie Lott. He also became involved in philanthropic work, particularly with charities focused on youth development. 

In 2011, he released a collaborative EP with rapper MC Jin, titled *The Sound of New York*. In 2014, he released a new single, “Light,” and followed it with the album *Stop Sign* in 2017, released independently through his own label, Unwritten Records. *Stop Sign* reflected a more mature and experimental sound, moving away from the pop sensibilities of his earlier work. 

Throughout his career, Daniel Bedingfield has received several awards and nominations, including two Brit Award nominations for Best Male Solo Artist in 2005 and 2007. He has also been recognized for his songwriting abilities. He continues to write and perform music, and remains active on social media, engaging with his fans. While he hasn’t consistently maintained the level of mainstream success he experienced in the mid-2000s, Daniel Bedingfield remains a respected figure in the British music scene, known for his honest songwriting and emotive vocal delivery. He currently resides in Los Angeles with his wife, actress Amanda Speratza, whom he married in 2011, and their two children.

title: Celâl Bayar
text:
Celâl Bayar was born on May 16, 1883, in Gumuşhane, a small town in the Ottoman Empire, located in present-day Turkey. His father, Mehmet Efendi, was a merchant, and his mother, Fatma Hanım, was a homemaker. He received his early education at local schools, demonstrating a keen aptitude for mathematics. In 1900, he enrolled in the Mülkiye Mektebi, the Ottoman Empire’s prestigious school for civil servants, in Istanbul, graduating in 1903. He continued his education at the School of Law, completing his studies in 1906 and qualifying as a legal professional.

Bayar began his career as a clerk in the Ottoman Ministry of Finance in 1908, quickly rising through the ranks due to his diligence and administrative skills. He held various positions within the ministry, including postings in different provinces, gaining valuable experience in financial management and local governance. A crucial period in his career began in 1919 when he was appointed as the Governor of İzmir, a strategically important port city.  This appointment came at a time of immense political turmoil following the defeat of the Ottoman Empire in World War I and the growing nationalist movement. 

During the Turkish War of Independence (1919-1922), Bayar played a pivotal role in organizing resistance against the Allied occupation forces in the Aegean region. He secretly supported the nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, providing crucial financial and logistical assistance despite officially remaining within the Ottoman administration. His discreet support proved vital in securing resources and maintaining morale amongst the resistance fighters.  Following the establishment of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, Bayar formally joined the new government.

He served as the first Speaker of the Grand National Assembly of Turkey from 1924 to 1935, a position he held for an unprecedented eleven years across four consecutive parliamentary terms. His calm demeanor and impartial leadership were instrumental in establishing parliamentary traditions within the newly formed republic.  He was a key figure in implementing Atatürk’s reforms, though he generally maintained a more conservative stance than some other prominent Republicans. 

In 1937, Atatürk appointed Bayar as Prime Minister, a position he held until 1939.  During his relatively short tenure, he focused on economic development and strengthening trade relations with neighboring countries. He oversaw initiatives to promote industrialization and agricultural modernization, laying the groundwork for future economic growth. However, his government faced challenges in balancing economic reforms with the existing political structure, and he ultimately resigned following disagreements with the Republican People's Party (CHP) leadership regarding economic policy.

After a period away from the forefront of politics, Bayar founded the Democrat Party (DP) in 1946, challenging the long-standing dominance of the CHP. The DP advocated for a more liberal economic policy, greater political freedoms, and a multi-party system.  The party gained significant popular support, particularly among rural populations and business owners. In 1950, the DP achieved a landslide victory in the general elections, marking the first time in Turkish history that power had been transferred democratically from one party to another.

Bayar became the third President of Turkey on September 23, 1950, and was re-elected in 1957. His presidency was characterized by economic growth, increased foreign investment, and closer ties with the West, including Turkey’s membership in NATO in 1952. However, his later years in office were marked by growing authoritarian tendencies within the DP government, led by Prime Minister Adnan Menderes.  

On May 27, 1960, a military coup d'état overthrew the DP government. Bayar, along with Menderes and other DP leaders, was arrested and put on trial. He was convicted of violating the constitution and sentenced to death. However, due to his age and health, his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. He was released from prison in 1966 following an amnesty. Celâl Bayar died on September 24, 1986, in Istanbul, at the age of 103, leaving behind a complex legacy as a pivotal figure in modern Turkish history.

title: Michael Coulson (barrister)
text:
Michael John Coulson was born on 21st June 1942 in Bradford, Yorkshire, to John and Margaret Coulson. His father was a solicitor, a profession that initially held little appeal for the young Michael, who instead harboured ambitions of becoming a professional cricketer. He attended Bradford Grammar School, an independent school for boys, from 1953 to 1960, where he excelled academically and captained the school’s first eleven cricket team. Despite his sporting prowess, a growing interest in debate and logic, fostered by a particularly influential English teacher, steered him towards a legal career.

Coulson proceeded to read Law at Jesus College, Oxford, graduating with a First-Class Honours degree in 1963. He then undertook the Bar Professional Training Course, completing it in 1964, and was called to the Bar at Gray’s Inn on 28th November 1964. He began his pupillage with John Haworth, a highly respected barrister specialising in commercial law at 4 Pump Court, a leading set of chambers in the Temple, London. He was formally taken on as a tenant at 4 Pump Court in 1965, remaining there for the entirety of his career. 

Coulson quickly established a reputation as a formidable and meticulous commercial barrister. Initially focusing on shipping and marine insurance, he rapidly expanded his practice to encompass a broader range of commercial disputes, including banking, finance, and contract law. He was known for his rigorous preparation, precise cross-examination, and a remarkably calm and persuasive courtroom manner. He eschewed flamboyant displays, preferring to win cases through the strength of his legal arguments and the clarity of his presentation. 

A pivotal moment in Coulson’s career arrived in 1979 when he was appointed Queen’s Counsel (QC), becoming a leading figure in the commercial bar. He handled numerous high-profile cases throughout the 1980s and 1990s, often involving significant sums of money and complex international transactions. He represented major banks in disputes arising from the secondary banking crisis of the early 1990s and acted for various parties in landmark cases concerning the interpretation of complex financial instruments. He appeared regularly in the Commercial Court, the Court of Appeal, and occasionally in the House of Lords (now the Supreme Court).

Coulson’s contributions extended beyond advocacy. He served as a Recorder, a part-time judge, from 1986 to 2002, hearing cases in both civil and criminal jurisdictions. He was also a Bencher of Gray’s Inn, the governing body of the Inn, from 1995, actively involved in the education and training of new barristers. He authored several articles and contributed to legal textbooks, notably co-authoring “Coulson on Commercial Arbitration” which became a standard text in the field. He was a highly respected lecturer, frequently invited to speak at professional development courses for lawyers.

In 2002, Coulson was appointed a judge of the High Court of Justice (Chancery Division), receiving the customary knighthood. He was assigned the judicial title Mr Justice Coulson. As a judge, he continued to specialise in commercial disputes, earning a reputation for his pragmatic and insightful judgments. He oversaw several significant cases involving insolvency, company law, and intellectual property rights. He was notably involved in the complex restructuring of Lehman Brothers International (Europe) in 2008, a case that required navigating unprecedented legal challenges in the wake of the global financial crisis. 

Michael Coulson retired from the High Court in June 2014, aged 72. Following his retirement, he remained active in legal circles, undertaking mediation work and providing advice to legal professionals. He died on 24th November 2018, at the age of 76, following a short illness. He was survived by his wife, Penelope, and their two daughters. His legacy remains as a highly respected barrister and judge, known for his intellectual rigour, professional integrity, and dedication to the law.

title: Khalid Mahmood Mithu
text:
Khalid Mahmood Mithu, a prominent Bangladeshi sculptor, was born on February 22, 1933, in Dhaka, British India (now Bangladesh). His father, Haji Mohammad Abdullah, was a businessman, and his mother, Laila Begum, was a homemaker. Mithu’s early life was steeped in the artistic atmosphere of Old Dhaka, a region known for its rich cultural heritage and traditional crafts. He received his initial art education at the Government Institute of Fine Arts, Dhaka, in 1950, studying under renowned artists like Zainul Abedin and Nalin Chandra Sharma. This foundational period profoundly shaped his artistic sensibilities, particularly his commitment to depicting the lives and struggles of ordinary people.

Mithu’s formal training continued when he secured a scholarship to study sculpture at the École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris, France, in 1954. He spent six years in Paris, honing his skills in classical sculpture techniques, working with materials like plaster, clay, and bronze. While embracing Western artistic traditions, he never abandoned his deep connection to the socio-political realities of his homeland. He graduated with a diploma in sculpture in 1960. During his time in Paris, he also briefly studied stone carving in Carrara, Italy, further broadening his technical expertise. 

Returning to Dhaka in 1961, Mithu joined as a teacher at the Government Institute of Fine Arts (later the Faculty of Fine Arts, Dhaka University), a position he held for over three decades until his retirement in 1994. This role allowed him to nurture generations of Bangladeshi sculptors and contribute significantly to the development of sculpture as a discipline in the country. He wasn’t simply an instructor of technique; he encouraged his students to engage with the social and political issues surrounding them, mirroring his own artistic approach. 

Mithu’s artistic career is marked by a distinctive style that blends realism with a powerful sense of social commentary. He is best known for his public sculptures, which frequently depict the struggles of the working class, the horrors of war, and the fight for independence. One of his most iconic works, “Shapla Chattar” (Lily Pad), erected in 1976 at the then Dhaka University's Charukala Institute, became a symbol of student protest and remains a landmark to this day. Although significantly damaged during political unrest in 2007, it was subsequently reconstructed. 

Another significant sculpture, “Mujib’s Smriti Stambha” (Mujib’s Memorial Pillar), a 15-meter high bronze work depicting Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the founding father of Bangladesh, was installed in 1982 at the National Press Club in Dhaka.  His work “Titumir” (1978), located in Dhaka’s Bahadur Shah Park, commemorates the 19th-century peasant leader Titumir, reflecting his dedication to portraying national heroes and historical events.  He also created the sculpture “Nirbhaya” (Fearless) in 1982, which stands as a tribute to the victims of the Liberation War of 1971. 

Throughout his career, Mithu participated in numerous national and international exhibitions, receiving several prestigious awards. These include the National Art Award of Bangladesh in 1978, the Ekushey Padak in 1997 (a national award recognizing contributions to literature, art, and culture), and the Shilpokala Academy Award in 2000.  He was also a founding member of the Bangladesh Sculpture Council.

In his later life, Mithu remained actively involved in the art community, mentoring young artists and continuing to create sculptures. He lived a relatively quiet life with his wife, Nasrin Mithu, a writer and journalist.  Khalid Mahmood Mithu passed away on January 29, 2018, at the age of 84, at the Square Hospital in Dhaka, following a prolonged illness. His legacy continues to inspire artists and remains a powerful testament to the role of art as a vehicle for social change and national identity in Bangladesh. His sculptures continue to be powerful and relevant symbols of Bangladeshi history and aspirations.

title: Rachel Weisz
text:
Rachel Hannah Weisz was born on March 7, 1970, in Westminster, London, England, to David Weisz, an inventor, and Catherine (née Samers), a teacher. Her father was born in Vienna, Austria, a Jewish refugee fleeing Nazi persecution, while her mother is of English and Italian ancestry. Weisz spent her early childhood in Hampstead, North London, and at the age of 14, she and her family moved to Cambridge when her father took a position at the University. This relocation proved pivotal, as she attended Cambridge Arts and Sciences Sixth Form and later, St. John's College, Cambridge, graduating in 1991 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in English Literature. 

During her time at Cambridge, Weisz’s interest in acting developed. She co-founded the amateur Cambridge Footlights dramatic club, following in the footsteps of notable alumni like Emma Thompson and Stephen Fry. While there, she performed in several productions, including a production of ‘Design for Living’ that caught the eye of agent Jane Hewland. After graduating, Weisz initially considered a career in law or journalism, but ultimately decided to pursue acting professionally, starting with small roles in television.

Her early television work included appearances in ‘Inspector Morse’ (1993) and ‘The Scarlet Pimpernel’ (1999). Her film debut came in 1994 with a minor role in ‘Death Machine’. She gained wider recognition with a supporting role in the independent film ‘Gas Land’ (1995), and further solidified her presence with roles in ‘Sense and Sensibility’ (1995), where she played Miss Pickering, and ‘Stealing Beauty’ (1996), directed by Bernardo Bertolucci. 

The late 1990s and early 2000s saw Weisz taking on increasingly diverse and challenging roles. She garnered critical acclaim for her performance in ‘The Mummy’ (1999) and its sequel, ‘The Mummy Returns’ (2001), becoming a commercially successful action star while simultaneously seeking out independent projects. A significant turning point came in 2005 when she won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Tessa Quayle in Fernando Meirelles’s ‘The Constant Gardener’, alongside Ralph Fiennes. This win cemented her status as a respected dramatic actress.

Following her Oscar win, Weisz continued to choose roles that showcased her range. She starred in ‘Proof’ (2005), a stage adaptation of David Auburn’s play, receiving a Tony Award nomination for her performance. Further film roles included ‘Eragon’ (2006), ‘Youth’ (2007), ‘The Lovely Bones’ (2009), and ‘Dream House’ (2011). 

In 2011, she began a relationship with Daniel Craig, whom she married in a private ceremony in New York City on June 22, 2011. The couple have a daughter, born in 2018. Weisz also has a son, Henry Aramis Knight, born in 1996, from a previous relationship with director Sam Mendes, whom she was with from 1998 to 2010. 

Weisz’s career continued to thrive in the 2010s and 2020s. She received further critical acclaim for her roles in ‘The Favourite’ (2018), earning her a BAFTA Award and another Academy Award nomination, and ‘Disobedience’ (2017). More recent work includes ‘Black Widow’ (2021), reprising her role as Melina Vostokoff from the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and ‘Dead Ringers’ (2023), a psychological thriller series for Apple TV+, where she plays both Beverly and Chad Mantle. 

Throughout her career, Rachel Weisz has consistently balanced mainstream and independent films, showcasing her versatility and commitment to challenging roles. She has received numerous awards and nominations, establishing herself as one of the most respected and accomplished actresses of her generation. Her filmography boasts over 50 film credits, alongside her stage and television work, demonstrating a sustained and impressive career spanning over three decades.

title: Diana Ivanova
text:
Diana Ivanova, born Diana Zharova on January 22, 1948, in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg), Russia, was a renowned Soviet and Russian figure skater, celebrated for her artistry and elegance on the ice. Her early life was deeply intertwined with the burgeoning Soviet figure skating program. Her father, Grigory Zharov, was a prominent coach, having trained several notable skaters, and her mother, Olga Zharova, was also involved in the sport. This familial connection provided Diana with a strong foundation and early access to training at the prestigious Dynamo Sports Society in Leningrad. She began skating at the age of four, quickly demonstrating a natural aptitude and dedication to the discipline. 

Diana’s competitive career officially began in the early 1960s. She initially skated in pairs with Vladimir Serkov, achieving modest success at the national level. However, her breakthrough came in 1964 when she was paired with Rodion Zaitsev. This partnership proved to be exceptionally fruitful, launching her to international prominence. Zaitsev, known for his strong jumping ability, complemented Ivanova’s lyrical skating style and expressive artistry. They were coached by Pyotr Orlov, a highly respected figure in Soviet skating, who refined their technique and choreography.

The pair's first major international success came at the 1966 European Championships in Bratislava, Czechoslovakia, where they secured the silver medal. This marked the beginning of a period of sustained dominance. In 1967, they claimed the gold medal at the European Championships held in Prešov, Czechoslovakia. Their real triumph, however, arrived at the 1968 Winter Olympics in Grenoble, France. Performing to a medley of Russian folk tunes, Ivanova and Zaitsev captivated the audience and judges alike. They won the gold medal, defeating the favoured Austrian pair, Ludowika Jakobsson-Eilers and Walter Eilers, by a narrow margin. Their free skate score of 125.45 was particularly lauded for its emotional depth and synchronization.

Following their Olympic victory, Ivanova and Zaitsev continued to compete successfully. They defended their European title in 1969 in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, West Germany. They also achieved silver at the 1969 World Championships in Colorado Springs, USA, finishing behind Ludowika Jakobsson-Eilers and Walter Eilers. Despite their continued success, the pair faced increasing competition from emerging teams, particularly from East Germany.  

In 1972, after several years of competing at the highest level, Diana Ivanova and Rodion Zaitsev retired from competitive skating. The decision was partly influenced by a desire to pursue other interests and also by the changing landscape of pair skating, which was becoming increasingly focused on technically demanding elements. 

After her competitive career, Diana Ivanova remained involved in the world of figure skating, though primarily outside of the spotlight. She dedicated herself to coaching, passing on her knowledge and experience to a new generation of skaters. She worked at the Dynamo Sports Society in Saint Petersburg, where she had begun her own skating journey.  She didn't achieve the same level of public recognition as a coach as she had as a skater, preferring a more understated role. 

Diana Ivanova’s impact on figure skating extended beyond her competitive results. She was celebrated for her grace, artistry, and the emotional connection she forged with audiences. Her performances are still remembered as exemplifying the beauty and elegance of Soviet-era skating. She was awarded the Order of the Badge of Honour in 1968 for her Olympic achievement.  She lived a relatively private life after retirement, rarely giving interviews. Diana Ivanova passed away on December 22, 2023, in Saint Petersburg at the age of 75, leaving behind a legacy as one of the most beloved and accomplished figure skaters in Russian history.

title: Jashubhai Dhanabhai Barad
text:
Jashubhai Dhanabhai Barad, a prominent figure in the cooperative movement of Gujarat, India, was born on November 29, 1903, in the village of Dhoraji, in the then-Kathiawar region of Bombay Presidency (now Gujarat). He hailed from a modest farming family belonging to the Patidar community, a traditionally land-owning caste. His father, Dhanabhai, was a farmer, and his mother, Maniben, instilled in him a strong sense of social responsibility and a commitment to the welfare of the farming community. Jashubhai received his primary education in Dhoraji, completing his primary schooling by 1917. He then attended the Alfred High School in Rajkot, finishing his secondary education in 1921. He subsequently enrolled at Gujarat Vidyapith, founded by Mahatma Gandhi, in Ahmedabad, where he pursued a degree in agriculture and economics, graduating in 1925. 

His exposure to Gandhian philosophy at Gujarat Vidyapith profoundly shaped his life and future work. Gandhi’s emphasis on self-sufficiency, village industries, and the upliftment of the rural poor resonated deeply with Jashubhai, who recognized the economic vulnerabilities faced by farmers in his region. Following his graduation, he briefly worked as a teacher at the Vidyapith itself, but soon felt compelled to return to his roots and dedicate himself to improving the conditions of farmers in Kathiawar.

Jashubhai’s career truly began in 1928 when he initiated the establishment of a cooperative credit society in his native village of Dhoraji. This marked the genesis of his lifelong dedication to the cooperative movement. He recognized that farmers were trapped in a cycle of debt due to exploitative moneylenders, and that access to affordable credit was crucial for their economic liberation. The Dhoraji society quickly proved successful, providing farmers with loans at reasonable interest rates and protecting them from the predatory practices of private lenders. 

This success spurred him to expand the cooperative network across Kathiawar.  He traveled extensively, organizing and establishing numerous cooperative societies, not just for credit, but also for marketing, processing, and distribution of agricultural produce. By 1948, he had facilitated the formation of over 300 primary cooperative societies in the region.  A key innovation he introduced was the concept of ‘joint liability’ within the societies, fostering a sense of collective responsibility and ensuring loan repayment. 

In 1953, Jashubhai played a pivotal role in the establishment of the Gujarat State Cooperative Bank, serving as its first Chairman.
